INTRODUCTION 
 
  
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Industry, having been aut horized by the Committee, hereby 
present this Two Hundred and Nine teenth Report on the Revival and 
Restructuring of C ement Corporation of India Limited pertaining to the 
Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public  Enterprises (Department of Heavy 
Industry)  
 
2. The Committee held de tailed discussion with C ement Corporation of 
India Limited at Guwahati on 25 th October, 2010.  The representative of the 
Department of Heavy Industry (Minis try of Heavy Industry and Public 
Enterprises) was also present there. 
 
3. I thank the Ministry of Heavy I ndustries and Public Enterprises 
(Department of Heavy Industry) and C ement Corporation of India 
Limited for furnishing the valuable inputs during the meetings.  
 
4.  The Committee in its meeting held on 15 th February, 2011 
considered and adopted the report. 
  
Tiruchi Siva 
Chairman                          
Department related Parliamentary 
                                         Standing Committee   on   Industry 
 
New Delhi 
15 February, 2011 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 

REPORT 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
One of the defining features of modern civilisation is the 
foundation of durable and concrete structures by extensively employing 
cement. As the construction activit y occupies central place in the 
expanding economic domain, the manufacture and use of cement assumes 
greater and critical importance. In fact it is well said that fifty per cent of 
all investment takes place in the cons truction sector which is nothing but 
steel and cement. Our accelerated constructio n activities and the 
expanding work in the infrastructur e projects are critically dependent on 
the quality and quantity of  cement used.  The i ndispensability of cement 
to further the modernisation process has been well documented.  Cement 
is, therefore, a critical ingredient for augmenting growth and development 
of our economy and advancem ent of the country as a whole. That is why 
our national leadership accorded due importance to the manufacture of 
adequate cement right since our independence. Within  the scheme of 
mixed economy conceived to rebuild  and modernise India the public 
sector was assigned crucial responsib ility to provide leadership in the 
sphere of cement production. A few y ears before the Cement Corporation 
of India was set up the se cond five year plan docum ent justly stated that 
“The output of cement ...is an im portant indicator of the volume of 
investment in the econo my...” and observed, “C ement ranks next in 
importance to iron and steel as a de velopmental commodity and hence a 
high place has to be given to it in the scheme of priorities.” The 
incorporation of the Cement Corpor ation of India (CCI) as a wholly 
Government of India Enterprise in 196 5, when the third five year plan 
was being implemented was a step to achieve that grand objective.  Later 
during 1970 and 1990 eleven cement plants were set up by the CCI in 
socially and economically backward regions of our country to produce  
 

2 
enough cement for meeting the growing demand in the market for this 
“developmental commodity”.  
 
2. It is important to note that as  part of a well formulated national 
plan for industrialisation of our co untry particularly of the backward 
regions’ a conscious decisi on was taken to locate i ndustrial units in areas 
which had no industry worth the name. Dispersal of industry was 
accorded importance for balanced regi onal development. In fact the third 
five year plan document observed, “P reference... has al ways been given 
to the location of the public sector pr ojects in relatively backward areas 
whenever this could be done without  significant prejudice to technical 
and economic considerations; and this  will be the guiding principle for 
the future also. Similarly in the li censing of private sector projects the 
claims of underdeveloped regions have generally been kept in view to the 
extent possible”.   
 
3. The eleven cement plants established in the remote and 
economically backward areas were to be  the nucleus of development of 
those regions. It was expected that  those units would spur economic 
activities and help remove their back wardness. Therefore, the decision to 
set up these units were taken not so lely on the basis of economic 
considerations but also on the basis of the larger objective of promoting 
development and growth of areas untouched by industrial development.  
 
4. The units of the Cement Corpor ation of India were established in 8 
States/Union Territories of India. Th e details of the locations of each 
plant are given below.  
 
 
  

3 
1.Bokajan                                    Assam 
2.Rajban                                Himachal Pradesh 
3.Tandur                                Andhra Pradesh 
4.Mandhar                              Chhattisgarh 
5.Kurkunta                              Karnataka 
6.Nayagaon                            Madhya Pradesh 
7.Akaltara                               Chhattisgarh 
8.Charkhi Dadri                       Haryana 
9.Adilabad                             Andhra Pradesh 
10.Delhi                                        Delhi 
11.Yerraguntla                       Andhra Pradesh 
 
5. It is extremely significant to note that out of th e abovementioned                     
11 plants only three plants at serial numbers 1 to 3 ar e operational. The 
Yerraguntla plant at serial number 11 was sold out to M/s India Cements 
Ltd. on 21 January 1998 for R s. 200.70 crore to meet  the demand of 
creditors as per the directions of Ho n’ble BIFR. Therefore, as of now,   
seven units are non-operating plants. The total installed capacity of all the 
plants was 42.48 lakh MT which is less than 2% of total installed capacity 
of India.  However, the installed cement capacity of three operating plants 
is 14.46 LMT and in contrast the in stalled capacity of 7 non-operating 
plants stands at 24.52LMT. The authorised share capital of the CCI is Rs. 
900 crore, whereas its net wo rth as on 31 March 2010 is (-) Rs.213.61 
crore and its net profit during 2009-10 is Rs. 52.75 crore. In spite of 
incurring heavy losses for several ye ars it could genera te profit during 
2006 and 2010 which is a positive sign. Its manpower as per the 
presentation made before the Committe e in Guwahati stands at 1037 as 
on 30 September 2010 with 117 Exec utives, 174 supervisiors and 746 
workers.  The figures for productivity per  employee  are going  up  from  

4 
600 MT during 2005-06 to  898 during 2009-10.  A ll the above facts have 
to be seen in the context of the vi sion and mission of the Corporation.  
While its vision is “To emerge as one  of the leading cement companies 
committed to contribute to the eco nomy and to enhance value for the 
stakeholders” its mission is “To a ugment the wealth creation for the 
company, deliver superior product and sustain market value.” 
 
6. The vision and mission sound audaci ous in the face of the installed 
capacity of only three operating plants and many other complex 
challenges confronting the Corporati on. However, its performance has to 
be seen against India’s position as th e second largest cement producing 
country in the world after China.  The per capita consumption of cement 
in our country is 156 kg which is quite low as compared to Thailand, 
Vietnam, USA and Dubai. While in case of Thailand and Vietnam, per 
capita consumption of cement is 400 kg, in case of  the USA and Dubai it 
is 800 kg and 4000 kg, respectively.  The Eleventh Five year Plan 
document noted that “Cement consum ption has generally grown at 2%-
3% higher than growth of GDP. Ke eping the past trends in view and 
taking into consideration the rene wed emphasis on infrastructure, the 
cement industry can be e xpected to grow at a bout 11% corresponding to 
the GDP growth of 9%”. With the accelerated growth  of construction 
work the requirement for cement will also get multiplied.  Therefore, the 
prospect for cement indu stry is very bright. In  the context of growing 
demand for cement, the Cement Corporat ion of India has to take the best 
foot forward for taking advantage of the situation and for becoming a key 
player for supplying quality cement to the expanding market. 
 
7. The Committee painfully notes that the Cement Corporation of 
India suffered huge losses right since the inception of the operation of  
 

5 
its plants.  The Corporation cited ho st of reasons for incurring such 
losses.  One of the key reasons, ac cording to the Corporation, was the 
very location of the cement fact ories in areas which did not have 
ample infrastructural facilities.  Th ose areas where these plants were 
set up did not have minimum ameniti es and conveniences in the form 
of township, communit y centres and health centres, etc. The 
investment made by the Corporation for the availability of such basic 
facilities added extra cost to its primary responsibility for producing 
cement. Over and above the cost required for the manufacture of 
cement, these facilities escalated its expenditure and, therefore, 
contributed to the over-capitalisat ion of the project. The Committee 
was informed by the officials of the Corporation that such extra 
burden in building up bare minimum facilities constituted a major 
factor behind the higher cost of production of cement. The 
background note supplied to th e Committee noted “Almost every 
plant of CCI has been over-capitali sed due to time and cost overrun 
resulting in very high interest an d depreciation costs. This has 
resulted in very high fixed costs of these plants as compared to the 
industry standards”.   
8. It is rather sad to note that some of the plants had to bear 
enormous expenditure for the purpo se of getting access to quarry 
which is located in a very difficult  and rough terrain .  For instance, 
the topography of the quarry for the Bokajan and Rajban Plants was 
such that it required extra cost  for mining the raw material and 
transporting it by employing ropeways. It seems that these plants had 
to face a hurdles race for producing  cement and at the same time 
develop the region by their manufactur ing activities.  It is distressing 
that owing to such factors the company could never register profit up 
to the year 2004-05 barring insignificant profits on few occasions.   
 

6 
9. The Corporation continued to incur loss which subsequently 
assumed proportion of a crisis.  Earlier in 2006 the Committee expressed 
its serious concern on the recurring lo sses of the CCI when it presented 
192nd Report after examining The Dalmia Dadri Cement Limited 
(Acquisition and Transfer of Undert aking) Amendment Bill, 2006. Over 
the years the mounting losses sharply eroded its net worth.  By the middle 
of 1990s the Committee wa s informed that the CCI suffered accumulated 
losses to the tune of Rs. 527.16 crore.   That staggering amount was more 
than it’s paid up capital of Rs.  406.74 crore and reserves worth Rs. 0.99 
crore.  The collapse of the net wort h sounded alarm bell to safeguard the 
very survival and commercial viability  of the Corporation.  It graduated 
from a loss making Corporation to a sick industrial undertaking. It, 
therefore, resulted in its reference to the BIFR under section 15(1) of 
CISA and was declared sick in August 1996.   
 
10. The crisis was further aggravated  when the accumulated loss of the 
Corporation by 31 Marc h 2005 mounted up to Rs. 2152.86 crore which 
sharply stood in contrast to its paid up capital of Rs. 429.28 crore.  Its net 
worth went to the sub-zero level and became nega tive.  It was worth               
Rs. 1723.58 crore.  All those catastr ophic developments took place even 
before the rehabilitation scheme was approved by the BIFR.  
 
11. In face of such gathering crisis of negative net worth, the 
Corporation had absolutely no mean s of modernising its units or 
upgrading technology and production and operation process.  At a time, 
when the cement industry in Indi a was looking up due to accelerated 
economic, industrial and construction activities, the Cement Corporation 
of India was in dire straits. Its difficult conditions were further 
compounded  by  its  inability to  have  its  captive  power  plants  and  its  
 

7 
reliance on the power s upplied by the electricity  boards of different 
States.  Erratic supply of power a nd even frequent breakdown of power 
made available to the plants  becam e one of the important factors behind 
its reduced output which over a period of  time led to the closure of some 
of its plants. 
 
12. In 1990, the Government of India came out with a slew of 
measures in favour of the cement i ndustry in the form of transport 
subsidy and capital subsidy and waiver of excise duty  and sales tax.  The 
new plants commissioned in remote and backward regions or the old ones 
already functioning there and expa nding their capacity for producing 
more cement were eligible for those benefits. While the  private players 
could avail of those incentives the Cement Corporation of India, however, 
lagged behind as it hardly could take any step for capacity addition.   
 
13. The Committee was also  told that the Corporation could not at all 
match up to the cut throat compe tition in the relatively open market 
which witnessed more supply of cement  much in excess of the demand.  
It was further accentuated by the r ecession which affected very badly the 
cement industry till 2004-05.  
  
14. The escalating loss of the Corpora tion remained at the root of its 
multiple problems.  It went from one cris is to another.  Even its working 
capital declined to an alarming leve l and eventually got depleted. There 
was no option for the Corpor ation to overcome it other than resorting to 
short term borrowings at  very high interest rate. The Committee was 
informed that the taking over of the sick Charkhi Dadri Unit of the 
erstwhile Dalmia Dadri Cement Ltd. and the failure of the management in  
 
 

8 
making available functional Directors to carry out key responsibilities 
such as Marketing, Finance and Oper ations also constituted major factors 
behind the sickness of the Corpora tion. Absence of clear guidelines to 
deal with non-operating un its which have been cl osed down for almost a 
decade and thereby imposing a heavy burden on the functioning units and 
draining their working capital further compounded the financial crisis. As 
a result employees had to go without salaries and arrear s in this respect 
went up to a very high level. The loss of morale of the employees hit hard 
the operations of the Corporation and contributed to its decline.   
 
15. The Committee notes with concern that the Cement 
Corporation of India which was est ablished to be a leading player in 
manufacturing cement and pr omoting balanced regional 
development had to go through such tr agic state of affairs.  It also 
notes with concern that no attempt was made for renovation, 
replacement and modernisation of its plants .  In the background note 
supplied to the Committee, it has been  stated under the heading ‘Future 
Strategy for Sustainable Revival’ that  “The company learning from past 
mistakes plans to continue to invest  a part of its pr ofit for renovation, 
replacement, modernisation of its plan ts so as to keep them updated and 
avoid occurrence of obsolescence  of technology in future”. The 
Committee feels that the Corporation committed a costly mistake.  It 
is heartening to note that the Corporation has adopted a future 
strategy for sustainable revival one of the key components of which is 
to use part of its profit fo r modernisation and renovation.  In fact, the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan dealing w ith the cement i ndustry has observed 
that “The industry has been modernising and some units can now boast of 
having the state of the art technol ogy plants with energy consumption 
comparable  with  the  best in  the  world”.  The  Committee is happy to  
 

9 
note that the officials of the Corporation are hopeful to not only 
register profit but also compete wi th the key players in the market.  
In fact, in its presentation befo re the Committee, the Corporation 
outlined the measures taken to turn around the company. The 
Committee sincerely feels that the stress given on expansion and 
modernisation of the operating plants would result in its revival and 
progress.   
16. The Committee also takes note of  the fact that the Corporation 
is introducing new product range su ch as 53-S Grade, special cement 
for manufacturing Railw ay sleepers and also introducing cement 
brand names Maha shakti (43 Gr ade), Param shakti (53 Grade), 
Poorna shakti (33 Grade) and Jal shakti (33 Grade PPC) for better 
brand image.   
17. The Committee was informed of the follow ing additional 
measures taken by the Corpor ation to make it buoyant and 
profitable.    
(1) Adopting aggressive marketing by entering into 
marketing alliance with reputed industrial houses. 
(2) Advertising campaign, TV hoardings, glow signs, wall 
paintings, etc., by allocating a budget of Rs.0.50 per bag. 
(3) Reducing employees’ strength  by introducing Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme with the assistance of Government of 
India. 
(4) Boosting of employee’s morale by clearing their dues and 
cultivating confidence amongst them. 
(5) Employees’ participation in decision making process. 
 

10 
(6) Cost reduction in all areas of activities, i.e., controlling of 
operational and non-operational costs. 
(7) Revenue generation by utilising idle infrastructure.   
18.  The rehabilitation scheme sanc tioned by the Hon’ble BIFR on 3 
May 2006 suggested closure of seven unviable plants located in Mandhar, 
Kurkunta, Akaltara, Charkhi Dadri , Delhi Grinding  Unit/Bhatinda 
Grinding unit, Nayagaon and Adilabad and sale of assets of those plants 
through Asset Sale Committee. Th e employees working in those units 
were kept under the category of Volunt ary Separation Scheme to get rid 
of unproductive fixed expenses. Th e liabilities of the company were 
further reduced due to the waiver of interests, penalties and surcharge on 
the Government dues.  The revival pa ckage also consisted of concessions 
from the Government, financial institutions, banks and creditors. 
 
19. The other three operating plan ts such as Rajban, Tandur and 
Bokajan are to be continued as these ar e viable.  The scheme stressed on 
expansion, technological upgradati on and modernisation of these three 
units to make them competitive and enhance the margin of profit. 
 
20. The Committee notes that the host of measures adopted to 
support the CCI has helpe d it to transform th is ailing Corporation 
and bring it to a level of profitable company at present. This is a 
noteworthy success.  It has to be  carried forward and the momentum 
of its revival has to be sustained.   
 
21. The Committee finds that the BIFR recommended for infusion 
of funds. While Rs. 153.62 crore have  been  given   as   non-plan  
loan  for  repayment  to  secured  and   unsecured  creditors  and  for  
 

-11- 
meeting the VRS/VSS expenses, the plan assistance involving Rs. 
30.67 crore for expansion of Ra jban and Bokajan plants and 
upgradation of Tandur plant have been provided for. It is also 
envisaged that the CCI would pay to the Government of India the 
existing plan loan of Rs. 150.90 cro re and fresh non-plan loan of Rs. 
153.62 crore out of sale proceeds of seven non-operating plants.   
 
22. The Committee while taking note of the measures of the 
Government of India for revival and r estructuring of the CCI, would like 
to know the outcome of the money spent. It recommends that the 
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI ) must closely monitor the way 
in which money is being spent fo r achieving the targeted goal and 
submit a detailed report in this regard to the Committee.   
 
23. On the basis of the information supplied to the Committee it is 
evident that the recommendation of  the BIFR to close down the 
aforementioned seven unviable units  (at para 18) was revisited.  
Based on the revised assessment it was found that it would be 
possible to revive the five non-op erating units (Adilabad, Kurkunta, 
Nayagaon, Akaltara and Mandhar Plants) and other three remaining 
non-operating units such as Char khi Dadri, Delhi Cement Grinding 
Unit and Bhatinda Cement Grinding Unit would be sold out after the 
re-evaluation of their assets. 
 
24. The Committee felt that it is a worthwhile effort as the 
aforementioned five non-operating units  have access to vast reservoir of 
limestone which is essential for manufacture of cement. The Techno 
Economic Feasibility Report for revi val of these units have been 
prepared and such repor ts indicate the possibility  of their revival to 
address the rising demand for cement in our country. The feasibility  
 

12 
report outlines the plan for next ten years which would enhance the 
capacity of the cement plants and increase its economic operations.    
 
25. It is worthwhile to refer to the Eleventh Five Year Plan document.  
Under the heading ‘Issues and Challe nges for the Cement Industry’ it 
observed that “Achievement of gr owth and targets for the cement 
industry is crucially dependent on vari ous inputs such as limestone, coal, 
power, and last but not the least, on transportation of limestone. Coal 
continues to be the main fuel for th e cement industry and will remain so 
in the near future”. Since the revival packag e for the above-mentioned 
five non-operating units, factor th e availability of limestone as a key 
issue, it is important that the CCI ta ke inspiration from the observation of 
the Eleventh Five Year Plan which also  lays emphasis on the inputs such 
as limestone for producing more cement.   
 
26. The CMD of the CCI informed the Committee vide letter 
No.Ref.CMD/CCI/12 (13)/2011, dated February 01, 2011 that the revival 
of non-operating plants was reviewed  in the Asset Sale Committee 
meeting held on 07 December 2010 wher ein it was decide d that the sale 
process for the disposal of non-operating  plants has been restarted. This 
would mean that the three plants which are functioning would be allowed 
to manufacture cement an d the other non-operating plants would be sold 
out.   
27. The Committee strongly recommen ds that due attention must 
be paid to the Techno Economic Feasibility Reports for the revival of 
non-operating plants either by starting production process there 
through joint ventures or by le asing them to the other cement 
manufacturing  bodies.   The Committee would like to get a detailed  
 
 

13 
report in this regard, both from the Cement Corporation of India 
and the Department of Heavy Industries.  
  
28. One of the reasons cited by the Ce ment Corporation of India for its 
uninterrupted loss is the absence of captive power and critical dependence 
on the electricity boards of the resp ective States which quite often could 
not supply adequate power for th e operation of the cement plants 
functioning under the CCI. The point advanced by the CCI in the meeting 
of the Committee is well taken.  The Eleventh Five Year Plan document 
also takes note of the point and obser ves “The producti on of cement is a 
continuous process requiring unint errupted power supply. Since the 
availability and quality of grid power  supply continue to be a problem, 
the use of captive power has been increasing.  Most of the cement units 
have installed captive power generation capacities to the extent of 60% to 
100% of their requirement. The cap tive power generation capacity of 
cement industry is estimated to be  1825 MW at present, of which 61% is 
based on diesel and the rest 39% on co al.  With growing uncertainties of 
grid power availability, it is estim ated that 2000 MW captive power 
would be required during Eleventh Plan”. 
 
29. The Committee strongly recomm ends both to the Planning 
Commission and the DHI to pay h eed to the above observations of 
the Eleventh Five Year Plan document and seriously undertake 
efforts for establishing captive power plants in the plants of the CCI.   
 
30. Human resource management is ke y to the revival and success of a 
company. It is noteworthy that the Cement Corporation of India has taken 
measures to improve the morale of its employees as part of its strategy for 
improving  its  performance. However,  the  Committee  notes  with  
 

14 
concern that due to si ckness of the company and the adoption of 
successive Voluntary Retirement Scheme the strength of executives of 
the CCI operated plants got reduced from 531 to 206 during 2000-04.  
The ban on recruitment and the absence of induction of new 
employees since 1998 has further added to the problem. The shortage 
of manpower has thus ba dly affected the operati onal function of the 
units.  It is sad to note that many employe es have left the CCI to join the 
private sector cement plants which have been doing well due to the 
upsurge of demand for cement.  There is another concern arising out of 
age profile and career stagnation of  executives which has resulted in 
serious lack of executive strength at  middle and senior management level 
which is key to the success of many ar eas such as operations, finance and 
human resource.  In te rms of manpower strength the CCI as of now has 
1037 employees consisti ng of 117 executives, 174 supervisors and 746 
workers.  The depletion of expert ha nd has been caused due to retirement 
age which is fixed at 58 years. During the presentation before the 
Committee it was strongly pu t forth by the CCI that the retirement age of 
the CCI employees should be raised to 60 years for retaining the ‘existing 
experienced, qualified and skilled ma npower at all the levels’. The CCI 
has already submitted a proposal for enhancement of retirement age to the 
administrative Ministry for seeki ng Cabinet approval. The Committee 
was informed by the Chairman and Managing Director Shri R.P. Tak vide 
his letter No.Ref.CMD/CCI/12(13)/ 2011 dated Februa ry 01, 2011 that 
“Due to upsurge in the cement i ndustry, experienced and technical 
manpower are likely to be or being attracted by the competitors as well as 
prospective entrepreneurs at very lucrative remuneration packages.  
Lateral entry from PSUs and private ceme nt industry is also not feasible 
since all the major PUSs and private companies are having retirement age 
of 60 years.   
 

15 
Even the existing employees who are retiring or have retired are being 
engaged by private sector cement companies on a handsome 
remuneration package. Even if the Corporation resorts to new recruitment 
for middle and senior level executives,  it is apprehended that it may not 
be able to attract expe rienced and qualified candi dates due to existing 
retirement age of 58 years as in most of the public sector and private 
sector companies, th e retirement age is 60 years and above. The 
employees working in such companies at  this level may not like to shift 
such organisations where retirement ag e is 58 years.  Therefore, the age 
limit should be immediately enhanced to 60 years to overcome the acute 
problem of manpower”.   
 
31. The Committee stro ngly approves the demand of the CCI 
seeking enhancement of retirem ent age from 58 to 60. The 
Committee also strongly supports  the stand of CCI for immediate 
posting of board level executive in  the key area of operations and 
marketing.  It is understood th at the public enterprises selection 
board is considering a proposal in this regard for creation of such 
posts. The Committee strongly recommends that the public 
enterprises selection board must clea r such proposals immediately.  
The Committee also would like to have a report from  the PESB in 
this connection.   
 
32. The Prime Minister of our country Dr. Manmohan Singh while 
giving away the MoU Excellence Awards and Scope Awards for the year 
2008-09 said that “It is no small measure due to th e robustness and 
resilience of our public sector ente rprise, and in particular, our public 
sector banks, that we did better  than most  other countries  in  weathering  
 
 

16 
the global economic crisis which s uddenly erupted in September 2008”.  
While underlining the vitality and inhere nt strength of our public sector 
enterprises he made a very signi ficant observation concerning quality 
human resources for making public s ector enterprises more competitive 
and viable.  He said “We must ensure that a vibrant private sector does 
not deprive our PSEs of our  best talent”.  He fu rther added, “But, the 
overall working environment in the company has now become an equally 
important factor for attracting and re taining employees. We must ensure 
proper succession planning in our compan ies. We must therefore ensure 
that we are able to recruit bright young men and women into public sector 
jobs, and must have the ability to re tain them there. I would urge the 
ministries and the public sector leader ship to give serious attention to 
human resource development issues at all levels”. 
 
33. The Committee feels that the demands and concerns of the CCI 
for posting of board level executives in the key area of operation and 
marketing and the immediate enha ncement of retirement age from 
58 years to 60 years to retain the qualified and experienced 
manpower are valid in the context of  the articulation of the Prime 
Minister of our country who has stro ng faith on the ability of our 
public sector to face the taste of market scrutiny.   
 
34. In fact, manifold measures ta ken by the CCI and the consultative 
and participative working culture it has fostered have contributed to boost 
up its productivity.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that the 
manpower productivity (MT per em ployee) has gone up from 672 in 
the year 2006-07 to 897 in the year 2009-10.   
 
 
 

17 
35. In the increasingly competitive atmosphere the public sector 
enterprises have to function with th eir own strength.  Many of the public 
sector enterprises which were referred to the Board of Reconstruction of 
public sector enterprises have success fully revived showing profits.  The 
Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh stated that the “The mantra of 
success for the success ful companies has been empowerment and 
enablement rather than mere financial assistance”.  
 
36. The Committee feels that the gradual revival of the Cement 
Corporation of India augurs well for its future.  Its confidence in 
itself that it can diversify its products, improve the capacity of its 
exiting operating plants to bring it at par with the competitors 
capacity, to replace its old equipment with energy efficient equipment 
constitutes its forward looking atti tude.  The Committee hopes that 
with its increasing profit, it can positively emerge as a major player 
in the cement industry of our country. 
 
37. The Eleventh Five Year Plan document dealing with ‘Demand 
Forecast and Investment Requirement for the Cement Industry’ observed, 
“Realization of capacity  projection of 298 mil lion tonnes would imply a 
capacity addition of 118 Million MT during the Eleventh Plan period.  Of 
the total capacity addition required  for the Eleventh Plan, 86 Million MT 
would come from new Greenfie ld units requiring an investment of         
Rs. 34400 crore and 32 Million tonnes through brown field 
expansions/de-bottlenecking requiring  investment of Rs. 6400 crore.  
Thus the total investment requirement during the Eleventh Plan works out 
to Rs. 52400 crore t ogether with Rs. 1100 crore and  Rs. 500 crore 
required for conversion of existing wet  process plants to dry process 
technology and setting up of coal washeries”.    

18 
38. There are bright prospects for th e cement industry in our country.  
This has to be taken advantage of by the Cement Corporation of India.  
Its gradual revival is a good sign.  It  can build on its achievements and 
contribute to the gigantic task of  nation-building and take forward our 
economic growth which would be dete rmined to a great extent by the 
quality and quantity of cement made  available for meeting our growing 
requirements.  
 
39. The Committee takes note of the fact that company’s Board in 
its 298th meeting held on 22nd July, 2010 has authorized C&MD of the 
company to take necessary action  for filling up of  vacant posts 
arising out of normal retirement, resignation, death, etc., at 
Operating Units and Corporate Office with effect from the year 2010 
as per Recruitment Rules and guide lines issued from time to time 
and the process of recruitment to fill up these posts is under progress.  
The Committee would like to have th e status of progress made in this 
regard.

REPORT 
Authorised by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry , 
I, Ashok Mitra, hereby present the Twenty-second Report of the Committee on the 
Demands for Grants for 1997-98 of the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines. 
2. The background of this joint report on the Demands for Grants of the three 
Ministries calls for some explanation. FoUowing the adjournment of Parliament on the 
conclusion of the general discussion of the budget proposals far 1997-98 on March 21, 1997, 
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Comminees were expected to avail of the 
period till April 21 to prepare and submit their reports on the Demands for Grants of the 
different Ministries alongwith the usual appraisal of the performance budgets for 1996-97 of 
each Ministry. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry 
accordingly met and examined witnesses on March 31, April1, April 2, April 3, April 7 and 
April 8, 1997. (See Appendix). The Standing Committee had scheduled meetings for April

3. In this circumstance, the Standing Committee has chosen to present to Parliament a 
brief joint report on the activities and proposed Demands for Grants of the three Ministries, 
namely, the Ministry of Mines, the Ministry of Steel and the Ministry of Industry. 
4. The Standing Committee is perturbed at the persistent signs of a slackening in the 
rate of growth in industrial production in recent months. The depressed condition, it was 
initially thought, was a feature of only infrastructural industries such as power and mining. 
Developments in the second quarter of 1996-97 suggest that the malaise is much more 
widespread, and recession appears to be enveloping the capital and consumer goods sectors 
as well, including consumer durables. The growth in the small scale segments of industry is 
assumed to have been over this period somewhat higher than in the organised sector. But 
the reasons underlying the hypothesis are at best wobbly. The time perhaps has arrived 
when an expert committe~ is invited to undertake a thorough restructuring of the index of 
industrial production; such restructuring should proceed far beyond merely shifting the base 
year and reassigning weights to the commodities covered by the index, and concentrate on 
improving the scientific basis of data collection from the small-scale industrial sector. 
5. A major issue of concern which came to the fore during the Standing Committee's 
discussions with representatives of the Ministries is the apparent lack of adequate functional 
coordination between the different Ministries and even between the Departments of the 
same Ministry. In the wake of the on-going liberalisation and the progressive dismantling of 
industrial and exchange controls, the Ministries, it would seem, are proceeding on the 
assumption that inter-ministerial and inter-departmental coordination need not be as greatly 
emphasised as was the wont in the pre-reforms days. Two trends are distinctly visible of late: 
(a) a gradual reduction in Plan allocations for each of the Ministries this Standing 
Committee is concerned with, or at least a perceptible fall in the rate of growth of these 
allocations; and (b) a growing reluctance on the part of the Ministries to assume 
responsibility for projecting the pace and pattern of industrial growth in the foreseeable

future; it is as if the en tire burden of responsibility in this area has already been shifted to 
the private sector and to foreign investors. What is equally dist urbing is the growing attitude 
that the promotion of infrastructural indus tries is a task that does not belong to any of the 
Ministries. 
6. The authofities may have, from their point of view, good reasons for withdrawing to 
such a positio n; contai ning the fiscal deficit must be one principal consideration. The private 
secto r may not necessarily concur with !he official view. For example, one or two major 
associations representing the chambers of commerce and industry in the organised sector 
had, on the eve of the presen tation of this year's budget proposals, pleaded for an across­
the-board increase in public investment so as to dispel the current spell of industrial 
recession. In the light of the many encouraging proposal s in the budget favouring indu.~try, 
art icula tion of the need for public investment o n a selective bas is in the infrastructural 
sphere as well as in basic industrial sectors has been temporarily halted; the lowering of 
interest rates may have also boosted the expectations with respect to private investment. 
What should, however , be discouraged is exaggerated expecta tion regarding the flow of 
direc t investment from over~eas. li essential investmen ts in key sectors are neglected in the 
immediate period on the ground that foreign investors would soon take up the slack, current 
perfornJ<mce might get still even depressed, thereby further inhibiting the intrusion of 
foreign capital. 
7. It is in view of such considerations that the Standing Committee does not have the 
least hesitation in recommending that Plan allocations indicated in the Budget for 1997-98 
for the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines, including allocations for the public 
undertakings under their umbrella, should be doubled . This would mean, other things 
remaining the same, realloc<Jtion, or fresh allocation, of around Rs. 1,500 crore ill favour of 
the three Ministries, which would still be less than one per cent of the Union Government's 
toral budgetary outlay proposed for the year.

(ii) 
 
 

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises  (Department of Heavy Industry) on 
the recommendations contained in the Committee’s Tw o hundred and Fifteenth Report 
on the Demands For Grants (2010-11)  pertaining to Department of Heavy Industry. 
 
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Heavy Industries and 
Public Enterprises (Department of Heavy Industry) in respect of the recommendations 
contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows: 
 
Chapter -I-  The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II -  The recommendation/observations which the Commit tee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic 
and explanations advanced by the Ministry and there fore does not want to pursue them 
for the present. 
 
Chapter -III -  The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has 
either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry should furnish 
logical explanations therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV - The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either 
furnished the interim replies or couched its langua ge in vague terms like noted for 
compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desir es that the Ministry should furnish 
Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations c ategorized in Chapter-IV in detail 
and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3.  The details of the ATR is being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
(iii) 

CHAPTER – I 
 
The Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
 
 
Impact of Budget proposal on Auto Sector  
 
Recommendations/observations 
 
1. The Committee appreciates that such an initiative o f the Department of Heavy 
Industry with the Ministry of Urban Development wil l not only boost the demand in the 
Auto sector but will also develop the public transp ort in the remote areas of the country.  
The Committee, therefore, desires that the scheme o f funding the purchase of buses for 
public transport by the States under JNNURM may con tinue for some more time in 
public interest.  The Committee at the same time st resses upon the Department of Heavy 
Industry to monitor the progress of this scheme wit h the Ministry of Urban Development 
and concerned State Governments. 
Para 7 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 As regards monitoring of JNNURM Scheme, it may be stated that whenever 
meetings are held in Ministry of Urban Development for monitoring the progress of the 
scheme, DHI is being invited and the meeting is bei ng attended regularly by a senior 
representative from DHI.  In addition, meetings are  also held in DHI with bus 
manufacturers to ascertain the supply order positio n, difficulties, if any, in timely supply 
of buses and decisions communicated to Ministry of Urban Development for necessary 
action.  Moreover, recently Ministry of Urban Devel opment has moved a Note for 
Cabinet committee on Infrastructure for review of t he JNNURM scheme wherein, 
Secretary, DHI or his nominee has been proposed to be included as a member in the 
Central Sanctioning & Monitoring Scheme (CSMC) for the subject relating to 
procurement and supply of buses under this scheme. . 
 
 
Scooter India Limited 
 
 
Recommendations/observations 
 
2. The Committee is surprised to know that despite of its serious concern for the 
revival of Scooters India Ltd., the Department has made the provision of Budgetary 
support to this company to the tune of only Rs.4 cr ore which Committee feels is very 
meagre amount for its revival.  Committee,  therefo re, recommends that the Department 
of Heavy Industry should make adequate Budgetary su pport for this company at the time 
of RE stage and at the same time,  should  seriously    pursue its 70  crore rupee project  
 
 
 

2 
proposal for revival through joint venture.  In fac t, this important PSE has to diversify its 
activities because it is manufacturing three wheele rs which are being phased out in 
various parts of the Country. Mini four wheelers fo r transporting goods have fairly good 
market and with the help of Government this PSE may  examine the diversification issue 
in right earnest. 
Para-18 
Action Taken Note 
 
            Scooters India Limited (SIL) engaged in  manufacturing 3-wheelers is not 
performing well for over a period of time and is incurring losses.  As a result, the net worth 
of the company has completely eroded.  The company,  at present, has been registered as a 
sick company with BIFR and is under reference to BR PSE.  As regards, the provision of 
Rs. 4 crore, the same had been budgeted for SIL, on  account of Renewals & Replacements 
(R&R), as part of the exercise for repairing and up-grading the old and obsolete machinery.  
The Business Plan of SIL for revival of the company , has been prepared by the consultant 
engaged by the company, in consultation with the ma nagement of SIL and has also been 
presented to BRPSE on 28.07.2010.  The recommendati ons of the BRPSE will be taken up 
for consideration and approval of the Government. 
 
 
Capital Good sector 
 
 
Recommendations/observations 
 
3. The Committee feels that such imported machines/plants although imported at the 
lower cost but importers have to pay high prices fo r their maintenance contracts and 
spares.  The Committee notes that the DHI has raise d such issue in the Development 
Council of Automotive and Allied Industries (DCAAD)  meeting. The Committee 
recommends that suitable remedial measures be taken by imposing high import duty   and 
anti dumping duty on second hand machinery in consultation with Ministry of Commerce 
to grow our capital goods Industry.  The Committee impresses upon the Government to 
allocate sufficient fund for the engineering indust ry and R & D activities to sustain the 
Industrial growth in coming years.  
Para-20 
Action Taken Note 
 
 Textile Machinery Sector: 
  It is observed that textile machinery sector is p resently 
importing the machinery both new as well as second hand to the extent of Rs.4411 crore 
during the year 2008-09.  The Textile Machinery Man ufacturers Association (TMMA) 
has already raised the issue of huge import of seco nd hand textile machinery in the 
Development Council meeting held on 24.2.2010 which  was considered to be major 
detrimental factors preventing the development of t he local machinery with various 
factors such as the imported machinery about one-fo urth or one-fifth price of the new 
equipment in addition to coupled with old generatio n of technology that consumes more 
electricity per unit production.   The textile indu stry is being supported by the scheme 
under Ministry of Textiles viz. Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) in which  

3 
import of second hand textile machinery such as air  jet, projectile, rapier and water jet 
shuttleless looms up to 10 years old with expected residual life of 10 year are funded 
under the scheme.  During the year 2008-09, the new  looms imported to the extent of 
Rs.238 crores (1645 nos.) whereas second hand looms  valued Rs.90 crores (1354 nos.) 
had been imported.  It is also learnt that the seco nd hand looms of more than 10 years old 
had also been imported.   For the development of lo cally manufactured looms, the 
Department is taking up with Ministry of Textile wi th a suggestion not to fund the 
imported second hand looms through TUFS.  Moreover,  it is also being recommended 
that the second hand textile machinery not more tha n five years old with a minimum 
residual life of five years with the applicability of actual user condition only be allowed. 
The enhancement in customs duty rate is also recommended. 
 
 Machine Tools Sector: 
  The machine tools industry presently needs Govern ment 
support. It is noted that no big industrial house i s coming forward in the machine tools 
manufacturing activity.  During the year 2008-09, o f machine tools worth Rs.1424 crore

Recommendations/observations 
 
1. The Committee has made its serious concern on its l ong waiting list for 
establishment of power plants in the country. Commi ttee finds that it has a pending list 
for customers who are waiting for 2-3 years. 
Para-26 
Action Taken Note 
 
 The setting up of power plant is a complex process  and is dependent on the 
performance of several players. The developer has t o provide several inputs starting from 
making available encumbrance free land, civil work including foundations, raw water, 
construction power etc. using which the equipment s upplied by BHEL is to be erected 
and commissioned. Several other Balance of Plant (B OP) vendors have to supply 
equipment like coal and ash handling systems, water systems, cooling towers etc. 
 
 The scope of work of BHEL for major portion of pre sent orders on hand for 
power projects in the country is limited to design,  engineering, manufacture, supply, 
erection & commissioning of Boiler, Turbine Generat or & Auxiliaries packages (BTG) 
only. The remaining portion including all Civil wor ks & several sub-systems of Balance 
of Plants (BoPs) like Coal handling plant (CHP), As h handling plant (AHP), De-
Mineralisation (DM) Plant and Pre-treatment (PT) Pl ant, Switchyard etc. are under 
project developer scope.  
 
 Most products of BHEL are custom designed and only  after receipt of an order is 
the design/manufacture undertaken. These can be bro adly classified for 2 types of 
customer segments viz. power and industry. For the industrial segment products, the 
period of delivery is relatively shorter and orders  are generally executed within a year 
after an order is received. On the other hand the m ain power plant generating 
equipment/products catering to the requirements of power utilities, are generally long 
cycle items. In this context, the execution period of power sector orders on hand varies 
between 36-48 months for 500/660/800 MW projects (2 8-33 months for 250MW 
projects), and for some hydro projects, the execution period could be even longer. Hence, 
at any given point of time, different customer orde rs with BHEL are at different stages of 
implementation. 
 
  

10 
 There have been some rescheduling in supplies from  BHEL mainly due to non 
availability of critical castings and forgings of a lloy steels, pipes and fittings and CRGO 
sourced from limited number of foreign vendors. Inf rastructure inadequacies with respect 
to roads, ports, rail links coupled with limited in digenous capacity & capability for 
Balance of Plant (BoP) equipment ; limited number and capacity of qualified construction 
contractors and erection agencies in the country for taking up construction of large power 
plants in civil, mechanical, electrical works ; ava ilability of skilled manpower with the 
contractors for specialized jobs like high pressure  welders, fitters etc. also contribute to 
the timely implementation of project.  
 
 BHEL has also embarked on a plan for enhancing its  manufacturing capacity & 
capability for preparing itself to meet the country ’s power demand and providing “Power 
to all by 2012”. Towards this end BHEL has augmented to annual capacity and capability 
to manufacture power generating equipment from 6000  MW in 1999-2000 to 10000 MW 
in 2008 and 15000 MW in 2010. This is expected to go up to 20000 MW by 2012. 
 
 Inspite of various factors beyond the control of B HEL, the company puts in extra 
efforts to minimize the slippages in commissioning of the projects.

employment activities. Redeployment of trained VRS optees, in the first place, depends

10, in all 1,54,828 VRS optees have been imparted t raining and 69,484 have been 
redeployed so far under CRR Scheme. Advice of the Committee has been noted. 
 
 
 
Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE)  
Recommendations/Observations 
 
12. The Committee also finds that various posts of SCs/STs/OBC are lying vacant in 
PSUs since quite long and directs that DPE should t ake appropriate measures to fill them 
soon as per the guidelines of GOI in this regard. 
Para (63) 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 Department of Public Enterprises vide OM dated 25 th  February, 2009 had 
extended Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) instructions for launching fresh 
“Special Recruitment Drive” to fill up backlog rese rved vacancies of SCs/STs and OBCs 
in direct recruitment and of SCs/STs and OBCs in pr omotion quota existing as on 
1.1.2008 to the administrative Ministries/Departmen ts concerned with CPSEs to issue 
direction, if not already done, to the CPSEs under their administrative control in a time 
bound manner.  A number of such vacancies have been  filled during the Special 
Recruitment Drive.  The implementation of Drive is monitored by the DoPT. 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
13. The Committee hopes that its recommendations wi ll be well taken up by the 
Department of Public Enterprises in view of the rec ent scenario of the industrial sector of 
the country. 
 Para (64) 
Action Taken Note 
[ 
Advice of Hon’ble Committee has been noted.  DPE is  taking all policy  measures to  
strengthen CPSEs and  promote their growth and efficiency through delegation of powers 
to their Boards of Directors, while ensuring compli ance of   Corporate Governance, 
Professionalization of Boards and  incorporating a robust MoU system,  etc.  
7 

CHAPTER–II 
 
The Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government's replies  
 
 
Counselling, Retraining and Redepoyment (CRR) 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1. The Committee desires that DPE should ensure tha t funds earmarked under CRR 
Scheme and Research, Development and Consultancy on  Generic issue related to CPSEs 
must be utilized equally in each quarter. 
. Para (47) 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 Implementing nodal agencies, in various parts of t he country,  chalk out batch 
wise and module wise training programmes as per the ir schedule of 30/45/60 days; as 
these modules may not be equally distributed quarte r wise, equal release and utilization 
of funds on quarterly basis is not feasible.  
 
 Under the Scheme of Research, Development and Cons ultancy on Generic Issues 
of CPSEs, studies, evaluation, workshops, conferenc es etc. are undertaken. The 
periodicities of events undertaken under this Schem e are not evenly distributed in all the 
quarters of the year and hence equal utlisation of funds in each quarter may not be 
applicable. Advice of the Committee has been noted . 
 
 
Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE) 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2. The Committee has noted and appreciates the view s of the SCOPE. 
Para (56) 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
3. The Committee noted the retention of Rs. 1.00 cr ore for North-Eastern Region. 
The Committee, recommends that the Department should make efforts to utilise the funds 
instead of simply let them transfer to non-lapsable pool. 
 Para (59) 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 In NE Region, non-availability of sufficient VRS o ptees is a constraint.  
 
8 

 VRS is not very sizable in the units located in NE  region. However, DPE has made 
consistent efforts to have more coverage of VRS opt ees in NE Region under CRR 
Scheme. In 2009-10, for the first time 500 VRS opte es were trained under CRR in NE 
region and Rs. 0.43 crore was spent on this account. 
 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
4.  The Committee further recommends that selection  of CMDs of various PSUs 
should be done quickly by Public Enterprises Selection Board without any delay and with 
transparency. It is quite surprising that the Depar tment of Public Enterprises and Public 
Enterprises Selection Board do not play any role in  selecting and appointing the CMDs 
and EDs and Directors in the Boards of Public Sector Banks. 
 Para (62) 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 Since, this recommendation pertains to Public Ente rprises Selection Board 
(PESB), which is under the administrative jurisdict ion of Department of Personnel & 
Training (DOPT), advice of Hon’ble Committee has be en conveyed to DOPT/PESB for 
further necessary action 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
9 

CHAPTER–III 
 
The Recommendations/Observations in respect of whic h the Committee has either not      
accepted the replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its replies  
 
Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE) 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1. The Committee has discussed the issue of profess ionalization of Boards of PSUs 
many times in the recent past and has also made recommendations with regard thereto but 
expresses its concern that its recommendations have  not been implemented in letter and 
spirit. In the name of independent Directors only r etired bureaucrats are being 
accommodated in the Board. There is no compulsory i nduction of Directors from the 
Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and OBC and wom en categories to take care of at 
least the employees of these categories of the PSUs . Even the former Members of 
Parliament are not appointed as Directors to have t he benefit of their vast public life 
experience. So is the case of vast majority of shar eholders of the CPSEs. The present 
norms of professionalization of Boards are certainl y not satisfactory. The Committee 
desires that Department of Public Enterprises may c ome out with a proposal for 
amending the guidelines in this regard so that the Directors representing the SCs, STs, 
OBCs and ex-MPs and a public share holder can get t he opportunity to become 
independent Directors. For this purpose educational  qualification and experience should 
be prescribed. 
Para (60) 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 The Government has already laid down criteria in t erms of educational 
qualifications, age and experience for persons to b e considered for appointment as non-
official Directors on the Boards of CPSEs. These gu idelines do not preclude the 
appointment of SCs/STs/OBCs/Ex-MPs as non-official Director on the Board of CPSEs, 
provided they fulfil the laid down criteria, their names are proposed by the concerned 
Administrative Ministry and are recommended by the Search Committee. Thus, 
opportunity is already available to SCs/STs/OBCs/Ex -MPs for becoming non-official 
Directors on the Boards of CPSEs. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
The Committee has taken into account the fact that the Government has laid down 
certain criteria for the 
appointment of non-official Directors on the Boards  of CPSEs. 
But what the Committee would like to reiterate is that if persons from the categories  
of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and OBC and wom en categories come 
forward with the above mentioned criteria, they sho uld be given preference. There 
by the Committee wants to re-emphasis the need for representation of these 
categories in the Board of CPSEs.  
 
 
10

Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry 
have not been  received  
 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)  
Recommendations/ Observations

achievement against the MoU targets. The committee observes that there is a decreasing 
trend in the `Excellent’ rating in the year 2008-09  as compared to the year 2007-08. The

creating suitable atmosphere for CPSEs by the concerned administrative Ministries.

Action Taken Note 
 
 Advice of Parliamentary Standing Committee has bee n brought to the notice of all

th  August,

Recommendations/Observations 
 
2. The Committee takes note of the efforts made by the DPE and desires that it

Para (37) 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 The Government set up a Board for Reconstruction o f Public Sector Enterprises 
(BRPSE) in December, 2004 to advise the Government,  inter alia, on measures to be 
taken to restructure / revive sick CPSEs. The conce rned administrative ministries / 
departments of the sick CPSEs prepare proposals for revival of sick companies on case to 
case basis and refer them to BRPSE for its recommendations and thereafter seek approval 
of the Government. 
     The Board has, till May, 2010, given its recom mendations for revival of 58 CPSEs 
upon reference. Based on the recommendations of BRP SE, Government, till May, 2010, 
have  approved revival of 37 CPSEs  envisaging tota l fund/non-fund based assistance of 
Rs. 15253 crores (cash assistance of Rs. 2920 crore s and non-cash assistance of Rs. 
12333 crores) from Govt. of India. 
     
11 

  Out of the 37 CPSEs approved for revival, 20 CPSE s have posted profit in 2007-
08, 20 CPSEs have posted profit in 2008-09 and 15 C PSEs have posted profit in 2007-08 
& 2008-09 and 11 CPSEs have posted profit consecuti vely in 2006-07, 2007-08 and 
2008-09. 
      Further, signing of MoU has been made mandato ry for all sick and loss making 
CPSEs also. A separate Syndicate Group has been for med for “sick and loss making 
CPSEs” for the year 2011-12 to suggest the MoU format, parameters, inter se, weightage, 
etc. 
 
 
Counselling, Retraining and Redepoyment (CRR) 
 
Recommendations/ Observations 
 
3. The Committee finds that no information has been  provided regarding the 
expenditure incurred for the training modules since  last three years. The Committee 
desires that year-wise detail of expenditure incurr ed on each training modules shall be 
provided to it at the earliest. 
Para (48) 
 
Action Taken Note 
 
 Out of total expenditure incurred by implementing agencies under CRR scheme, 
module wise expenditure by the agencies for last th ree years is being collected separately 
from implementing nodal agencies.  
 
 
State Level Public Sector Enterprises (SLPSEs) 
 
Recommendations/ Observations 
 
4. The Committee recommends that DPE should issue g uidelines to the SLPSEs 
asking them to furnish the information on their per formance well in time for preparing 
the next Annual Survey of SLPSEs and also take up t he matter with State Governments 
to nominate one Department as the Nodal Department for data compilation on SLPSEs. 
Para (52) 
 
Action Taken Note 
  
 This Department (DPE) vide its D.O. letter dated 2 4.5.2010 has requested all the 
Chief Secretaries of State Governments/UTs to nomin ate one Department as the Nodal 
Department for data compilation on State Level Public Enterprises (SLPEs). 
       In response to the above request of DPE, 10 States and 3 Union Territories (UTs) 
have already nominated one Department as the Nodal Department for data compilation 
on SLPEs in their respective States / UTs. 
       
12 

 In addition, 10 States  already have one coordinat ing department (Department of 
Public Enterprises (DPE) / Department of Finance / Industry Department) as the nodal 
Department.   
      In respect of the remaining 13 States / UTs, the information is yet to be received. 
      With a view to solicit information from State s / UTs for preparing the next 
National Survey on SLPEs, Zonal Workshops on SLPEs have been organized in 
Guwahati on 5 
th  March 2009, in Kolkata on 20-21 January 2010, in B engaluru on 16-17

      The Department has supplied  all the States /  UTs an Input Sheet (Schedule) in 
three parts (on performance of the Enterprise) to be filled-in by their respective SLPEs

5. The Committee finds that the problems faced by S LPSEs such as absence of 
Board of Directors, short tenure of CMDs and lack o f both operational and strategic

Government and SLPSEs and recommends that DPE shoul d prepare a well articulated

performance of SLPSEs. 
Para (53) 
Action Taken Note 
 
 The Model MoU for State Level Public Enterprises,  prepared in the Department

Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE)  
Recommendations/ Observations  
 
6. At the same time the Committee recommends that i n order to play a meaningful 
role in the affairs of CPSEs the Department of Publ ic Enterprises should not remain a 
mere interface between the administrative Ministrie s and the CPSEs and therefore the

knowledgeable person as Director in the Board of every CPSE. 
Para (61) 
Action Taken Note 
 
 Presently, the proposals for appointment of non-of ficial Directors are initiated by

A proposal for empowering DPE to suo-moto initiate the proposals for

CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
1.  The Committee considered the views of associations  in MSME sector and   recommends 
that the recommendations of the Task Force should b e implemented in letter and spirit on 
priority basis.  
Para (9)   
 
Action taken/Comments 
 
 
 The Ministry of MSME has initiated action for impl ementing the recommendations of the 
Task Force in a time-bound manner. The report has b een circulated to all the Departments/agencies 
concerned and the State/UT Governments for implemen ting the recommendations, as per the time 
lines laid down in the report. The Ministry has als o organized a one-day meeting on 11 
th  May, 2010 
with the State Ministers and Secretaries (Industrie s/MSME) to discuss the recommendations 
concerning the State/UT Governments.  A Council on MSMEs under the chairmanship of Hon’ble 
Prime Minister has been constituted to lay down the  broad policy guidelines and review the 
development of the MSME sector. Further, for ensuri ng timely/speedy implementation of the 
recommendations of the Task Force and follow-up on the decisions of the Prime Minister’s Council 
on MSMEs, a Steering Group under the chairmanship o f Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister 
has also been constituted. The Steering Group has reviewed the progress made in the implementation 
of the recommendations in its meetings held on 6 th  April 2010 and 29 th  July, 2010.  Of the 85 
recommendations, action has been completed in respe ct of several recommendations and other 
recommendations are at various stages of implementation. 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
2. The  Committee  recommends  that  the  seminars/wor kshops  and  other  awareness

are  to  be  sensitized  to  create  more  awarenes s  among  the  MSME  entrepreneurs  and 
persons working in the managerial field.  
 
Para (54)  
 
 
 
-1- 

  
Action taken/Comments  
 
 Besides organizing Packaging for Exports Programme s through MSME-DIs, IIFT, IIP and 
FIEO have been requested to conduct training progra mmes on Packaging for Exports for MSE 
entrepreneurs to promote exports. Likewise, WTO awa reness programmes are being organized 
through field offices all over the country every ye ar so as to prepare MSEs to face challenges of 
globalization.   
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
3. The Committee observe that the main problem in impl ementation of any scheme 
pertains  to  low  level  of  awareness  about  the   schemes  and  negative  mind  set  of  field 
officers  dealing  with  the  entrepreneurs. The Co mmittee  therefore  recommends  that these  
problems  need  to  be  seriously  addressed  by  t he  management  be  it  Commercial 
Banks/Financial Institutions/Ministry.  
Para (55)  
Action taken/Comments 
 
 
 MSME-Development Institutes (MSME-DIs) located in different States are organizing 
Intensive Motivational Campaigns, Entrepreneurial S kill Development Programmes and 
Entrepreneurial Development Programmes. In the Inte nsive Motivational Campaigns, awareness on 
the MSME schemes such as MSE-Cluster Development Pr ogrammes, National Manufacturing 
Competitiveness Programme, Credit Guarantee Scheme,  Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme, 
Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme, R ajiv Gandhi Udyami Mitra Yojana, etc. is 
being created amongst the participants/entrepreneur s. MSME-DIs are also conducting Skill 
Development Programmes for weaker sections/women an d for the general category. In these 
programmes,  training is imparted to the prospectiv e entrepreneurs for setting up micro and small 
enterprises (MSEs), covering the aspects like finan cial management and procedures/formalities for 
availing loans from banks/financial institutions. 
The matter was discussed in the 11 
th  Standing Advisory Committee (SAC) on Flow of Credi t 
to MSME Sector held on May 5, 2010 and it was decid ed that the outcome of the special SLBC 
meetings on MSEs should be closely monitored to ens ure their efficacy.  CEOs of banks have been 
advised to sensitise the branch level functionaries  on various policies and schemes for the benefit of  
MSEs for effective implementation at the branch level. 
 
-2- 

  
For the wide publicity and creation of awareness am ong the beneficiaries, a number of steps 
are being taken by KVIC and Coir Board.  Towards th is direction they organise awareness camps, 
workshops, seminars and also participates in variou s exhibitions in the country. This is also 
supplemented by efforts made through advertisement in print and electronic media and people’s 
education programme.  As reported, some professional agencies have been empanelled by KVIC and 
publicity works are carried out through them from t ime to time. Advertisements of the schemes are 
also being made in the national as well as local ne ws papers from time to time. It is also under 
consideration for placing hoardings in Metro rails, important Railway Stations, Airports, Bus Stands, 
and Collectorate offices in the District levels.   
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
4. In  order  to  sustain  the  Khadi  sector  in  the   country  the  committee  recommends 
that all the Ministries, Departments, PSEs and othe r organizations should opt for Khadi items 
for curtains of  doors  and  windows,  dusters,  to wels,   dress material for the employees and 
give their annual requirements to  KVIC.  This will certainly boost the Khadi sector .  
Para (69)  
Action taken/Comments 
 
 
 With regard to procurement of KVI products by Gove rnment Departments, PSUs, Defence, it 
is to mention that a number of KVI items are covere d under the Rate Contract System of the 
Directorate General of Supply and Disposals, Govern ment of India and Government supply 
activities are undertaken in the Khadi Gramodyog Bh awans of KVIC. Based upon DGS&D Rate 
Contract, the items like dasuti khadi, dungari clot h, dusters, long cloth, bunting cloth and sheeting 
cloth, etc., are being supplied to Government Agenc ies and bed rolls, curtains, pillow covers, etc., 
are being made available to the Indian Railways.  T he instructions have been issued by Government 
of Kerala to all State Government Departments and s chools to instruct the employees and the school 
children to wear khadi at least for one day in a we ek.  Further to boost the khadi sector, KVIC has 
been insisting on the use of khadi and khadi produc ts in all State Government Departments and 
schools.  A target to supply KVI products was fixed  Rs.25 crore under DGS&D contract and against 
the target the supply was Rs.18 crore (provisional)  in 2009-10.  KVIC has been asked to achieve a 
two fold increase in Govt. Supply of Khadi and enco urage procurement of supply orders from 
Government Agencies, through a well planned strategy. 
 
-3- 

  
Recommendation/Observation  
 
5. While deposing before the Committee one of the w itness said that the Khadi has spread over 
in all those villages and huts which are in the tri bal areas, in the hill and border areas and in thos e 
remote areas where no industry is willing to go.  I n this field 75 per cent workers are women and 70 
per cent of them are Scheduled Castes and Scheduled  Tribes.  All of them are below poverty line.  
Majority of them are having traditional charkha on which they are spinning.  So their out put is very 
very low and they get meagre amount as wage.  The n eed of the hour is that the traditional charkhas 
should be replaced by new eight spindle charkha whi ch will increase their out put tremendously and 
naturally their wage will also increase substantially.  
 The Committee feels that the suggestion for replacement of traditional charkhas by new 
eight spindle charkha  is worth consideration and recommends that  a  sepa rate  fund  with  
substantial  funds  be  created  for  replacing  th e  traditional charkhas  of  the  poor  weavers  
throughout  the  country  within  a  time  frame  t o  improve their lot on priority basis as  the 
Khadi has spread over in all those villages and hut s which are in the tribal areas, in the hill 
and border areas and in those remote areas where no industry is willing to go.  
Para (72)  
 
 
Action taken/Comments 
 
 
 Khadi activity is spread all over the country incl uding those remote areas where setting up of 
Industries is extremely difficult. In this field mo st of the workers are from BPL and women and 
majority categories  are having traditional charkha s on which they are spinning yarns  and their 
output  also is very low and they get meagre amount  as wage.  With regard to the suggestion of the 
Committee for creation of a separate fund for replacing the traditional charkhas of poor weavers, it is 
submitted that a new scheme titled ‘Enhancing Produ ctivity and Competitiveness of Khadi Industry 
and Artisans’ has been launched in 2008-09 for  rep lacement of obsolete and old machinery and 
equipment and repair to/renovation of existing/obso lete machinery and equipment to make khadi 
industry more competitive with more market-driven, profitable, production and sustained 
employment for khadi artisans with a total plan out lay of Rs. 84 crore for a period of four years i.e. , 
2008-09 to 2011-12. Provisions for replacement of o bsolete charkhas/looms have also been made 
under Scheme for Strengthening of Infrastructure of  Existing Weak Khadi Institutions and 
Assistance for Marketing Infrastructure introduced in 2009-10 and the Scheme of Funds for 
Regeneration of  Traditional  Industries (SFURTI).   Besides, the ADB-assisted Khadi Reforms  and  
-4- 

  
Development Programme also has a sizable component of the outlay to provide improved 
equipments to artisans and upgradation of technolog y. KVIC/Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural 
Industrialization has also launched a pilot project  of testing solar charkhas for reducing drudgery of  
spinners. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
6. Looking at the performance of the KVIC in North Eas t Region the Committee is of the   
opinion  that KVIC should set up more central slive r plants in North East Region and  provide  
them  support  in  the  form  of  grant  in  lieu  of  working  capital  so  that  the production   
activities   in   North   East   Region   are   enh anced   and   thus   creating   more employment 
and development of economic conditions.  
Para (106)  
 
Action taken/Comments 
 
 
 Necessary measures have been initiated by the Gove rnment through the Khadi Reform 
Programme which includes production of quality raw- material in the Central Sliver Plants operated 
in PPP mode, besides sliver production at institutional level, opening of new sliver plants, opening of 
new sales, renovation, and modernization of institutional sales outlets, etc.  It is proposed to establish 
a new CSP in North East Region for timely availabil ity of quality raw materials to the khadi 
institutions located in these States.   
Recommendation/Observation
