1
REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of
Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises (Department of Public Enterprises) on the
recommendations contained in the Committee’s Two Hundred Thirty-third Report on the Demands
For Grants (2012-13) pertaining to Department of Public Enterprises.
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises (Department of Public Enterprises) in respect of the recommendations contained in the
Report. These have been categorized as follows:
Chapter-I– The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry.
The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry has accepted its recommendations
as mentioned in the Chapter–I of the Report.
Chapter-II – The recommendation/observations, which the Committee does not desire to
pursue in view of the Government’s replies.
In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and
explanations advanced by the Ministry and therefore does not want to pursue them for the present.
Chapter-III – The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has
either not accepted replies of the Ministry or has asked the Ministry to review its reply.
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of recommendations
contained in Chapter–III and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanations thereof.
Chapter-IV – The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the
Ministry have not been received.
In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either furnished
the interim replies or couched its language in vague terms therefore, the Committee desires that
the Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations categorized in
Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the
Committee.
3. The details of the ATR is being discussed in the succeeding pages.

2
CHAPTER-I
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Ministry
Recommendations/Observations
1. The Committee is given to understand that normally money earmarked for spending under
the plan head is not transferred to the non-plan head. Of course, the Department must have re-
appropriated the money under the explicit approval of the Finance Ministry. However, it is to be
borne in mind that the lack of funds to meet the non-plan expenditure is indicative of absence of
sound planning by the DPE. It must foresee and anticipate such spending and approach the Finance
Ministry for allocation of funds for the purpose of meeting non-plan expenditure. It strongly
recommends that the DPE must not divert funds from the plan to non-plan head. The officials of
the DPE must foresee the non-plan expenditure and accordingly submit their estimates to the
Ministry of Finance for adequate allocation of funds. The Committee hopes that the Department
will adopt a proper strategy so that it does not divert the plan fund for the non-plan expenditure.
The Committee strongly feels that the Department must spend the money put under the plan head
to achieve the desired results. (Para 14)
Action Taken Note
This Department is in agreement with the observations of the Hon’ble Committee. During
the financial year 2011-12, an amount of Rs.1.50 crore was earmarked for Plan head Research,
Development and consultancy on generic issues related to central Public Sector Enterprises and
State Level Public Enterprises (RDC). As Department envisaged not utilizing this amount, because
of some unforeseen and other reasons, Ministry of Finance was requested for surrender of
Rs.66 lakhs out of the total amount of Rs.1.50 crore under RDC. Ministry of Finance agreed to
the proposal. Further, as there was requirement of funds, in Non-Plan (11-12) this Department
requested the M/o Finance for providing the additional funds under the Non-Plan, which they
agreed. Nevertheless, the observations of the Hon’ble Committee about the anticipation and
foreseeing the spending under Non-plan have been conveyed to the concerned Divisions in this
Department and also noted for compliance. In the year 2012-13, a proper strategy is being framed
to utilize the funds under Plan head RDC to achieve the desired results.
Recommendations/Observations
2. The Committee takes note of the fact that the DPE intends to focus attention on the
deficiencies and weaknesses of the employees of the SLPES so that it could take measures to
mitigate or rectify them and improve their capabilities. But, while doing so, it would be self-
defeating to ignore the strengths of the employees whose skills are to be developed. In the syllabus
of the modern management discipline SWOT (Strength, Weakness, Opportunity and Threats) has
been adopted to get a broad view of the dark and brighter sides of the human resources deployed
in an enterprise. In ignoring the strengths the positive aspects would be completely lost sight of.
The concept of ‘Core Competence’ has been increasingly emphasized in the modern organization
to highlight the inherent resilience and capabilities of the employees. It would be appropriate for
the department to stress on ‘Core Competence’ while adopting the SWOT analysis. This would
enable the Department and the concerned enterprises to have a better grasp of the talent pool
2

3
available at their disposal and their plus and minus dimensions. The Committee recommends that
the good performance of the SLPEs may be factored into any decision to allocate funds for skill
development. Besides, the weightage also should be given to the enterprises which function in core
areas of our economy which are critical to economic growth and expansion. The Committee also
hastens to add that the SLPEs utilizing locally available resources and creating job opportunities
may be accorded priority. (Para 17)
Action Taken Note
The directions of the Standing Committee have been incorporated in the proposed new Plan
Scheme.
Recommendations/Observations
3. The figures in the Budget Documents at Table 2 shows that the allocation (RE) for the
Scheme of CRR for 2010-11 was Rs. 7.58 crore, but the Actuals for the year is shown as Rs.8.03
crore. The Committee fails to understand as to how the utilization figures for 2010-11 were higher
than the allocation made for year. Furthermore, if the Table 1 figures for allocation (Rs.8.90 crore)
is taken in face value, the Actuals for 2010-11 in the Budget Document should have been Rs.8.63
crore (96.97% of Rs.8.90 crore) instead of Rs. 8.03 crore. Similarly, while considering the figures
of Table-1, the allocation for 2011-12 as furnished by DPE is Rs.8.90 crore whereas in the Budget
Document puts it at Rs.7.80 crore. (Para 27)
4. The Committee observes that such variation in figures presented before a Parliamentary
Committee, engaged in scrutinizing the Demand for Grants is totally unacceptable. The Committee
expects a clear cut explanation in this regard. It is imperative that the Department shall take note
of this and ensure strict compliance in future. (Para 28)
Action Taken Note
In 2010-11, RE under CRR was Rs. 8.63 crore which includes Rs. 7.58 crore for
implementation of CRR Scheme in other than NE Region and Rs. 1.03 crore in NE Region. In
2010-11, actual expenditure of Rs. 8.03 crore under CRR includes Rs. 7.43 crore in other than
NE Region and Rs. 0.60 crore in NE Region. During 2011-12, RE budget allocation was Rs. 8.90
crore under CRR including allocation for all regions including NER. The position is given in a
tabular form as under:
(Rs. in crore )
Y ear BE RE Fund Remarks
utilized
2010-11 8.90 8.63 8.03* Allocation and utilization of funds is for all regions
including NE Region.
2011-12 8.90 8.90 8.17*
* Balance funds transferred to Non-lapsable Pool
Henceforth, the figures regarding allocation of funds and their utilization would be presented
with greater clarity.
Recommendations/Observations
5. The Committee has persistently noted that funds allocated to North Eastern Areas and are

4
taken forward to next financial years. Of course, the committee appreciates the fact that in case
of North Eastern Region, the funds allocated would not lapse. The North Eastern Areas of the
country do always get the special attention of the Union Government. Fund earmarked for this
region has to be utilized properly for the cause of improving that region and accelerating the
process of industrialization. It is important, therefore, to accelerate the process of utilization of
funds for training VRS optees. The Committee also finds it difficult to fathom as to why the
Budget Document reflects the Actual expenditure for the North Eastern Areas for 2010-11 as ‘nil’,
when the Department claims to have utilized Rs. 6 crore. This sort of anomalies in figure may lead
to misunderstanding and, therefore, the Committee demands an explanation from the Departments
concerned. The Committee firmly recommends that the Department should iron out such
incongruities and improve their performance in the North Eastern Areas. (Para 36)
Action Taken Note
In the year 2010-11, 700 VRS optees were trained in NE Region and Rs. 0.60 crore was
utilized under the CRR scheme. CRR Scheme has not got momentum in NE Region mainly because
of non-availability of substantial VRS optees in the region. VRS is not very sizeable in the units
located in NE Region and often, immediately after separation, they migrate to their native places/
states and change their domicile. DPE is making all efforts to cover the backlog of VRS
optees even though it is sometime difficult to locate them in a sizable number in a cluster. Nodal
agencies have been motivated to operate and cover more candidates in NE Region. Besides CRR,
in 2012-13, some state specific proposals involving CPSEs and SLPEs have also been planned to
be implemented in NE Region.
As per the existing norm, 10% of total plan fund is earmarked for NE region. This
allocation is provided in the Account Head – North Eastern Areas. As given to understand by the
Ministry of Finance, this being non-functional head, the expenditure cannot be booked directly
under it and the same is to be met from functional head, i.e. head under CRR in the instant case.
Since total actual expenditure, including that towards NE was within the allocation of functional
Head, the re-appropriation from NE was not sought. As such, even though the expenditure in NE
Head is ‘nil’, expenditure for NE region under CRR Scheme was incurred.
Recommendations/Observations
6. (i) The Committee takes note that the MoU System as it exists today is broadly based on
the recommendation of NCAER made in the year 2003. It is the considered opinion
of the Committee that the MoU system, which has an overarching influence on the
performance of the CPSEs, has to be in tune with the latest trends for successful
operation of the PSEs.
(ii) Accordingly, it is recommended that DPE may engage an accredited organization to
revisit the MoU system and assess it for the purpose of revitalizing it and making it
more effective.
(iii) The system should be more flexible and receptive to the feedback received from the
CPSEs. It is worthwhile to note that certain profit making organizations must not be
allowed to opt for soft targets solely on the ground that they have performed better.
In fact, in a highly competitive environment such organizations need to set better
targets for themselves for full flowering of their potentialities. The Prime Minister of
our country while giving away the MoU and SCOPE Awards to best performing
Central Public Sector Enterprises referred to MoU system and said that, “We cannot

5
be satisfied with the status quo”. He made that observation in the context of the
determination of the Government to make CPSEs stronger and competitive. An
overhauled MoU system must serve this cause. (Para 41)
Action Taken Note
(i) MoU System as it exists now is predominantly based on NCAER recommendations of
2004, but it has evolved and changed over the years and new initiatives have been
introduced from time to time. The parameters selected are a good mix of financial,
dynamic and efficiency indicators which are strategically important for CPSEs. Thus,
under the present system, an attempt has been made to strike a balance between
financial and non-financial parameters. Targets include performance of the CPSE under
Corporate Social Responsibility, R&D, Sustainable Development, Human Resources
Management, Corporate Governance and Compliance of DPE Guidelines.
As CPSEs have to operate in a free market, they cannot continue to depend upon
Government assistance. The MoU also emphasizes on projects management and fresh
order book from Government/Private/Foreign with corresponding weightages. MoU
appears to be an appropriate instrument where the issues involving inter-ministry/inter-
CPSEs coordination can be taken up more effectively.
Adoption of innovative practices is included as a new parameter with some weightage
in the MoU. Customer satisfaction, quality, safety, Capital expenditure/Joint Ventures,
Globalization, etc. are also taken as MoU Parameters.
Thus, MoU System is now a performance driven, forward looking management tool to
facilitate empowerment and enhancement of performance of CPSEs.
(ii) and (iii) These pertinent issues are under examination by DPE. DPE has formed a
Working Group headed by Chairman Task Force to review the existing MoU System
and to suggest improvements to make it more effective.
Besides, DPE is also in the process of engaging an External Agency to conduct the
evaluation of MoU System. Request for Proposal is being issued.
Reports/Recommendations received will be examined by DPE in consultation with the
administrative Ministries/departments of concerned CPSEs and placed before the High
Power Committee on MoU headed by Cabinet Secretary for bringing in suitable
changes in the MoU System.
Recommendations/Observations
7. (i) The Committee was constrained to note that there are certain Central Public Sector
Enterprises which do not subscribe to the MoU discipline and protocol. It has noted that
such departure from MoU discipline has taken place in spite of the intervention of the
Cabinet Secretary. It is sad commentary on the functioning of our system. The
Committee finds it unacceptable that certain PSEs are not amenable to the MoU regime.
(ii) The Committee is sad to note that certain CPSEs do not submit certain documents at
the time of evaluation of their functioning. The Committee was informed that 36
CPSEs failed to submit the required document to the DPE for evaluation. The
Committee feels that action must be initiated against such organizations which remain
out of the ambit of the MoU. The Committee notes that incentives are there for CPSEs
to submit to the MoU system. The Committee strongly recommends that there must
be stringent action and disincentives as well to enforce the MoU system. (Para 42)

6
Action Taken Note
(i) and (ii) For CPSEs, which do not sign or delay in signing the MoU, their
performance in MoU is rated as ‘Poor’ and the same to be reflected in Annual
Performance Appraisal Report (APAR) of the Chief Executive of CPSE.
MoU Guideline issued by DPE provides that those CPSEs which do not
submit performance Evaluation Report with annual audited data by the
prescribed date will not be evaluated by DPE and CPSEs will be rated ‘Poor’
in the MoU and they will not be eligible for Performance Related Pay (PRP).
Recommendations/Observations
8. Further, the Committee is strongly in favour of introducing disincentives and punitive
measures against those PSEs which desist from entering into MoU discipline and those which do
not comply with the MoU agreements already signed. (Para 43)
Action Taken Note
As regards initiating disincentives and punitive measures against such defaulting CPSEs,
DPE has been writing to the concerned administrative Ministry/Department under whose jurisdiction
they fall.
The Working Group on MoU formed by DPE is, examining inter alia , this issue of not
subscribing to discipline of MoU by CPSEs. Their recommendations will be examined by DPE and
suitable measures will be taken.

7
CHAPTER-II
Recommendations/Observations, which the Committee does
not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies
Recommendations/Observations
1. The Committee strongly feels that the vision and mission of the DPE must be further
expanded to include issues like research and development capabilities and manpower planning in the
absence of which the CPSEs quite often do not generate greater productivity and incur loss leading
to their sickness and closure. The issue of research and development is of course the responsibility
of the concerned public sector enterprises. But if the DPE is guided by vision and mission to
enhance the research and development capability and other critical factors which are essential for
making our PSEs technologically advanced and competitive, then it would better help the DPE to
take the cause of public sector enterprises forward. The Committee feels that the vision and
mission of the DPE incorporating such factors would be more impactful on the CPSEs for making
them competitive and result oriented. It would also make the CPSEs more aware of the fact that
for their survival and growth these have to stand on their own and prove their worth in the
expanding market and global economy. Such a modified vision and mission statement would also
enable the DPE officials to emphasise on the issue during their interactions with CPSE
representatives. (Para 6)
Action Taken Note
DPE is primarily concerned with the policy formulation on general matters pertaining to
CPSEs and in line with this mandate DPE lays down policy guidelines on performance improvement
and evaluation, autonomy and financial delegation and personnel management in CPSEs. DPE has
already finalized its Results-Framework Document (RFD) for the year 2012-13 on 2nd May, 2012
as per direction of Cabinet Secretariat. It may also be pointed out that the Vision statement of any
organization is having long term relevance. As per its mandate, DPE’s Vision is to evolve policies,
reform programmes, guidelines and mechanisms towards the establishment of a strong and
effective public sector. The aspects of Research and Development activities and Manpower
Planning are covered by the Vision Statement presently incorporated in RFD of DPE. It may also
be mentioned that Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) has already issued Guidelines on
Research and Development (R&D) and Human Resource Management (HRM) for Central Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) as a mandatory component of MoU which is applicable from the year
2012-13. It is further pointed out that DPE has already issued Advisory on professionalization of
the below Board level management in CPSEs which covers the issue of Manpower Planning.
Therefore, a proposal to suitably incorporate Research and Development and Manpower
Planning in the Mission statement of DPE at the time of finalizing RFD for the year 2013-14 will
be submitted for the approval of competent authority.
Recommendations/Observations
2. The Committee, while taking note of the programme for skill development of SLPEs, is
constrained to observe that the Department of Public Enterprises has no scheme for training its
own officers both at the national level institutes and in the reputed training establishments located
7

8
in some of the world class universities and institutes. The officials of the DPE are quite often
engaged in imparting training facilities. They are also engaged in finalizing the MoUs where
weightage is given to several parameters which are indispensable for enhancing growth,
productivity and competitiveness of the PSEs. If these officers are not adequately trained, both at
the national and international levels, their expertise and competence will remain stagnant. It is,
therefore, strongly recommended that a separate scheme for the employees and officers of the DPE
should be formulated for their training within India and abroad. (Para 18)
Action Taken Note
DPE has very small establishment with a total 126 sanctioned staff strength. All these posts
except Group ‘D’ posts have been encadred with various organised Service Cadre like CSS, CSSS,
CSCS, D/o Official Language, IES, ISS, SSS, IAS, IRS, IRTS, ICoAS etc. Matters relating to
training of Officers/Officials are observed by relevant Service Cadres. However, once joining the
DPE officers are sent for attending Workshops, Seminars etc in India/abroad, as per the office
exigencies. Nevertheless, now special emphasis is being given to such training areas.
Recommendations/Observations
3. The Committee takes note of the fact that the DPE is periodically reviewing the CRR
scheme to make it useful to the beneficiaries. A scheme like CRR becomes more meaningful when
the targeted beneficiaries are made employable through training imparted to them. The skills they
acquire need to be certified by an accredited agency so that the training they received is recognized
and valued. (Para 24)
Action Taken Note
The scheme is reviewed on continuous basis. From 2012-13 onwards, a system for Third
Party Evaluation is being introduced for the first time to make the CRR Scheme more robust and
effective. Further improvements in the Scheme including post training certification of candidates is
under consideration for introduction in phases.
Recommendations/Observations
4. The Committee is surprised to note that there is failure on the part of the DPE to secure
the Annual Compliance Reports from the CPSEs. An appropriate strategy has to be devised to
receive such Reports from the concerned PSEs. It is important that Committee must be informed
about the action taken in this regard. (Para 45)
Action Taken Note
The Department of Public Enterprises had issued the guidelines regarding submission of
Annual Compliance Report by the CPSEs vide its OM dated 29.07.2010. This OM was issued by
DPE in compliance of the recommendation made by the Department Related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry (DRPSC) in its 216th Report to the effect that DPE should ask for the
Annual Compliance Reports from the CPSEs about the implementation of the Policies and
Guidelines formulated by DPE from time to time. While accepting the above recommendation of
DRPSC, DPE had requested all CPSEs to furnish the Annual Compliance Reports within 30 days
from the end of the preceding financial year to their concerned administrative Ministry, and the
administrative Ministries/Departments were requested to furnish the consolidated Compliance Report
in respect of all CPSEs under their respective administrative control to DPE by 30 June every year.
The OM dated 29.07.2010 was followed by another OM dated 28.06.2011 wherein DPE prescribed

9
the format for submission of Annual Compliance Reports by the concerned administrative
Ministries/Departments. As, the Reports were received from only a few Ministries/CPSEs, all
administrative Ministries/Departments were reminded on 29.03.2012 to furnish the consolidated
Annual Compliance Report for the year 2011-12 in the prescribed format.
Secretary, Department of Public Enterprises has taken up the matter of delay in the
submission of Annual Compliance Reports with Secretaries of Administrative Ministries/Departments
vide DO letter dated 29.05.2012. Secretaries of all Administrative Ministries/Departments were
requested to depute their senior officers to furnish Annual Compliance Reports to DPE. In a series
of meetings convened by Secretary (DPE) with all Administrative Ministries/Departments from 8th
June to 26th June, 2012 senior officers of all 39 administrative Ministries/Department were
sensitized about the need of timely submission of Annual compliance Reports in respect of CPSEs
under their administrative control. As a result, compliance reports have been received in respect of
38 CPSEs, and DPE has issued another reminder on 12.07.2012 to the concerned administrative
Ministries from which replies have not yet been received. It is proposed to establish a system of
convening meetings with all Administrative Ministries/Departments on an annual basis to ensure
timely receipt of Annual Compliance Reports from all administrative Ministries.

10
CHAPTER-III
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee
has either not accepted the replies of the Ministry or has asked
the Ministry to review its replies
Recommendations/Observations
1. The Committee is given to understand that the Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
is part of the Department of Personnel and Training. The Committee is surprised to note that it
is the DoPT which is the administrative Ministry for the PESB. Possibly the PESB was made part
of the DoPT when there was no Department of Public Enterprises. Now, that the DPE is in
existence for several years, it would be prudent to bring the PESB under the control of the DPE.
The Committee strongly recommends that such a change must take place for the purpose of
streamlining and quickening the process of succession planning in the PSEs. Apart from the PSEs
and their administrative Ministry the domain knowledge concerning the functioning of the PSEs is
with the DPE. It finalises their MoUs and sets their targets both in the financial and non-financial
sectors. It is, therefore, appropriate that PESB must function under the jurisdiction of DPE. At a
time when the Government of India is emphasizing on the need to reform the functioning the
Central Public Sector Enterprises, it is extremely important to include within the reform process
the decision to transfer the PESB from the control of DoPT to DPE. Realising the importance of
the recommendation it must be done irrespective of any resistance from any quarter.
(Para 20)
Action Taken Note
This issue was taken up at highest level in the Ministry of HI&PE with the highest level
in the Government, for consideration of the matter of transfer of Public Enterprises Selection Board
(PESB) from Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) to Department of Public Enterprises
(DPE). The matter was duly examined at highest level in consultation with concerned stake holders.
It has been conveyed that no change in the existing allocation of business in respect of PESB is
considered necessary.
Further Recommendation
The Committee, for two reasons, considers this reply of the Government to be far
from satisfactory. Foremost, the reply only states that the issue of transfer of Public
Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) from Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) to
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) was considered at the highest level in the
Government and it has been decided that no change in the allocation of business to this
effect was necessary, whereas, the rationale behind the decision is not reflected in the reply.
The Committee expects a reply from the Department with regard to its recommendation to
be explanatory and want it to contain the logic behind the decision taken on the
recommendation.
Further, the Committee is of the firm and considered opinion that the transfer of
the Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) from Department of Personnel & Training
(DoPT) to Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) is a functional prerequisite in the
10

11
professionalization of the management of CPSEs and thus can have a cascading effect on
the efficient running of various CPSEs. Taking these into account, the Committee reiterates
its recommendation in the strongest terms.
Recommendations/Observations
2. The Committee is not happy to note that the reduction in expenditure took place because
some States organized their workshops on their own due to delayed approvals of the workshops
to be conducted by the DPE. It also established the point that there was a lack of coordination
between the DPE and the States concerned. Even earlier the Committee has observed that lack of
coordination among Ministries and several Departments of Governments have resulted in policy
paralysis and adversely affecting the functioning of PSEs. The Committee recommends that funds
allocated for such important schemes should be fully utilized. (Para 32)
Action Taken Note
The recommendations of the Committee to (fully) utilize the funds allocated for such
Schemes will be adhered to in all earnest.
Further Recommendation
Though the reply of the Government commits that funds provided for training
programmes will be fully utilized, the Committee would like the Government to comment
on the aspect of lack of coordination between Departments of the Government of India and
the Union and State Governments in implementing such schemes to the full.

12
CHAPTER-IV
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which
final replies of the Ministry have not been received
Recommendations/Observations
1. The Committee finds that the time taken to process the proposal for revival and
restructuring of a PSU is too long. The delay caused in this regard compounds the problem. The
Committee was given to understand that BRPSE cannot take punitive action or even a strong view
if its recommendations are not followed. In contrast, the views of BIFR are given importance due
to the fact that it has a statutory backing. The Committee is given to understand that the BIFR
is soon to be replaced by the National Company law Tribunal (NCLT). In this scenario, the
Committee recommends that when NCLT is put in place, its mandate should avoid any duplication
of work with BRPSE. The Committee also strongly feels that the revival proposal of sick PSEs
must be disposed of within a specified time avoiding unnecessary delay. (Para 48)
Action Taken Note
The observation and recommendation of the Committee on National Company Law Tribunal
(NCLT) has been brought to the notice of the M/o Corporate Affairs for consideration in the
formulation of mandate of NCLT.
The administrative Ministries/Departments of the CPSEs are informed to take note of the
concern of the Committee for necessary action to dispose the revival proposals of sick CPSEs
under their control in a time frame.
Recommendations/Observations
2. It is deplorable that there are 300 vacant positions of non-official Directors on the Board
of more than 100 scheduled CPSEs. However, the recommendations of Search Committee for
filling up 100 of these vacant positions have already been conveyed to the concerned Ministries for
obtaining approval of competent authority. This must be done expeditiously. (Para 50)
3. The Committee is of the view that professionalization of Boards of CPSEs is an
indispensable necessity for making them more competitive and viable in the emerging market
economy. The good corporate governance can be ensured by professionalization of board of
directors. The existing vacancies of 300 posts of non-functional Directors must be filled up
urgently without which the effective performance of CPSEs would be adversely affected. These
vacancies indicate lack of vision, planning and non responsive attitude to vital issues concerning
the functions of PSEs. The Committee would like to reiterate the point that DPE has to be the
nodal Department under the jurisdiction of which must function the Public Enterprises Selection
Board. The Committee strongly recommends for the filling up of vacancies of non-officials
Directors in CPSEs within a minimum period of one month and also to ensure that such vacancies
do not exist beyond the period of a financial quarter in any case. (Para 51)
Action Taken Note
The selection and appointment of non-official Directors on the Boards of CPSEs is a
12

13
continuous process involving furnishing of proposals by the concerned administrative Ministry,
recommendations by the Search Committee and approval by the competent authority. Following the
above recommendations, the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) has taken the following
actions to expedite filling up of vacant positions of non-official Directors on the Boards of CPSEs.
Secretary, Department of Public Enterprises has conveyed the above recommendation to Secretaries
of all administrative Ministries/Department in May, 2012 and requested them to take necessary steps
to ensure that requisite numbers of non-official Directors are appointed on the Boards of CPSEs
under their respective administrative control. Thereafter, DPE organized interaction meetings with
senior officials of all (39) administrative Ministries/Departments during the month of June, 2012
wherein the urgent need to fill vacant positions of non-official Directors as recommended by the
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry was reiterated. As a result, there
has been significant increase in the number of proposals for appointment of non-official Directors
being submitted to DPE. Further, Secretary, Department of Public Enterprises, in July, 2012 has
again taken up this matter with Secretaries of those Ministries/Departments in whose CPSEs there
are substantial number of vacant positions of non-official Directors, impressing them again to take
immediate steps to fill such vacant positions.

REPORT
The architecture of mixed economy providing space both to the private and public sectors
served the nation well in reviving our growth and development which suffered irreparable damage
due to colonial rule. The private sector which is the engine of economic growth in 21
st century
India was in no position to invest monetary resources and employ skills and expertise to address
the challenges of our economic growth in the formative stage of our independence. Therefore, the
State relied on public enterprises for the primary purpose of building infrastructure, generating
employment opportunities for people, promoting balanced regional development and above all for
industrializing remote and backward areas of our country. It is due to public sector enterprises that
the nation could create conditions for emergence of private players to shape our economic growth
and take it forward. The first Prime Minister of our country Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru justly
described the public sector enterprises as the commanding heights of our economy.
2. With the onset of economic reforms in the 1990s, a more liberalized and market
environment was created. It is worth noting that the PSEs have proved their worth in the new
environment and successfully met the challenges posed by globalization and competition arising out
of private sector led economic growth. There is now a more expanding market where competition,
innovation, technological upgradation and above all improved customer preferences define the
course of business, trade and commerce. In this age, which is known as the age of geo-
economics, the wide variety of choices available to a customer and the continuously improved
quality of products and accelerated delivery of services become important factors for the
advancement of business practices. In fact, these factors have transformed the way in which
business transactions are maintained, sustained and taken forward. The public sector enterprises
have proved their worth in face of these challenges. While upgrading their performance they have
to improve their productivity and competitive edge and at the same time discharge their obligations
to society at large. Acknowledgement of the good performance of the public sector enterprises by
none less than the Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh is indicative of the positive assessment of
their contributions to our country at the highest political level.
3. It is worthwhile to place in record the statement of Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh
that due to the resilience of the public sector enterprises the country could withstand the challenges
of financial crisis which originated in the United States of America. Therefore, public sector
enterprises are as relevant today as they were relevant in the mixed economy of 1950s.
4. The PSEs have grown from 5 in the First Five Year Plan to 260 by the end of March,
2012. Out of these 220 are in operation. It is heartening to note that 158, which come to 70 per
cent of the operating PSEs, are making profits. In other words, majority of the PSEs are generating
profits. It is found that, “The profit of these 158 CPSEs increased from Rs.895.8 billion in
Financial Year 2007 to Rs.1137.7 billion in Financial Year 2011, led by robust performance by
mining companies, power companies and select oil and gas companies.” Apart from profits, the
PSEs have made important contributions to the nation exchequer by paying excise and custom
duties and dividends and royalties. These also account for over 20 per cent of country’s GDP,
around six per cent of total employment in the organized sector and 20 per cent of direct and
indirect tax collection. In fact, it is worthwhile to observe that the performance of the profit
making PSEs are favorably compared with their private sector counterparts.
5. The genesis of Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), the nodal agency for all CPSEs in
India, can be traced to the formation of a Bureau of Public Enterprises in 1965 pursuant to the
recommendations of the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha.

2
The vision of the DPE is:
“To enable PSEs to become strong, effective and globally competitive”.
While their Mission is:
“To continuously improve the management of public sector enterprises facilitating
better corporate governance, human resource management (HRM), research & development,
innovative efforts and reviving sick PSEs”.
The core functions of the Department are as under:–
• Co-ordination of matters of general policy of non-financial nature relating to public
sector enterprises.
• Formulation of policies, pertaining to public sector enterprises, in areas like board
structures, personnel management, performance improvement, financial management,
wage settlement, etc.
• Conferring and review of Maharatana, Navratana and Miniratna status to CPSEs.
• Policy relating to delegation of powers to Board of Directors.
• Policy relating to deputation of Government officers to public sector enterprises.
• Publication of the annual survey of CPSEs known as Public Enterprises Survey.
• Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the public sector enterprises and the
administrative Ministries/Departments.
• Policy relating to Counseling, Retraining and Redeployment Scheme (CRR) for
rationalized employees of CPSEs.
• Policy relating to Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE).
• Policy relating to reservation of posts in the public sector enterprises for certain
classes of citizens.
• Settlement of disputes through Permanent Machinery of Arbitration (PMA) among
Public Sector Enterprises and between Public Sector Enterprises and government
departments except disputes relating to tax matters.
• Matters relating to International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE) and
Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE).
• Bringing out annual Survey of CPSEs/SLPEs to create a reliable time series data on
their performance.
• Organizing capacity building programmes for CPSE/SLPE executives.
6. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department of Public Enterprises has
paid heed to its recommendation to include R&D issue in the mission of the DPE and
accordingly the issue of R&D finds in an appropriate place in the mission statement of the
Department.

11. The Committee regrets that Non-plan funds have been increased and the plan funds

functioning of the PSEs are not getting adequate budgetary allocation. It is even more

money put under the plan head to achieve the desired results.” It is rather unfortunate that

12. During the course of discussion on Demands for 2013-14, it has been submitted to the

Rs.1.0123 crore and Rs.1.6778 crore, respectively as ‘savings’. While explaining the usage of the
word ‘saving’ the Committee was informed that in certain schemes such as Counselling,
Retraining and Redeployment Scheme for the North Eastern Region the money could not be
utilized and, therefore, that money was treated as saving. With regard to underutilization of Plan
expenditure of CRR the Secretary, DPE stated that “As figures, which you might have seen,
show, there have been shortfalls in all these three. We have not been able to utilize even the
curtailed resources at the RE stage. I take full responsibility for that But I took courage from
the Committee’ s guidance that these schemes are not just to push money and achieve physical
numbers or targets; these schemes are for ensuring qualitative change that for whatever purpose
these monies are to be spent, those changes are achieved, and, therefore, I would like to
enlighten the Committee that in CRR, I received certain complaints on telephone, by mail and
I found that there were problems. Wherever I found these complaints, we verified them and we
found that the monies were not being spent objectively.” The Committee was also informed that
in certain other projects the objectives could be met and the money meant for such projects
could not be fully utilized. For instance, a project like the review of the role and responsibilities
of non-official directors being undertaken by the Institute of Chartered Accountants India could
be completed and whatever money could not be utilized for the completion of such a project was
treated as savings.
13. The Committee notes that the money earmarked for any scheme for the North
Eastern Region does not lapse. However, non-utilization of such money is a poor reflection
on the ability and expertise of the Department. The North Eastern part of India has always
been given special attention for its development and progress. Any scheme meant for that
region has to be seen in this broader context. While it is true that funds meant for schemes
of the North Eastern Region would be carried forward, it is equally important that
determined efforts need to be taken to use the funds allotted for a particular year. The
unutilized funds cannot be treated as ‘saving’. Rather, the Committee feels that such
unutilized funds are indicative of lack of seriousness of purpose and action on the part of
the Department. In case of money which remains unspent after meeting the objectives of
a scheme that money, in true sense of the term, can be called as savings. Accordingly, it
is recommended that that Ministry may use terms which should be exact in terms of
nomenclature and terminology.

counselling, retraining and redeploying them. It was supposed to prepare them to take up new
vocations or to become self-employed.

22. The Committee notes that the CRR scheme has been an important initiative for the
welfare of the VRS optees of CPSEs. However, it is apparent that the scheme in its present

DPE intends to reinvent the scheme by identifying fresh pockets of beneficiaries, revision
of course curriculum, national level certification of training, etc. The Committee
recommends an objective assessment of the scheme must be made. The Committee also
recommends that the Department must ensure that the VRS beneficiaries are properly
redeployed. In this context, it is strongly recommends to monitor the scheme and submit
a report to the Committee.
23. The Committee notes that the implementation of the scheme in the North Eastern
part of India is highly unsatisfactory. Year after year, the funds meant for the North
Eastern part are not utilized for implementation of the scheme and these are transferred
to the non lapsable pool without producing any significant results. This is not at all a
heartening development. The Department officials must be more sensitive to the North
Eastern Region. In this context, the Committee recommends that the revamped CRR
Scheme must be more effective in the North Eastern Region of our country.
Scheme for Skill Development/Training programme of Executives of State Level Public
Enterprises (SLPEs)
24. The Standing Committee of Principal Secretaries of Public Enterprises/Departments in State/
Union Territories recommended in 2008 that the Government of India should supplement the effort
of the State Governments for training Executives and employees of State Level Public Enterprises.
Accordingly, DPE submitted a proposal to the Planning Commission in 2009. This submission
resulted in preparation of a scheme called Skill Development/Training programme of Executives of
State Level Public Enterprises (SLPEs) in Bhopal, Delhi and Shimla.
25. Regarding the future progress of the scheme, the Department submitted before the
Committee that the Planning Commission while approving the Annual Plan 2012-13 of DPE
provided a token amount of Rs. 1 crore (in BE) for the Scheme. The Hon’ble Minister of HI&PE
on 29.01.2013 thereafter granted administrative approval for the scheme and Guidelines on the
Training of SLPEs Executives were devised and finalised. Accordingly, five training programmes
under this Scheme were held during 2012-13 resulting in a total expenditure of Rs.10.86 lakhs (out
of which Rs.5.97 lakhs for 3 programmes are still pending for financial approvals). Also a Seminar
on Training Need Assessment in SLPEs was organized by DPE on 16th November, 2012, in New
Delhi. The recommendations of the TNA Workshop have been made the basis for selecting/
designing the training programmes during the FY 2013-14.
26. During the course of examination of Demand for Grants, 2013-14, the Department also
stated that they tried to launch the scheme in 2012-13, but the approval was received only in
December 2012. The Department also took time to give its approval to the scheme. It may be
mentioned that the Committee on Industry had recommended that the Department, instead of
focusing only on the weakness of the beneficiaries must take into account their strength and
experience. Such a recommendation resulted in the formulation of a scheme called Objective
Training Need Assessment under which training programmes would be conducted as per the needs
of the trainees. It was also decided that the resources would be spent for the purpose of training
in requisite areas and building capacity by taking into account the needs and based on SWOT
analysis.

could be finally approved only in January, 2013. It is also being observed that the
Department would do well to avoid any further delay in the implementation of the scheme.
The Committee also observes that the feedback of respective State Governments and State
level Public Sector Enterprises must be taken to further fine tune the scheme. Stress
should be laid for time bound implementation of the scheme and it should be reflected in
the Result-Framework Document of the Ministry/Department.

Utilization of Funds in the North Eastern Region (NER)
31. As per the existing norm, 10% of total Plan funds of the Department have to be earmarked

9
for utilization in the NER. This allocation is provided in the Account Head – NE Areas. As directed
by the Ministry of Finance since this is a non functional head, the expenditure cannot be shown
directly under this head and the same is to be re-appropriated under a functional head before
disbursement.
32. While responding to a query regarding utilisation of Funds in the NER during examination
of Demands, DPE submitted that they have received a proposal from Public Enterprise
Department, Government of Assam in the year 2012-13 for providing funds under Non-lapsable
Central Pool for N.E. region for computerization of the State Level Public Enterprises (SLPEs)
with a view to strengthening I.T. Infrastructure. The Government of Sikkim also sent a similar
request. The proposal received from Government of Assam was examined in DPE and
concurrence of the competent authority (IFW/CCA) was sought for opening a new Sub-head
under Major Head 2552 (NER) and for re-appropriation of the requisite budget allocation from
NER-CRR Head to NER-SLPE Sub-head. Against this submission, the IF Wing/CCA raised certain
queries regarding approval of the Planning Commission on the concept note of the scheme,
outlay and guidelines of the scheme and whether the funds would be released in the form of
grant-in-aid, etc. DPE have resubmitted the proposal to IFW after incorporating above
suggestions for concurrence of the Planning Commission. The Secretary, DPE, further assured
the Committee that if these proposals are approved and implemented, it would lead to effective
utilization of funds for North Eastern Region for the purpose of capacity building of the State
level Public Sector Enterprises.
33. The Committee takes note of the fact that opportunities are now being created for
effective utilization of funds by the North Eastern Region. However, it regrets that the
failure on the part of the DPE to stick to standard budgetary proposal such as placing it
under the proper head, labeling the nature of scheme, etc., led to non-utilization of the
funds for such a long period. In this context, the Committee would like to observe that
development of the North Eastern Region must not suffer due to non adherence to standard
budgetary process. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department must take
measures to comply with such procedures and the proposals received from the States of
Assam and Sikkim must be taken up on a priority basis.
MoU System
34. The MoU regime has served the Public Sector Enterprises very well. The entire architecture
of MoU is based on negotiated agreement between the Government and the management of the
Enterprises specifying clearly the objective of the agreement and obligation of both the parties. The
MoU is used as a tool for assessment of performance of CPSEs against a predecided set of
objectives. The system was introduced in India in 1986 and underwent a major revamp in 2003.
The Committee has been informed by the Department that the MoU system is again set to undergo
a thorough revamp to make it more effective.
35. The Committee while analysis the working of the MoU system understood that
policies followed by the Government impact the performance of CPSEs. For instance, the
import policy of the Government allows import of capital goods and equipment to our
country in a more liberal manner with hardly any duty on the imported item. As a result,
the capacities of the domestic industry which includes the PSEs remain underutilized. Such
policies of the Government adversely affect the MoU performance of the PSEs. As a result,
the concerned PSEs get a poor rating for no fault of theirs. Accordingly, the Committee
recommends that while rating a PSE under a MoU regime the Government policy should be
included as a measurable parameter. In other words, the Government policies must be
factored in the process of evaluation of the MoU performance.

10
36. During the course of the discussion on Demands for Grants many industry associations
submitted the point before the Committee that in our country the level playing field between an
importer and domestic industry is not there. It was suggested that the concept of deemed imports
may be introduced for the goods or equipments supplied by the domestic supplier whose prices
are competitive with the global supplier. The idea that if the prices of the domestic supplier are
competitive of the global supplier, then the equipments supplied by the domestic supplier may be
described as deemed imports sounds good. The Committee is mindful of the fact that this is an
issue which involves the Ministry of Commerce. However, taking into account the larger issue of
Indian market where both the public and private sectors of our country are facing the absence of
a level playing field, the Committee strongly feels that the idea of deemed import may be introduced
for providing opportunities to the domestic industry and strengthening our indigenous industrial and
entrepreneurial base.
Annual Compliance Reports
37. DPE had issue guidelines on 29th July, 2010 that all CPSEs would submit Annual
Compliance Reports within 30 days from the end of the preceding financial year to their concerned
administrative Ministry/Department which in turn would furnish the consolidated Compliance Report
in respect of all CPSEs under their respective administrative control by 30th June every year to
DPE.
38. The Committee regrets to note that only 78 CPSEs have furnished ACRs till now.
The Committee observes that the efforts of DPE till now have failed to generate the desired
response from CPSEs. It is strongly felt that DPE should make all efforts to secure the
Annual Compliance Reports regarding implementation of DPEs guidelines from all CPSEs in
the country.
Revival and Restructuring of CPSEs
39. The CPSEs perform within the rules and guidelines framed by the Government and at the
same time are expected to remain competitive and generate profit in a highly globalised and market
environment. These are also expected to fulfill social objectives. It is not easy to show impressive
performance in such situations. The problem is further compounded by the fact that most of the
CPSEs suffer from structural inefficiencies which arise out of outdated technology, poor
management methods and overstaffing. As a result, many such CPSEs have been incurring huge
losses.
40. Two institutions take care of the revival and restructuring of sick and loss incurring CPSEs,
namely, the Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) and Board for Reconstruction
of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE). BIFR is a statutory body and considers those CPSEs whose
accumulated losses are equal to or have exceeded their net worth under the provisions of SICA
(Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985. The BRPSE on the other hand considers
CPSEs whose accumulated losses in any financial year is equal to 50% or more of its average net
worth during 4 years immediately preceding such financial year, and/or is a company within the
meaning of Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 (SICA).
41. During the discussion on Demand for Grants (2013-14), BRPSE submitted that it is
mandatory for them that they submit their recommendations on CPSEs referred to them by the
respective administrative Ministry within a period of two months. But, thereafter, Government takes
a time period ranging from 3 months to 4 years for acting on the recommendations of BRPSE.
However, while going through the materials furnished by BRPSE, it was found that revival of many
CPSEs are still pending with the Government despite the lapse of 6 years after the
recommendations of BRPSE. Regarding the reasons for delay on the part of the Government, the

11
representatives of BRPSE informed that the dichotomous policy prescriptions of successive
Governments are a major reason of delayed approval from the Government. Due to delay, the
revival packages have been rendered infructus and required another review by BRPSE. ( Annexure–I)
42. The Committee while taking note of the mechanism available for revival and
restructuring of CPSEs in India found that there is inordinate delay in getting approval
from the Government which is effecting revival proposals after receipts of recommendations
for revival from the BRPSE. In this regard, the Committee is of the firm opinion that this
state of affairs defeats the very purpose of revival. Delayed action by the Government
exceeding period upto 6 years can render the financial packages redundant. The highly
dynamic market environment in which the CPSEs operate also makes delayed revival
attempts meaningless. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that DPE should take
initiative to establish an appropriate time line for the Government to take action on the
revival recommendations of a sick CPSE.
Boards of PSEs
43. As the nodal Department of the CPSEs, DPE brings out policy guidelines on the Board
structure of CPSEs. Several initiatives had been taken for professionalization of Boards since the
economic liberalization of 1991. A detailed guideline which provided for the induction of Non
Official Directors (NODs) in the Boards of CPSEs was issued in 1992, which was reviewed in
December, 2012.
44. While examining Demands for Grants (2012-13), the Committee has found that there were
250 vacant positions of NODs on the Boards of more than 100 Scheduled CPSEs. Out of this,
the Search Committee recommended candidates to fill up 100 positions. When queried about the
status of implementation of the above recommendations of the Search Committee by the
administrative Ministries concerned, DPE submitted that they do not monitor the status of
vacancies after the recommendations of Search Committee have been conveyed to the
administrative Ministry/Department.
45. In the opinion of the Committee, it is imperative that the status of action taken by
the administrative Ministries or Departments on the recommendations of the Search
Committee needs to be invariably monitored. In this regard, it is recommended that DPE,
being the nodal Department and policy formulator responsible for the general functioning
of CPSEs, should be empowered to follow up the status of implementation of the
recommendation of the Search Committee for the appointment of the NODs. It is also
advisable that in the MoU signed by the concerned CPSEs must reflect the action taken by
the administrative Ministry in appointing NODs. The Government must also be held
accountable in filling up such vacancies.
46. The Public Enterprises Selection Board is part of the Department of Personnel and
Training. Last year the Committee had observed that such a scheme came into existence
when there was no Department of Public Enterprises. Now, that a full-fledged Department
of Public Enterprises is there in the Government it is important that the Public Enterprises
Selection Board must be made part of the Department. The Committee would like to
reiterate the recommendation which it made last year. The Committee strongly recommends
that such a change must take place for the purpose of streamlining and quickening the
process of succession planning in the PSEs. Apart from the PSEs and their administrative
Ministry, the domain knowledge concerning the functioning of the PSEs is with the DPE. It
finalizes their MoUs and sets their targets both in the financial and non-financial sectors.
It is, therefore, appropriate that PESB must function under the jurisdiction of DPE. At a

12
time when the Government of India is emphasizing on the need to reform the functioning
the Central Public Sector Enterprises, it is extremely important to include within the
reform process the decision to transfer the PESB from the control of DoPT to DPE.
Realizing the importance of the recommendation it must be done irrespective of any
resistance from any quarter.
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
47. The DPE guidelines on CSR for CPSEs require that all profit making CPSEs mandatorily
earmark, through a Board resolution, budgetary allocation as a percentage of Profit After Tax for
the previous financial year to undertake CSR activities. The administrative Ministries are expected
to monitor the CSR activities of their CPSEs. The MoU system also gives weightage to CSR
initiatives.
48. DPE submitted before the Committee the information furnished by Maharatana and
Navratana CPSEs on the funds allocated and utilized by them for CSR activities during 2010-11 and
2011-12 (Annexure-II).
49. While going through the information it was found that Coal India Ltd, ONGC and BHEL had
not utilized the funds allocated for CSR to a desirable level. The Secretary, DPE stated in this
regard that the new guidelines of DPE on CSR had come into force on 1st April, 2013 wherein
if there is a shortfall in spending the funds set aside for CSR, that amount will get deposited in
a Sustainability Fund operated by an implementation mechanism of the Government of India. The
Department expects this new measure to improve efficient utilization of CSR funds.
50. In the course of examination of DFG it was queried if the CPSEs have any difficulty in
funding good CSR projects and whether that was the reason for CSR funds remaining unspent.
In this regard, the DPE submitted that they were not aware of any such difficulty being faced by
the CPSEs. According to the Department, the CPSEs were free to take the help of the National
CSR Hub located at Tata Institute of Social Science (TISS), Mumbai to select suitable CSR
projects.
51. The Committee regrets to note that some of largest CPSEs in India are not utilizing
the funds earmarked for CSR activities. This can be viewed as an unhealthy trend having
a direct bearing on the commitment of the CPSEs towards India’s social and environmental
wellbeing. It is even more disheartening to note that this situation exists despite 5%
weightage being accorded to CPSEs for CSR activities in their MoU evaluation. Therefore,
the Committee observes that the Department of Public Enterprises has to take cognizance
of this aspect and keep a tab in the future efforts of these CPSEs to improve their
performance in this area. It is expected that the Sustainability Fund would evolve as a
handy tool in this process.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
1. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department of Public Enterprises has
paid heed to its recommendation to include R&D issue in the mission of the DPE and
accordingly the issue of R&D finds in an appropriate place in the mission statement of the
Department. (Para 6)
2. The Committee regrets that non-plan funds have been increased and the plan funds
have been reduced. The implication of this trend is that loans, salaries, interest payments,
etc., are getting more funds and schemes/projects/programmes which are central to the
functioning of the PSEs are not getting adequate budgetary allocation. It is even more
discouraging to find that only 50% of the curtailed allocation under plan funds could be
utilized by the Department with only a month remaining in the financial year. Analyzing the
broader picture, the Committee feels that the utilization figures of DPE under the plan head
could have been done with vision and foresight. In the Demands for Grants Report of the
Committee 2012-13 the Committee had observed that, “The Department must spend the
money put under the plan head to achieve the desired results.” It is rather unfortunate that
the funds earmarked for the plan category have not been utilized in spite of the
recommendation of the Committee to do so. (Para 11)
3. The Committee notes that the money earmarked for any scheme for the North
Eastern Region does not lapse. However, non-utilization of such money is a poor reflection
on the ability and expertise of the Department. The North Eastern part of India has always
been given special attention for its development and progress. Any scheme meant for that
region has to be seen in this broader context. While it is true that funds meant for schemes
of the North Eastern Region would be carried forward, it is equally important that
determined efforts need to be taken to use the funds allotted for a particular year. The
unutilized funds cannot be treated as ‘saving’. Rather, the Committee feels that such
unutilized funds are indicative of lack of seriousness of purpose and action on the part of
the Department. In case of money which remains unspent after meeting the objectives of
a scheme that money, in true sense of the term, can be called as savings. Accordingly, it
is recommended that that Ministry may use terms which should be exact in terms of
nomenclature and terminology. (Para 13)
4. The Committee notes that the Department could get only 68.98% of the Plan fund
sought for the Twelfth Plan period. Other than the flagship schemes of CRR, DPE has
relatively two new schemes such as Skill Development/Training programme of Executives of
State Level Public Enterprises and Scheme for Research, Development and Consultancy
(RDC) on Generic issues concerning CPSEs & SLPEs which have been approved. The
Committee notes that the DPE is going to review the scheme of CRR because of its poor
implementation. The Committee notes that the issue of skill development must be given top
priority. It is, therefore, important that paucity of funds should not come on the way of
effective achievement of targets fixed for the Twelfth Plan period. (Para 15)
5. The Committee notes that the CRR scheme has been an important initiative for the
welfare of the VRS optees of CPSEs. However, it is apparent that the scheme in its present
form is not serving the purpose for which it was created. The Committee is aware that the
DPE intends to reinvent the scheme by identifying fresh pockets of beneficiaries, revision
22

23
of course curriculum, national level certification of training, etc. The Committee
recommends an objective assessment of the scheme must be made. The Committee also
recommends that the Department must ensure that the VRS beneficiaries are properly
redeployed. In this context, it is strongly recommends to monitor the scheme and submit
a report to the Committee. (Para 22)
6. The Committee notes that the implementation of the scheme in the North Eastern
part of India is highly unsatisfactory. Year after year, the funds meant for the North
Eastern part are not utilized for implementation of the scheme and these are transferred
to the non lapsable pool without producing any significant results. This is not at all a
heartening development. The Department officials must be more sensitive to the North
Eastern Region. In this context, the Committee recommends that the revamped CRR
Scheme must be more effective in the North Eastern Region of our country. (Para 23)
7. In this regard, the Committee notes that the scheme which was proposed in 2009
could be finally approved only in January, 2013. It is also being observed that the
Department would do well to avoid any further delay in the implementation of the scheme.
The Committee also observes that the feedback of respective State Governments and State
level Public Sector Enterprises must be taken to further fine tune the scheme. Stress
should be laid for time bound implementation of the scheme and it should be reflected in
the Result-Framework Document of the Ministry/Department. (Para 27)
8. The Committee finds from the above table that since the beginning of the scheme
in 2008-09, there have been huge gaps between allocation and expenditure. However, the
Department maintained that they have been saving lot of funds allocated for the scheme.
The Committee notes that the Department intends to have a comprehensive re-look at the
scheme. The scheme has lot of potential which needs to be tapped for deriving maximum
benefit. In light of the above, it is recommended that a comprehensive reassessment of the
scheme has to be done on a priority basis and the efforts for publication of SLPEs survey
has to be given importance. (Para 30)
9. The Committee takes note of the fact that opportunities are now being created for
effective utilization of funds by the North Eastern Region. However, it regrets that the
failure on the part of the DPE to stick to standard budgetary proposal such as placing it
under the proper head, labeling the nature of scheme, etc., led to non-utilization of the
funds for such a long period. In this context, the Committee would like to observe that
development of the North Eastern Region must not suffer due to non adherence to standard
budgetary process. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department must take
measures to comply with such procedures and the proposals received from the States of
Assam and Sikkim must be taken up on a priority basis. (Para 33)
10. The Committee while analysis the working of the MoU system understood that
policies followed by the Government impact the performance of CPSEs. For instance, the
import policy of the Government allows import of capital goods and equipment to our
country in a more liberal manner with hardly any duty on the imported item. As a result,
the capacities of the domestic industry which includes the PSEs remain underutilized. Such
policies of the Government adversely affect the MoU performance of the PSEs. As a result,
the concerned PSEs get a poor rating for no fault of theirs. Accordingly, the Committee
recommends that while rating a PSE under a MoU regime the Government policy should be
included as a measurable parameter. In other words, the Government policies must be
factored in the process of evaluation of the MoU performance. (Para 35)

24
11. The Committee regrets to note that only 78 CPSEs have furnished ACRs till now.
The Committee observes that the efforts of DPE till now have failed to generate the desired
response from CPSEs. It is strongly felt that DPE should make all efforts to secure the
Annual Compliance Reports regarding implementation of DPEs guidelines from all CPSEs in
the country. (Para 38)
12. The Committee while taking note of the mechanism available for revival and
restructuring of CPSEs in India found that there is inordinate delay in getting approval
from the Government which is effecting revival proposals after receipts of recommendations
for revival from the BRPSE. In this regard, the Committee is of the firm opinion that this
state of affairs defeats the very purpose of revival. Delayed action by the Government
exceeding period upto 6 years can render the financial packages redundant. The highly
dynamic market environment in which the CPSEs operate also makes delayed revival
attempts meaningless. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that DPE should take
initiative to establish an appropriate time line for the Government to take action on the
revival recommendations of a sick CPSE. (Para 42)
13. In the opinion of the Committee, it is imperative that the status of action taken by
the administrative Ministries or Departments on the recommendations of the Search
Committee needs to be invariably monitored. In this regard, it is recommended that DPE,
being the nodal Department and policy formulator responsible for the general functioning
of CPSEs, should be empowered to follow up the status of implementation of the
recommendation of the Search Committee for the appointment of the NODs. It is also
advisable that in the MoU signed by the concerned CPSEs must reflect the action taken by
the administrative Ministry in appointing NODs. The Government must also be held
accountable in filling up such vacancies. (Para 45)
14. The Public Enterprises Selection Board is part of the Department of Personnel and
Training. Last year the Committee had observed that such a scheme came into existence
when there was no Department of Public Enterprises. Now, that a full-fledged Department
of Public Enterprises is there in the Government it is important that the Public Enterprises
Selection Board must be made part of the Department. The Committee would like to
reiterate the recommendation which it made last year. The Committee strongly recommends
that such a change must take place for the purpose of streamlining and quickening the
process of succession planning in the PSEs. Apart from the PSEs and their administrative
Ministry, the domain knowledge concerning the functioning of the PSEs is with the DPE. It
finalizes their MoUs and sets their targets both in the financial and non-financial sectors.
It is, therefore, appropriate that PESB must function under the jurisdiction of DPE. At a
time when the Government of India is emphasizing on the need to reform the functioning
the Central Public Sector Enterprises, it is extremely important to include within the
reform process the decision to transfer the PESB from the control of DoPT to DPE.
Realizing the importance of the recommendation it must be done irrespective of any
resistance from any quarter. (Para 46)
15. The Committee regrets to note that some of largest CPSEs in India are not utilizing
the funds earmarked for CSR activities. This can be viewed as an unhealthy trend having
a direct bearing on the commitment of the CPSEs towards India’s social and environmental
wellbeing. It is even more disheartening to note that this situation exists despite 5%
weightage being accorded to CPSEs for CSR  activities in their MoU evaluation. Therefore,
the Committee observes that the Department of Public Enterprises has to take cognizance
of this aspect and keep a tab in the future efforts of these CPSEs to improve their
performance in this area. It is expected that the Sustainability Fund would evolve as a
handy tool in this process. (Para 51)

REPORT
The capital goods and engineering industry constitute the building block of our economy.
A strong capital goods sector is indicative of the health and vibrancy of a robust market. Rights
since our independence our leadership accorded priority to build capital goods industry by setting
up key public sector units. In the economic environment of 21
st century India, it is the private
sector which is driving the growth and development. However, it is found that the public sector
units are as relevant in the private sector led economy as they were in the mixed economy of the
1950s. The engineering and capital goods PSEs assume critical role in nation building.
 2. The Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) under the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises is the nodal department of the Heavy Industries Sector in India, which can be generally
classified into two broad segments, Capital Goods and Equipments. The Department deals with
nineteen industrial sub-sectors that comprise of boilers, cement and dairy machinery, electrical
furnace, freight containers, material heading equipments, metallurgical and mining machinery,
machine tools, oil field equipment, printing, pulp and paper machinery, rubber machinery,
switchgear and control gear, locomotive, sugar machinery, turbine and generator set, transformers
and textile machinery. Besides these, the very important sector of automobiles is also under the
oversight of DHI.
3. The Heavy Industries sector in India has quite a few important CPSEs, the number of
which adds up to thirty two under the administrative control of Department of Heavy Industry. Of
these, eighteen are profit making and fourteen incur losses, currently. The performance of the
heavy industries sector is a crucial marker of the total industrial growth of the country. Therefore,
the Government makes continuous efforts to create a facilitative environment for this sector
through initiatives like NATRiP, the Automotive Mission Plan 2006-16, the National Electric
Mortality Plan 2020, Schemes for Modernization of Capital Goods Sector, etc.
4. The growth of the user industries like infrastructure, oil and gas power, mining,
automotives steel and consumer durable are key to the health of the heavy industries sector. The
Government’s thrust on these areas coupled with India being seen as an outsourcing destination by
global companies due to lower labour cost and availability of quality manpower acts as growth
drivers of this important sector.

the BE for 2012-13 of Rs. 25.00 crore was curtailed to Rs. 20.00 crore at the RE stage, as only
four months of the financial year were left. The DHI is of the opinion that the BE has to be
enhanced as number of R&D proposals are in pipeline to be implemented. The on-going scheme
of Research and Development of Automotive Industry is under review in the Technical Committee
and Cess Committee. Further, DHI also submitted that it can utilize more than Rs. 24.00 crore
under the head in 2013-14 as adequate number of shelf of projects/schemes are ready for
implementation.
16. Though the Committee takes into consideration that funds for 2011-12 (Rs. 18.30 crore)
were released in the last month of the financial year, it remains a fact that the Department
could not fully utilize this amount till November, 2012. The Department has quoted this
underutilization as the reason for curtailment of funds for the year 2012-13. In this context,
the Committee is of the opinion that if DHI faced any problem for the release of funds from
the Ministry of Finance that could have been taken up at the appropriate juncture. Once
funds are released there cannot be an excuse for under-utilization as the attainment of the
defined objectives would be affected, especially, in an area as important as R&D. Further,
under this scheme till February, 2013 out of the Rs. 20 crore (RE), no money has been
actually allocated. Accordingly, the Committee is constrained to note that the R&D has been

5
compromised by not getting the amount released for the year 2012-13. Therefore, the
Committee recommends that the Department should take strong measures to avoid a
repetition of this mistake in future and impress upon the Ministry of Finance for prompt
release of funds. Also, the Committee is hopeful that the review of the ongoing scheme will
help the Department to grapple with the problems that it faced earlier.
National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP)
17. NATRiP envisages setting up of world –class automotive testing and homologation facilities
in India. Its principal facilities will come up in the three automotive hubs of India, in the south,
north and west. The project aims at (i) creating critically needed automotive testing infrastructure
to enable the Government in ushering in global vehicular safety, emission and performance
standards, (ii) deepening manufacturing in India, promoting larger value addition leading to
significant enhancement of employment potential and facilitating convergence of India’s strengths
in IT and electronics with automotive engineering, (iii) enhancing India’s considerably low global
outreach in this sector by de-bottlenecking exports and (iv) removing the crippling absence of basic
product testing, validation and development infrastructure for automotive industry. The scheme was
introduced in August, 2005, with an investment of Rs. 1718 crore and it was to be completed by
30.09.2011. Thereafter, Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), in its meeting held on
5.4.2011, revised the project completion date to 31.12.2012 along with the revised cost estimate
to Rs. 2288 crore. However, it is understood that the scheduled date of completion of the project
is again proposed to be extended by a couple of years to 31.12.2014. It is not clear whether there
will be also be a further revision of the cost.
18. The BE 2012-2013 for NATRiP was Rs. 488.48 crore which was reduced to Rs. 341.94
crore in RE stage. During 2012-13, an amount of Rs. 341.94 crore has been released to NATRiP
on 28.9.2012 and the actual expenditure made was Rs. 146.54 crore. Representatives of NATRiP
informed the Committee that allocation of Rs. 341.94 crore of 2013-14 is not sufficient and
informed that Rs. 753.19 crore is required for effective achievement of targets for the project for
the year. The Committee notes that a cumulative amount of Rs. 1512.38 crore has been released
for NATRiP till Jan, 2013. Out of this, the Department could utilize Rs. 1246.32 crore till January,
2013. Considering that the total funds earmarked for NATRiP is Rs. 2288.06 crore and that the
Cabinet would grant extension of time completion till Dec., 2014, an amount of Rs. 775.68 crore
remains to be released within 2 years.
