20. The Committee notes that DHI’s flagship project of NATRiP has been severely plagued
by delays and cost overruns. The main reasons for the delays as cited by Department of Heavy
Industry are delay in acquisition of land and clearance and shifting of utility. Moreover, the
Committee is extremely disturbed to observe that the Actual expenditure year wise since
2005-06 for NATRiP has been abysmal. Barring one year (2008-09), the Actual expenditure has
been well below 50% of the corresponding RE figures. After an analysis of this scenario, the
Committee observes that the performance of the planning machinery for NATRiP has not
been satisfactory and lack of long term vision has crippled the implementation of the scheme,
which has been one of the most awaited projects of the automobile sector. The Committee
recommends that at least at this late point in time, in comparison with the original date of
completion, NATRiP should strictly adhere to the revised completion date of December, 2014

Modernization of Capital Goods Sector (CGS)
21. The Capital Good Sector contributes 12% to the total manufacturing Capacity (approximately
15% of GDP) of India. Accordingly, the domestic CG Industry would be having a size of $30 billion.
However, India’s import dependence in CGS is increasing over the years and stands close to $45
billion in a year. In view of this, the CG Sector is identified as a strategic sector by National
Manufacturing Competition Council (NMCC). Despite, such acknowledgments a lack of long term
road map to develop indigenous manufacturing base in this sector is a glaring lacuna.
22. Some of the important reasons isolated by the Department for the laggard performance of
the CG sector in India are:
(1) Lack of world class cutting edge technology and no R&D initiatives;
(2) Increasing trend in import of capital goods including second hand capital goods in
some sub sectors, e.g., shuttle less looms;
(3) Lack of skilled manpower;
(4) Lack of level playing field vis-à-vis global players.
23. Taking these issues on board, DHI has introduced a Scheme for enhancement of
competitiveness of the Indian Capital Goods Industry on the basis of recommendations of the
working group on Capital Goods and Engineering Sector. The components of the scheme include
setting up of infrastructural facilities, e.g., common facility centre, product development centre,
industrial cluster park, etc. The Scheme also envisages setting up of such facilities for several
sectors of capital goods, e.g., Machine Tools sector, Earthmoving and Construction Machinery and
Textile Machinery. The Department has also been raising the issue of second hand import of capital
goods with NMCC and Ministry of Textiles. A meeting of the Committee of Secretaries took place
in May, 2012 which recommended several measures to arrest the growth of second hand imports
in capital goods sector. DHI has also been taking follow up action on this as well as on the issue
of zero import duty on construction machinery which are being made indigenously.
24. Regarding the current status of the scheme, the DHI submitted to the Committee that in
January 2013 Planning Commission communicated in principle approval for the Scheme and a
budgetary allocation of Rs.1081.22 crore for the Scheme has been made during 12
th FYP. DHI also
placed before the Committee that a plan is already in place to efficiently utilize the BE of Rs. 70.00
crore for the year 2013-14 under the scheme, by preparation of Detailed Project Report for
implementing the many components of the scheme. The various industrial associations who were
heard by the Committee during the course of discussion for Demand for Grants 2013-14 also
emphasized the importance of successful implementation of this scheme.

7
25. The Committee finds that though the scheme for Enhancement of the Competitiveness
of the Capital Goods Sector was originally slated to have been in operation during 2012-13,
the inprinciple approval of the Planning Commission was obtained only in January, 2013. Now
that a beginning has been made, it is expected that DHI will strive to attain all the
parameters intended for 2013-14 by effective use of Rs. 70.00 crore provided for the Scheme.
The Committee observes that considering the magnitude of the problem faced by the CG
Sector in India and the enormity of the steps to be taken to counter these problems, the
Twelfth Five Year Plan allocation of Rs. 1081.22 crore looks highly inadequate. Meanwhile, it
is felt that while Government can play the role of facilitator and take the initiatives as it has
already done, the participation of the private sector can also to be roped in to achieve the
modernization of the CG Sector of the country at appropriate juncture. The Committee also
takes into cognizance the apprehensions expressed by various industry associations about the
Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs) being inked by the
Government of India with various countries. Therefore, it is recommended that the
Government should take all necessary steps to protect the interests of our Capital Goods
industry as well as the domestic industry as a whole, while entering into such agreements.
26. The problem of capital good industries of our country is compounded by the dumping of
capital goods from many other countries like China and South Korea. Many industry associations
who appeared before the Committee expressed grave concern on this issue. The Committee notes
that the import policy is determined by the Ministry of Commerce and other concerned Ministries.
Import duties on the capital goods imported from abroad is quite less. As a result, the domestic
industry consisting of the private and public sector units are suffering very badly. The Committee
strongly recommends that the Government of India must impose duties on imported capital
goods as per the WTO agreement. It is understood that by adhering to the provisions of
the WTO agreement, we can protect the domestic capital industry which is central to our
industrial activities and technological capability and security. The Committee wants the
Department of Heavy Industry to place the recommendation of the Committee while taking
up this issue with the concerned Ministries.
Scooters India Ltd. (SIL)
27. The Scooters India Ltd. is a company engaged in designing, manufacturing and marketing of
three wheelers, their spares and engineering goods. SIL is the only automobile company in the country
operating in the Public Sector. Incorporated in 1972, it was first declared sick by BIFR in 2010 and
thereafter was referred to BRPSE. In line with the recommendations of BRPSE, the Government
decided to identify a strategic partner for SIL through a resolution in Parliament. However, the resolution
introduced in Monsoon Session 2011 was withdrawn under directions from Prime Minister’s Office and
also on account of several representations. Subsequently, a revised revival proposal for SIL was
prepared and placed before the Cabinet on 19.05.2012, which was approved.
28. The following are the salient features of the Revival Plan:–
1. To infuse fund of Rs. 70.38 crore as equity by GOI for capital expenditure.
2. To provide Rs. 20 crore as interest free plan loan by GOI for working capital. The
plan loan may be recovered in 5 equal annual instalments commencing from
31.03.2015 after moratorium of three years.
3. To convert plan loan of Rs. 1.93 crore, outstanding as on 31
st March, 2012 into equity.
4. To convert non plan loan of Rs. 83.28 crore outstanding as on 31 st March, 2012 into
equity.
5. To waive interest accrued and due of Rs. 22.17 crore as on 31 st March, 2012.

8
6. To waive interest accrued and not due of Rs. 4.20 crore as on 31 st March, 2012.
7. Enhancement of superannuation age from 58 years to 60 years in relaxation of DPE
guidelines.
8. Implementation of 2007 Pay Revision as per DPE guidelines.
29. As part of the examination of Demand for Grants, the Committee interacted with
representatives of various PSEs including, SIL. During the discussion, the representative of SIL
submitted that the business of the Company was severely hampered as the permits for three
wheelers were controlled by State Governments through their Regional Transport Authorities.
30. Regarding the revival of SIL, the Committee feels that along with prompt and time
bound execution of the revival plan, it is important that the matter of three wheeler
permits controlled by the Regional Transport Authorities of State Governments is also given
urgent attention. The Committee recommends that the following two requests of SIL shared
with the Committee shall be examined and given due consideration as these aspects are
important for the future business prospects of SIL.
(a) The permits for three wheelers in passenger categories (6+1) may be released
as per the demand/need of the city/town and in a way should be deregulated and
decontrolled as is the case with four wheelers and two wheelers.
(b) The State Governments and Registration authorities may be advised to release
passenger permits for three wheelers in 6+1 category for outside city limits
areas where Hon’ble Courts has enforced a ban. This assumes significance as
the city buses which occupy more volume/space on roads because of its designs
features could not provide last mile solution to common man and where only
three wheelers can approach because of its design and constructional advantages.

coordination is missing. However, the Committee was informed by the officials of the DHI
that instead of going to the court the inter-departmental dispute mechanism available in the
Cabinet Secretariat may be used to sort out the issues among Ministries. The Committee got
the assurance from the Secretary, DHI that he would look into it. The Committee strongly
recommends that the matters involving several PSEs must be resolved in a time bound
manner for the completion of the projects and for improving the efficiency and performance
of the PSEs. The Committee would like to get a detailed report in this respect from the DHI.
Heavy Engineering Corporation (HEC)
39. The HEC Ltd. was incorporated on 31
st December, 1958 for the manufacturing of steel

10
plant equipments. The company never performed well financially till the year 2005. Due to the
inability of the company to face challenges of economic liberalization of 1991, the Company was
referred to BIFR in February 1992. The revival plan proposed therein did not take off. However,
another plan was submitted to BRPSE in September, 2005, with the initiatives of DHI. The plan
was approved by the Government in December, 2005 and by the High Court of Jharkhand in
November, 2009.
40. The Committee notes that HEC has been making profit, though small, since 2006-07. The
sales performance of the Company has increased from Rs.178.18 crore in 2005-06 to Rs. 759.75
crore in 2012-13. However, it is given to understand that the achievements of the HEC comes from
operations of outdated plants and machinery and it will not be able to sustain the marginal profits
for a very long time without modernization and upgradation of those plants and machinery.
Meanwhile, a Working Group under the Secretary, DHI has recommended the Planning Commission
to build HEC as a National Champion.
41. Subsequently, the modernisation plan of the HEC to be undertaken at a cost of Rs.1516.13
crore during the 12
th Five Year Plan has been cut down to Rs.763.66 crore, owing to downward
revision of the allocations for DHI. Out of this, budgetary support is for Rs.350 crore and Rs.300
crore is allotted for EBR (loan from FI) and Rs.113.66 crore is to be generated internally. In tune
with this a budgetary support of Rs.200 crore was sought for 2013-14, against which only a token
provision Rs.0.01 crore has been kept aside for HEC in the Budget. Meanwhile, HEC is trying to
complete the Techno Economic Viability (TEV) Report and Detailed Project Report (DPR). If the
required approvals from Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance come through, the Company
hopes to seek more funds during the supplementary demand.
42. The Committee views the case of HEC as a classic example of turn around of a
CPSE, through a revival package. The progress the HEC has achieved despite obsolete
technology and machinery inspires confidence that the PSEs can do much better with
upgradation of plant and machinery. Accordingly, the Committee is of the firm opinion that
HEC has earned the right to seek budgetary support and necessary funds for capital
expenditure without which it would not be possible for the HEC to increase its production.
The Committee strongly recommends that the Government and the Planning Commission
must extend all support to the HEC to emerge as a role model in the public sector. If the
HEC can show impressive results by using obsolete technology then it is quite sure that it
can show much better results by using modern and updated equipments. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry, Ministry of Finance and the
Planning Commission should expedite the requisite approval for timely infusion of funds to
the HEC. Timely support to HEC will send a positive message to all CPSEs. The HEC, on
their part should be ready with the TEV and DPR at the earliest.
43. Many PSUs are incurring losses. Government has plans to revive them. There are many
steps which are taken to revive a sick industry. It involves going to Board for Reconstruction of
Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSC), Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR), the
Cabinet and consultation with experts and other concerned people. The Committee found that such
a long drawn out process takes lot of time and in the process the calculation of the cost for revival
is done several times. As a result, the cost goes up. The Committee strongly recommends that
decision in such matters must be taken on time.
Issues placed before the Committee by the Industry and Auto Associations
44. The Committee heard the views of various associations like ASSOCHAM, FICCI, CII,
ACMA, SIAM, IMTMA,  etc., as part of the examination of Demands for Grants, 2013-14, to get
the views of the industrial units of the private sector.

11
45. The collective grievance of the industry included lack of the level playing field in the
capital good sector which rendered domestic companies uncompetitive. The import of second
hand machinery compounded these problems. The industry was also extremely worried about the
signing of Foreign Trade Agreements (FTAs) and Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs) with
various countries that would lead to lower or nil import duties and other countries routing their
products through FTA countries. Lack of effective R&D, absence of necessary infrastructure and
shortage of skilled manpower weakened the capability of the Indian industry to compete at the
global level. It was also submitted before the Committee that the educational institutions
particularly the engineering colleges do not produce the required skilled youth who would be
useful to the industry. The Committee suggested that the industry associations should
interact with the educational institutions in developed curricula to minimize the gap
between skill requirement and availability. The Committee also suggested that a core
group of the industry consisting of selected skilled people may draft educational curricula
and send it to all educational institutions for their adoption and incorporation in the
syllabus for engineering students.
46. The industry associations wanted our embassies abroad to inform through their websites
opportunities available in foreign countries to do business. They pointed out that no such
consolidation information is available in the website of the MEA or the website of our
embassies.
47. The industry associations also put their specific grievances before the Committee. The auto
industry associations referred to the lack of standardization in the auto components and demanded
adoption of standards for auto components in the pattern of European countries. Some of the
associations stated that they have been launching a campaign called Asli Naqli  to sensitise the
buyers of auto components about the genuineness of auto parts. The Committee commends such
initiative and recommends that the Government must take measures for standardization of
auto components.  The bottlenecks in the Construction equipment industry included lack of speedy
project implementation, import of second-hand machinery and lack of tariff and non-tariff
incentives. The issues bothering Textile machinery sector included cheap and second-hand Chinese
machinery, duty reduction on shuttle less looms, price disadvantage to local manufactures, lack of
R&D support and absence of FDI, etc.
48. The Auto associations of the country also placed many issues of relevance before the
Committee. These related to demand for reduction in excise duty on vehicles and SUVs, help of
Government to overcome difficulties in valuation of excisable goods, inclusion of automobile CBU
(completely built up units) trade in FTA with EU, etc. The points raised by the Auto component
industry included interest subvention for technology upgradation and development, export
allowances, input credit on diesel, protection while entering into FTAs, encouragement for in-house
R&D, increase in depreciation rate in the cost of plant and machinery, etc.
49. Having heard the grievances of both the industry and auto associations, the Committee
understands that certain problems cut across all sectors of industry be it in the private or in
the public sector. Of the most pressing issues is the low duty on imported goods, in adequate
R&D, import of secondhand Capital Goods, free trade agreements and skill deficit. The
Committee recommends that the domestic industry must be protected and in this regard the
Government can take sufficient measures by following the WTO norms. The Committee is
also of the firm opinion that due consideration should be given to the suggestions put forth
by the Committee of Secretaries in its meeting held on 23
rd May, 2012 for letting NMCC
separately examine the impact of FTAs on domestic industries and thereafter to have an
inter-ministerial consultations on those findings. The Committee, in tune with the industry’s
interests, favours non-tariff trade barriers and effective implementation of the Scheme for
Modernization of the Capital Goods Sector to strengthen the indigenous industry.

urgent attention. The Committee recommends that the following two requests of SIL shared
with the Committee shall be examined and given due consideration as these aspects are
important for the future business prospects of SIL.
(a) The permits for three wheelers in passenger categories (6+1) may be released
as per the demand/need of the city/town and in a way should be deregulated and
decontrolled as is the case with four wheelers and two wheelers.
(b) The State Governments and Registration authorities may be advised to release
passenger permits for three wheelers in 6+1 category for outside city limits
areas where Hon’ble Courts has enforced a ban. This assumes significance as
the city buses which occupy more volume/space on roads because of its designs

14
features could not provide last mile solution to common man and where only
three wheelers can approach because of its design and constructional advantages.
(Para 30)
8. The Committee finds that BHEL’s IEBR figures during 2011-12, 2012-13 and 2013-14
are at variance with the corresponding figures in expenditure budget supplied by DHI.
Accordingly, the Committee observes that such difference in figures should have been
reconciled with the Department and thereafter presented before Committee along with an
explanation. The Department also, on their part should have noticed the variance in figures
and taken it up with BHEL. (Para 34)
9. Since, the IEBR figures of BHEL are at variance, the Committee refrains from
commenting on it. But the reasons quoted for the shortfall in IEBR figures for 2011-12 and
2012-13 are common. The Committee observes that the BHEL should take measures to
address the problem which has caused shortfall. The Committee feels that the avoidable
delay cited by the BHEL should not be allowed to spill over to another year by a Maharatana
Company like a BHEL. (Para 35)
10. In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the DHI, which is the
administrative Department for BHEL should extend all support to the efforts of the
company to convince the Ministry of Defence regarding the relevance and utility of the
BHEL for the defence sector. It is expected that the presentation to be made by BHEL
before the Ministry of Defence, in presence of Hon’ble Minister of HI and PE would be a
beginning in this regard. Besides, the BHEL must further expand its activities for
generating power from renewable sources of energy. (Para 37)
11. The Committee observed that there are many problems involving BHEL, Rashtriya
Ispat Nigam Ltd., Neyveil Lignite Corporation, etc. It is understood that the orders placed
by many PSEs with the BHEL are not being completed in time. As a result, several PSEs
are not able to improve their performance. The Committee is constrained to note that the
inter PSE coordination is missing. However, the Committee was informed by the officials of
the DHI that instead of going to the court the inter-departmental dispute mechanism
available in the Cabinet Secretariat may be used to sort out the issues among Ministries.
The Committee got the assurance from the Secretary, DHI that he would look into it. The
Committee strongly recommends that the matters involving several PSEs must be resolved
in a time bound manner for the completion of the projects and for improving the efficiency
and performance of the PSEs. The Committee would like to get a detailed report in this
respect from the DHI. (Para 38)
12. The Committee views the case of HEC as a classic example of turn around of a
CPSE, through a revival package. The progress the HEC has achieved despite obsolete
technology and machinery inspires confidence that the PSEs can do much better with
upgradation of plant and machinery. Accordingly, the Committee is of the firm opinion that
HEC has earned the right to seek budgetary support and necessary funds for capital
expenditure without which it would not be possible for the HEC to increase its production.
The Committee strongly recommends that the Government and the Planning Commission
must extend all support to the HEC to emerge as a role model in the public sector. If the
HEC can show impressive results by using obsolete technology then it is quite sure that it
can show much better results by using modern and updated equipments. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry, Ministry of Finance and the
Planning Commission should expedite the requisite approval for timely infusion of funds to
the HEC. Timely support to HEC will send a positive message to all CPSEs. The HEC, on
their part should be ready with the TEV and DPR at the earliest. (Para 42)

15
13. The Committee strongly recommends that decision in such matters must be taken on
time. (Para 43)
14. The Committee suggested that the industry associations should interact with the
educational institutions in developed curricula to minimize the gap between skill
requirement and availability. The Committee also suggested that a core group of the
industry consisting of selected skilled people may draft educational curricula and send it to
all educational institutions for their adoption and incorporation in the syllabus for
engineering students. (Para 45)
15. The Committee commends such initiative and recommends that the Government
must take measures for standardization of auto components. (Para 47)
16.  Having heard the grievances of both the industry and auto associations, the
Committee understands that certain problems cut across all sectors of industry be it in the
private or in the public sector. Of the most pressing issues is the low duty on imported
goods, in adequate R&D, import of second-hand Capital Goods, free trade agreements and
skill deficit. The Committee recommends that the domestic industry must be protected and
in this regard the Government can take sufficient measures by following the WTO norms.
The Committee is also of the firm opinion that due consideration should be given to the
suggestions put forth by the Committee of Secretaries in its meeting held on 23
rd May, 2012
for letting NMCC separately examine the impact of FTAs on domestic industries and
thereafter to have an inter-ministerial consultations on those findings. The Committee, in
tune with the industry’s interests, favours non-tariff trade barriers and effective
implementation of the Scheme for Modernization of the Capital Goods Sector to strengthen
the indigenous industry. (Para 49)

REPORT
Overview of the MSME sector
1. Fourth Census of MSME (2006-07) estimates provide insight into the composition and
structure of MSME sector in the country. Estimated 361.76 lakh units provide employment to
805.24 lakh persons at an average of 2.23 persons per unit with fixed investment of Rs 6.90 lakh
crore. 55 % of units are located in rural areas. 7.36% of the Units are owned by the women. 95%
of the enterprises are proprietary organizations.
2. 67% of the registered MSME enterprises were engaged in manufacturing whereas 33%
were involved in service sector. However, the situation was opposite in case of unregistered units,
of which 70% were engaged in service activities and remaining 30% in manufacturing business.
Among the Registered enterprises about 55% employment was located in urban areas whereas
remaining 45% was located in rural areas. The situation was opposite in case of unregistered
enterprises where rural enterprises provided for about 56% of employment, and remaining 44%
employment was in urban areas.
3. Between the third All India Census of SSI (2001-02) and the Fourth Census (2006-07), in
terms of number of enterprises and employment the sector grew at an impressive annual
compounded growth rate of 28% and 26.42% respectively. Though the scope of the sector was
greatly enhanced with the inclusion of micro, small and medium enterprises.
4. In terms of number of enterprises and employment potential retail trade including repair of
household and consumer goods is the leading industry. Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu
are the three leading states in terms of number of enterprises and employment.
5. Another important indicator of growing prominence of this sector in economy, is
exponential growth in filing of Entrepreneur Memorandum–II after the commencement of a project.
The number of EM II have grown from 1.74 lakh in 2007 after the commencement of the MSMED
Act, 2006 to 2.82 lakh in 2011-12. The most encouraging sign has been exponential growth of
EM-II in Micro sector, from 1.56 lakhs in 2007-08 to 2.42 lakh in 2011-12.
6. The Chairman of the Committee recognized the comment made in the Economic Survey
(2012-13) that “too many firms in India stay small, unregistered, unincorporated, largely informal
or in the unorganized sector because they can avoid regulations and taxes. These firms have little
incentive to invest in upgrading skills of largely temporary workers or investing in capital equipment
that could bring them into tax net, so their productivity stays low.”
7. The Committee also took cognizance of the incentives given to firms to grow, in this years
Budget. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech announced “To encourage them to grow, I
propose that the benefits or preferences enjoyed by them will stay with them upto three years after
they grow out of the category in which they obtained the benefit. To begin with I propose that
the non-tax benefits may be made available to a MSME unit for three years after it graduates to
a higher category.” In his submission before the Committee, the DC, MSME sought extension of
Tax benefits as well.
8. The Committee recognises that Section 8 of the MSME Development Act, 2006 makes
filing of memorandum optional for micro, small and those medium enterprises engaged in
service sector. However, in view of large number of un-registered units, who are excluded
from the benefits given to registered units, the Committee recommends that registration of
MSME units should be encouraged. The Ministry should make registration simple and

2
nonintrusive.  It should facilitate online registration of unregistered units. The  Ministry
should also take the help of industry associations in this regard. The Committee also
recommends that in addition to non-tax benefits as announced in the Budget, tax benefits
too should be extended to the Units who have graduated from their category.
Allocations and Utilisation
9. In year 2010-11, Rs. 2648.70 crores was the allocated to the Ministry at BE stage which
was raised to Rs. 2678.95 crores at RE stage. However, actual expenditure was Rs. 2552.67
crores, with significant under-utilisation of Planned allocation.
10. Similarly in year 2011-12, total Rs. 3001.29 crores were allocated at BE stage, which was
reduced to Rs. 2759.25 crores at RE stage. The actual expenditure was Rs. 2240.42 crores, which
was about Rs. 500 crores lower than the Revised Estimates. Again, there was significant under-
utilisation of Planned allocation.
11. In 2012-13 too, the Ministry demanded about Rs. 6379 crores as Planned expenditure but
was allocated Rs. 2835 crores in BE, which was reduced at RE stage to Rs. 2542 crores and
provisional expenditure in the year has been only about Rs. 2257 crores, a gap of almost Rs. 4000
crores between demand and actual utilization.
12. It was informed that the Ministry had proposed a plan outlay of Rs.5263.61 crore for
2013-14. However, the Planning Commission has reduced the outlay and allocated Rs.2977.00 crore
only.
13. The Committee notes with reservation that despite its critical observation in 235th
Report on Demands for Grants for the Ministry for 2012-13, regarding non-utilisation of
funds and its recommendation that Ministry must use the money allocated to it for meeting
its targets, the situation in 2012-13 remained the same. Scarce funds still remain un-
utilised. The Committee has always supported Ministry’s demand for more funds as it
considered MSME sector critical for the inclusive and equitable socioeconomic development.
However, it observes a consistent under- utilization funds. The Committee reiterates its
reservation over possible pattern of inflated demands by the Ministry.
Achievement of targets as given in Outcome Budget (2012-13)
14. The Committee also noted that despite massive under-utilisation of funds, the annual
achievements have been exceeding the target. For year 2012-13, in case of Assistance to Training
Institutions upto 31st December 2012, only Rs. 35 crores out of allocated Rs. 71 crores were
spent. However, as per the Annual Report (2012-13) of the Ministry 1,75,315 persons were trained
against annual target of 55000. The Outcome Budget put the figure at 1.41 lakh persons. Under
Rajiv Gandhi Udyami Mitra Yojna, upto 31st December 2012, 8465 new Udyamis were registered
against the target of 3000 with an expenditure of Rs. 1.37 crores out of Budget allocation of
Rs. 3 crores.
15. In case of Village Industries Grant Rs. 20.77 crores out of Budget allocation of Rs. 74.84
crores was spent upto 31st December 2012, which was less than a third of allocation but 70%
of production and Sales targets and 90% of employment targets were already met.
16. Similarly, in case of Khadi grants upto 31st December 2012, only Rs. 64.64 crores was
spent out of Revised allocation of 168.90 crores, however 70% of the production target, 75% of
the sales targets and 90% of employment targets were met with that amount. On the other hand,
in case of PMEGP, Rs. 914.28 crores out of annual allocation of Rs. 1276.28 crores had been
spent by 31.12.2012 but only 35% target in terms of projects assisted and employment

3
opportunities were created. However if compared with performance in PMEGP for previous year
2011-12, 128% of the target in terms of project assisted and 115% of target in terms of
employment opportunities was achieved with Rs. 1057 crores as against Revised allocation of
Rs. 1215.95 crores. The Committee has reason to be circumspect about the figures provided
by the Ministry. There have been year-end rush in spending the allocation. There is
legitimate apprehension about the quality of expenditure. Also, in view of excessive
achievement with lesser actual expenditure, the Committee apprehends if annual targets are
kept at modest levels vis a vis annual budgetary allocations.
17. The Committee took note that the Economic Survey 2012-13 stated that the PM’s Task
Force on MSME would be the basis of XII Plan Policy Framework. It sought to know the status
of implementation of these recommendations of the Task Force during the XII Plan period
considering that the Task Force had even identified nodal Ministries/Departments to implement its
recommendations and had also indicated deadlines.
18. The Ministry informed that the Prime Minister’s Task Force (PMTF) made 85
recommendations under various areas including credit, marketing, labour, rehabilitation and exit
policy, infrastructure/technology/skill development, taxation and special measure for North-Eastern
Region and Jammu & Kashmir. Out of the 85 recommendations action on 39 recommendations
have been completed, recommendations dropped/delinked. It was informed that to monitor
implementation of the recommendations, a Steering Group under the Chairmanship of Principal
Secretary has been constituted.
19. However, the Development Commissioner, MSME, in its oral evidence before the Committee
on the 16th April, 2013, submitted that there were significant slippages in Task Force’s
recommendation in respect of 10% Year on Year hike in terms of micro enterprise accounts and
volume of credit. And that the micro enterprises accounts were actually coming down in case of
certain bigger Public Sector Banks.
20. The Committee may be informed about the eight recommendations that have been
dropped/delinked and rationale for dropping the same. The Committee may also be informed
about the status of implementation of remaining recommendations through the Action
Taken Note. The Ministry must closely work with the Steering Committee in implementing
the recommendations. The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the prominent
Public Sector Banks are not adhering to the recommendations of PM’s Task Force and RBI
guidelines in respect of credit to Micro sector. It recommends the Ministry to take up the
issue with RBI and Steering Committee.
Demands for Grants 2013-14
21. The Committee took note of the composition of the Ministry’s expenditure. There is a huge
gap between proposed Revenue (Rs. 3210.91 crores) and Capital expenditure (Rs. 78 crores) on
one hand. On the other hand there is equally large gap between proposed Planned (Rs. 2977
crores) and Non-planned (312.71 crores) expenditures.
22. In previous years, except for 2012-13 only when Non-Planned Revenue expenditures
increased from BE to RE stage and the Actual expenditure exceeded even the revised
estimates, in other categories of allocations like Planned Revenue and Capital and Non-
Planned Capital have been always been reduced in revised estimates and yet remained
under-utilized.
23. The Ministry informed that Plan expenditure has been less than RE due to less number of
proposals received in some of demand driven schemes i.e. Performance & Credit Rating Scheme,
Quality of Technology Support Institution & Programme, MSME Cluster Development Programme

4
and MSME Growth Poles, MDA Programme, Khadi Grant including MDA for khadi, Village
Industries Grant, workshed Scheme for khadi Artisans, Rejuvenation, Modernisation & Technology
Upgradation of Coir Industries and some new Scheme are not approved i.e. National Innovation
Fund.
24. The Committee recalled that the Ministry had given similar excuse of lack of
demand, in respect of under utilization of funds in 2011-12. It expresses serious concern
that situation has not changed much over last year. This trend goes against the
Government’s policy of promoting this important sector as reflected in enhanced year on
year allocations. The Committee is concerned over the lack of enough demand for the
Government’s schemes even to the extent of annual allocation. If the Ministry is seeking
year on year enhanced allocation for these Schemes, it is obviously on the basis of enhanced
estimated demand for the scheme. The reply is an implicit admission that the Ministry has
not been able to reach out to the targeted group or it has not been able to educate people
about these schemes or the procedures in schemes are not sufficiently seamless and
streamlined so as to attract potential users. The Committee also noted that the Ministry
had commissioned a third party evaluation of these schemes. The Committee would like to
know the outcome of such evaluation what were the infirmities identified and the steps
taken to remove them.
MSME Enterprises
25. Total Rs. 1087.22 crores were allocated in BE 2012-13 of which Rs. 986.55 crores was
Planned allocation and Rs. 100.67 crores was Non-Planned allocation. However at RE stage the
Planned component was drastically reduced to Rs. 824.65 crores but Non Planned component
was marginally enhanced to Rs. 102.06 crores. Over all the RE were reduced to Rs. 926.71
crores.
Credit Support Programme
26. The Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme is the prominent scheme under this Scheme. The
Credit Guarantee Scheme operated by Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small
Enterprises (CGTMSE) guarantees collateral free and/or third party guarantee free credit facilities
upto Rs. 100 lakh per MSE borrower sanctioned by its Member Lending Institutions (MLIs). The
Trust has been receiving corpus contribution since inception from its Settlors i.e., GoI and
SIDBI in the ratio of 4:1. The corpus contribution received by CGTMSE and the net income
earned by the Trust have been invested in FDs of Banks/Institutions. In the event, the borrower
account turns into NPA, the MLIs can invoke the guarantee cover after expiry of lock-in–period
of 18 months and compliance of other terms and conditions for settlement of claim. The cost
of guarantee cover is to be paid by MLIs to CGTMSE. However, the amount equivalent to the
guarantee fee and/or the service fee payable may be recovered by the MLI, at its discretion from
the eligible borrower. A composite all-in Guarantee Fee of 1% per annum of sanctioned credit
facility shall be paid upfront to the Trust by the Institutions availing of the guarantee cover for
credit facilities sanctioned by MLIs on or after January 01, 2013 as per the modified provisions
of the scheme. This is lower at 0.75% per annum for credit facility upto Rs. 5 lakh and 0.85%
per annum above Rs. 5 lakh and upto Rs. 100 lakh for women, Micro enterprises and units in
NER including Sikkim.
27. It was informed that as on February 28, 2013, 11,431 claims preferred by MLIs for an
amount of Rs. 302.53 crore (1st installment) have been settled. The quarter-wise claims settled
during 2011-12 and 2012-13 are as under:

29. The Committee also observed that there was a sharp reduction in the allocation over the

33. The Committee also noted the demand for enhancing the existing credit ceiling upto

was a need of raising the credit ceiling in view of inflation, it must also be borne in view that
majority of beneficiaries of this Scheme were in the credit bracket of Rs. 10 lakh credit and an
extension of credit ceiling may dilute the participation of small and micro units. The Additional
Secretary from the M/o MSME however cautioned and informed that the Ministry with assistance
from the World Bank, on the exoperimental basis has enhanced ceiling to Rs. 2 crores.
34. In view of inflation, the Committee concurred with the view of Ministry to enhance
the credit ceiling to Rs. 2 crores from existing Rs. 1 crore.
SIDBI/India Microfinance Equity Fund (IMEF)
35. The Committee noted that another Rs. 100 crores were being provided to SIDBI for the
IME Fund Scheme .
36. In this regard the Ministry informed that to enhance credit flow to Micro and Small
Enterprises (MSEs) by augmenting refinancing capability of SIDBI, a fund would be made available

6
to SIDBI out of the contribution made by scheduled commercial banks having shortfall in

margin money subsidy for a given state is released is two instalments of 50% each. The first
instalment is released when the State has utilized at least 50% of the margin money subsidy
released to it during the previous year after fully utilizing all previous years’ releases. The second
instalments is released after the State has utilized 50% of the current years’ release after fully
utilizing all previous years’ releases. These releases are made by the Ministry to KVIC which in
turn transfer the funds state-wise to the concerned PMEGP accounts in nodal bank branches.
Financing branches after sanctioning and making the first disbursement to the beneficiary, submits
the claims to its nodal branch. The nodal branch then settles the claims and transfers the fund to
the financing branch. Financing branch then keeps the entire subsidy in the name of beneficiary
in his TDR account. However, the Committee also came across the instances like Tamil Nadu
were no fresh applications were being entertained for last few years for the need of
adequate funds. The Committee takes strong view over such instances which will defeat the
very objective of the Scheme and bring it down in the esteem of people. Instead of turning

Interaction with Select Industry Associations
152. The Committee had useful interaction with the representatives of select industry
associations, who expressed their concerns and gave suggestions.
Difficulty in doing the business
153. There Associations impressed upon the Committee that despite its socioeconomic
importance, the growth of sector has remained stunted due to multiple constraints which has been
recognized in the Economic Survey 2012-13 which states “India has not improved significantly in
terms of the ease of doing business and ranks very low in comparison to other industrial peers.
The MSME sector in particular faces multiple approval and operational restrictions. The process of
setting up and exiting business is time consuming and complicated requiring expensive third party
assistance. Since states have the major role in administering MSME sector, the prevailing ecosystem
therefore varies from state to state.” It further acknowledges that the MSME sector suffers due
to costly finance, “Sourcing of finance at competitive cost is another major constraint for both the
organized and the unorganized MSME enterprises. Financing other than internal accruals is costly
and prohibitive.” The Survey also recognized the technological constraints faced by sector.
“Research and technology upgradation activities also need to be scaled up. Presently only a small
number of incubators operates in the country which is very low relative to other countries. New
incubators will need to be set up on a Public-Private Partnership basis.”
154. DC, MSME concurred and suggested Self certification by entrepreneur instead of recurrent
inspections by multiple inspectors. He particularly pointed out inspections by Departments pertaining
to pollution control and labour.

Summing up
177. The Committee reiterates the pivotal role MSME Sector will play to bring about
inclusive and equitable development, and in giving opportunity to self employed
entrepreneurs to express their skills and innovation. In the spectre of overall economic slow
down, only MSME could be a redeeming factor. With little support, it shows resilience to
withstand the recession. This sector provides the foundation on which new corporate sector
will be built. There are innumerable inspiring success stories, where small entrepreneurs
have achieved exemplary and inspiring success with their sheer resilience and acumen. As
the spectre of jobless growth and informalisation of job market continues, the Government
has recognized the vitality of this sector. Several Committees and instruments have been
set up to suggest ways to support this Sector. Government has increasingly been proving
budgetary support to schemes. The Committee has always supported the demand of the
Ministry for higher funds. However, the constraints not only about money, it is more about
management, monitoring and delivery of the schemes. It is issue of implementation and
financial discipline, which rests squarely on the Ministry and implementing agencies. The
structure of Schemes is complex and involves multiple funding agencies who more often
lack coordination. Scarce Finds remain unutilised for most part of the year, there is year-
end rush to spend. Balance unspent money is carried forward to subsequent year. Whether
there is a approval of Ministry of Finance, to roll over the unspent balance of a continuing
scheme to next year. Money is deposited in joint Bank accounts and remains un-used. Yet
the Budget estimates for next year are retained at same level. Umbrella allocations are
made in Budget, under which independent schemes are allocated independent meagre funds,
but same is not reflected in the Budget document. These funds remain unutilized supposedly
for lack of demand as indicated in Outcome Budgets. Yet the allocation is retained at same
level. As the Ministry seeks more funds for the MSME sector, the Committee is circumspect
about the argument of lack of demand.  There is a prevalent practice of seeking allocations
for successive years, for Schemes like Special Scheme on PM’s Task Force, Virtual SME
Univerisity etc. which does not have the approval of Planning Commission or other
competent authority. Also, there are recurrent discrepancies in figures provided by the
Ministry vis-a-vis the Budget figures.

27. The Committee expresses its disappointment over repeated under-utilization of funds
meant for critical S&T projects. The Committee apprehends year-end expenditure. The
Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry must make Planned expenditures more
discreetly. (Para No. 91)
28. The Committee expresses reservation over the practice of retaining meager ‘Token
allocations’ for successive years for Planned schemes, without approval of Planning
Commission. Such practice obviously violates the very concept of Parliamentary approval
and oversight of Budget. (Para No. 94)
29. The Committee suggests that the Ministry too should intervene in resolving the long
pending issues of MGIRI. (Para No. 97)
30. The Committee notes that annual allocations are being made to meet only committed
obligations, yet there has been gross under-utilisation in successive years. The money is
deposited in joint bank accounts of representatives of institutions, which is carried forward
to next years. The Committee wonders if the nodal agencies or Scheme Steering Committee
can monitor the expenditure from joint bank accounts. The Ministry should specify if such
practices of depositing money in joint accounts and carrying the unused funds over to
subsequent year, have the approval of the Ministry of Finance. (Para No. 102)
31. The Committee notes that there was no expenditure during half the Financial Year
and that unspent balance has been carried over this year. The Ministry may clarify if it
adhered to the norms set by the Ministry of Finance in this regard. (Para No. 106)
32. As per the Outcome Budget (2013-14), till 31.12.2012, no money was spent nor any
achievement was reported. The Committee has observed a persistent trend of under
achievement of targets and under-utilisation of funds. Yet the allocation in BE 2013-14 has
been retained at Rs 7.42 crores. The Committee expresses its anguish over general
prevalence of underutilisation of Planned funds, despite budgetary support remaining at the
same level. The Committee expects the Ministry to make proactive intervention to reach
out to intended beneficiaries. (Para No. 109)
33. The Committee recommends that the views of stakeholders in Khadi sector should
be factored while formulating the implementation. (Para No. 113)
34. The Committee expresses its reservation over repeated difference in figures
contained in Budgetary documents that are presented to Parliament. The Ministry should
explain the recurrence of this difference in figures. (Para No. 116)
35. The Committee insists that the core objective of the scheme is to provide
opportunities to self employed entrepreneurs and to generate job opportunities. The success
of the scheme shall always be judged in terms of these parameters and not in terms of
utilization of margin money only. The Committee expresses its anguish over under
achievement. (Para No. 120)
36. However, the Committee also came across the instances like Tamil Nadu were no
fresh applications were being entertained for last few years for the need of adequate funds.
The Committee takes strong view over such instances which will defeat the very objective
of the Scheme and bring it down in the esteem of people. Instead of turning the applicant
away, implementing agencies including Banks should proactively reach out to them.
(Para No. 123)

29
37. The Committee finds that these proposal regarding financing the expansion of
existing PMEGP Units and synergizing PMEGP with schemes of rural development in the
naxal effected areas, should be acceptable to the Ministry, provided that implementation
should be efficient and target oriented. (Para No. 128)
38. The Committee considers that PMEGP is an important scheme. In view of significant
under-achievements in meeting physical targets, the Committee recommends that efforts
should be made to simplify the procedure and streamline the processes. There appears to
be disjoint at every level of approvals. The Committee recommends that DTFC should
mandatorily meet and approve the applications at quarterly basis. And should evaluate the
applications after due diligence. The application should be considered against determined
check-lists and benchmarks. There should be time bound approval at every level. It would
be helpful if the DTFC assigns local Udyami Mitras for this scheme. In case of rejection the
reasons should be communicated to the applicant in writing within a time-limit. The KVIC
alongwith the Banks should use Bank’s publicity platforms to publicise PMEGP. So far only
KVIC has been publicizing the PMEGP. The PMEGP should be promoted and publicized as
a viable Banking product. The Committee also recommends that issue of relaxing Service
area norm should be settled and notified expeditiously. This procedural issue must not
hamper the Scheme. For PMEGP entire district should be considered as one unit. Every
approved project should automatically stand covered under CGTMSE. However, the
guarantee fee should be absorbed by the Bank. The Committee also suggests that Ministry
may consider having a Sub-Plan for the revivable sick PMEGP units. (Para No. 129)
39. For better and more efficient performance of the PMEGP, there was suggestion that
was discussed in Committee that instead of giving the margin money, the Government
should provide interest subvention beyond a certain rate. Considering that there is a ceiling
on the value of project, the total liability on interest rate subvention can be estimated. The
Committee would like the Ministry to consider this suggestion, for better performance of
scheme. (Para No. 130)
40. The Committee wonders reduction in Non-Planned allocation considering that
committed expenditures including salary and other statutory dues of employees are met out
of this allocation. In view of increase in the Non-Planned allocations over RE 2012-13
pertaining to other agencies under the Ministry, reduction in respect of Coir Board is
noticeable. The Ministry may clarify if these obligatory expenditures are being duly met.
(Para No. 132)
41. The Committee notes that the target for 2012-13 was 900 units, however, till
31.12.2012, only 63 units (7% of the target) could be assisted. Almost 10 fold increase in
last quarter without spending any money under the scheme. However, the Secretary, Coir
Board in his presentation before the Committee stated that the target of 900 was surpassed
and 934 units were established. The Committee seeks explanation on such difference in
figures. (Para No. 135)
42. There is a difference between the figures for 2012-13 as provided by the Ministry and
those given in the Budget documents. The Committee reiterates its reservation over this
recurrent trend. The Ministry ought to reconcile its figures as given in the Expenditure
Budget (II) for the Ministry. Further the Committee notes significant reduction in Planned
allocation at RE stage to Rs. 32.51 crores. However, the Ministry released only Rs. 19.31
crores to Coir Board. It has been stated that the Coir Board spent unutilized balance of
previous year. Whether this recurrent practice of utilizing unused balance of previous year,

30
in the Ministry, has the approval of Ministry of Finance. At RE stage only in case of Coir
S&T the allocation was retained at Rs 7 crores. However, no money was spent in I and III
quarters and total expenditure was Rs 2.31 crores uneven expenditure of Planned allocation.
No money was spent under the important REMOT scheme through out the year. The
Committee feels that Coir industry is a promising sector for employment generation and
export market. While the Committee supports greater allocation for this Sector, it can not
ignore the less than optimal performance on the part of Ministry and concerned agencies.
These issues pertain the management, monitoring and financial efficiency by the Ministry
and concerned agency. (Para No. 140)
43. The Committee appreciates the export performance in Coir sector particularly
considering the structural, technological and financial limitations. The Committee impresses
that efforts should be made to realize full potential of this Sector. (Para No. 142)
44. The Committee finds the scope and prospects in NE promising. The MSME and KVIC
could prove to be most important vehicles for inclusive development of this region which
has immense scope and skill. However, as per the Expenditure Budget (II) of the Budget
document, the actual expenditure in 2010-11 and 2011-12, has been Nil. Even for year
2013-14 the Planned allocation is shown as Rs 31.83 crores, instead of Rs 297.70 crores as
indicated above. The Committee would like clarification on the yet another difference in
figures between Budget documents and those furnished by the Ministry. (Para No. 151)
45. The Committee found its interaction with select industry associations a useful
experience. It received feedback from the ultimate consumers of these schemes. The
Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider and respond to their suggestions
and concerns. (Para No. 176)
46. The Committee reiterates the pivotal role MSME Sector will play to bring about
inclusive and equitable development, and in giving opportunity to self employed
entrepreneurs to express their skills and innovation. In the spectre of overall economic slow
down, only MSME could be a redeeming factor. With little support, it shows resilience to
withstand the recession. This sector provides the foundation on which new corporate sector
will be built. There are innumerable inspiring success stories, where small entrepreneurs
have achieved exemplary and inspiring success with their sheer resilience and acumen. As
the spectre of jobless growth and informalisation of job market continues, the Government
has recognized the vitality of this sector. Several Committees and instruments have been
set up to suggest ways to support this Sector. Government has increasingly been proving
budgetary support to schemes. The Committee has always supported the demand of the
Ministry for higher funds. However, the constraints not only about money, it is more about
management, monitoring and delivery of the schemes. It is issue of implementation and
financial discipline, which rests squarely on the Ministry and implementing agencies. The
structure of Schemes is complex and involves multiple funding agencies who more often
lack coordination. Scarce Finds remain unutilised for most part of the year, there is year-
end rush to spend. Balance unspent money is carried forward to subsequent year. Whether
there is a approval of Ministry of Finance, to roll over the unspent balance of a continuing
scheme to next year. Money is deposited in joint Bank accounts and remains un-used. Yet
the Budget estimates for next year are retained at same level. Umbrella allocations are
made in Budget, under which independent schemes are allocated independent meagre funds,
but same is not reflected in the Budget document. These funds remain unutilized supposedly
for lack of demand as indicated in Outcome Budgets. Yet the allocation is retained at same

31
level. As the Ministry seeks more funds for the MSME sector, the Committee is circumspect
about the argument of lack of demand. There is a prevalent practice of seeking allocations
for successive years, for Schemes like Special Scheme on PM’s Task Force, Virtual SME
University etc. which does not have the approval of Planning Commission or other
competent authority. Also, there are recurrent discrepancies in figures provided by the
Ministry vis a vis the Budget figures. (Para No. 177)

(i) 

 
INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamen tary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred 
and Forty Fifth Report on Review the implementation  of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development Act, 2006 pertaining to Min istry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises. 
 
2.  The Committee heard the representatives of Mini stry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises, organizations under the adminis trative control of Ministry of 
MSME and received valuable inputs from select MSME Associations on the issue.   
 
3.  The Committee in its meeting held on 2
nd  July, 2013 considered and adopted the 
report. 
 
 
 
 
 
TIRUCHI SIVA        
Chairman 
Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry 
 
 
New Delhi,  
July, 2013 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(ii) 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Report  
 
The MSME Sector accounts for 45% of the country’s m anufacturing output, 40% 
of the exports and 8% of our GDP. The 26 million enterprises employing some 60 million 
people, have investment to the tune of Rs. 6.89 lak h crores, yet about 94% remain 
unregistered with large number of them being establ ished in unorganized and informal 
sector. The Report of Prime Minister’s Task Force o n MSME brings out the  largest 
significant of MSMEs for economy and states :  
 
“….   The labour to capital ratio in MSMEs and the over all growth in the MSME 
sector is much higher than in the large industries.  The geographic distribution of 
the MSMEs is also more even. Thus, MSMEs are import ant for the national 
objectives of growth with equity and inclusion. 
 
…. The MSME sector in India is highly heterogeneous  in terms of the size of the 
enterprises, variety of products and services produ ced and the levels of 
technology employed. While one end of the MSME spec trum contains highly 
innovative and high growth enterprises, more than 9 4 per cent of MSMEs are 
unregistered, with a large number established in th e informal or unorganized 
sector.”  
 
2. Until 2006, the small scale industries sector wa s being regulated by two sections 
of Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951.  There was absence of an 
institutional regulatory and consultative mechanism  to capture and guide the organic 
progress of the sector from a micro enterprise to s mall scale enterprise to eventually a 
medium scale one. It also excluded the fast emergin g service sector. It was therefore 
considered essential to provide an exclusive legisl ation for the micro, small and medium 
enterprises. Such Bill was introduced in Lok Sabha on 12 
th  May, 2005 and was referred 
to this Committee. The Committee had held extensive  consultations on the provisions of 
the legislation which  included provisions pertaining – 
 
• statutory definitions of “small enterprise” and “medium enterprise”; 
• establishment of a National Small and Medium Enterp rises Board, a high-level 
forum consisting of stakeholders for participative review of and making  
 
• recommendations on the policies and programmes for the development of small 
and medium enterprises; 
 
• Classification of small and medium enterprises on the basis of investment in plant 
and machinery, or equipment  
 
• establishment of an Advisory Committee to recommend on the related matter; 
 
• The Act also sought to empower the Central Governme nt to notify programmes, 
guidelines or instructions for facilitating the pro motion and development and 
enhancing the competitiveness of small and medium enterprises; 
 
 
 

• The Act  also made provisions for ensuring timely a nd smooth flow of credit to 
small and medium enterprises to minimize the incide nce of sickness among and 
enhancing the competitiveness of such enterprises; 
 
• The Act also provided that the Central and State Go vernments may notify 
preference policies in respect of procurement of goods and services, produced and 
provided by small enterprises, by the Ministries, d epartments and public sector 
enterprises; 
 
• The Bill had a provision for the Central Government to create a Fund or Funds for 
facilitating promotion and development and enhancin g the competitiveness of  
small enterprises and medium enterprises; 
 
• It made further improvements to ensure timely payme nts to Small Scale 
enterprises.  
 
3. The Committee had acknowledged that the Bill was  an important and forward 
looking initiative. In its discussions with various  stake-holders, Industry associations and 
representatives of State Governments, there was gen eral approval for the Bill. In its 
Report to the Parliament, the Committee made follow ing recommendations for the 
Government:  
 
“…. certain States and industry associations sought  greater elaboration of the 
provisions of Bill particularly on the enabling Cla uses for promotion, 
development and enhancement of competitiveness of t he tiny, small and medium 
enterprises.   
 
….the Ministry of SSI should hold wide consultation s with the industry 
associations and State Governments while framing th e rules, so as to incorporate 
the views of the State Governments who shall be exe cuting the provisions of the 
Bill.  
 
….Having formulated the enabling rules, the Ministr y should continue to monitor 
their execution by agencies at local level and shou ld ensure that the agencies 
evolve processes / procedures that are simple and i n consonance with the 
objectives of the Act.  
 
….in order to encourage tiny, small  and medium ent erprises to adhere to 
pollution control norms, as per the Order dated the  10 
th  December 1997 of the 
Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, the cost of pollution control and 
R&D devices should not be included while calculatin g the investments in plant 
and machinery. Similar exemption should be made wit h respect to industrial 
safety devices to promote such units to adopt industrial safety norms.  
 
… The Industrial Facilitation Council should evolve  into an effective forum of 
arbitration, to resolve the issue of delayed paymen ts to small and tiny enterprises, 
conferred with sufficient mandate to execute its aw ard, appeal against which 
could be filed only in the High Court of the State where IFC is located” 
 

 
4. The Act was passed and notified on 16 th  June 2006. The Act provided advisory 
and regulatory framework and had enabling provision s which needed subordinate 
legislations in form of Rules, Regulation and polic ies on the part of Union and State 
Governments.   
 
5. After passage of six years of the notification o f the MSME Development Act, 
2006, the Committee decided to review the implement ation of the Act in July, 2012. The 
Committee held four meetings on the subject on 6 
th  July, 13 th  July, 20 th  July and 27 th  July, 
2012 with the representatives of select industry associations and the representatives of the 
Ministry of MSME. The Committee also received a lar ge number of written 
representations. The Ministry of MSME was asked to furnish their comments on the 
suggestions made by the representatives of  industry associations.  
 
6. In its written submission to the Committee, the Ministry of MSME informed that 
in order to provide greater efficacy to some import ant provisions of the MSMED Act 
particularly in respect of delayed payments,  a pro posal to amend the relevant Sections of 
the Act was under consideration. It also submitted that in pursuance of different 
provisions of the Act the Government has been issui ng periodic notifications regarding 
operationalisation of the Act from 2 
nd  October 2006, constitution of National Board of 
MSME and Advisory Committee, classification of the micro, small and medium 
enterprises and exclusion of items while calculatin g the investment in plant and 
machinery. The Government has also notified the aut hority in the States/UTs with whom 
the medium enterprises are to be registered and the Format of memorandum to be filed by 
the micro, small and medium enterprises. The Govern ment has also notified rules for 
National Board of Micro, Small and Medium Enterpris es. However,  the Committee 
notes that the National Board of MSME had so far he ld only nine meetings at 
random intervals as against the statutory requireme nt of one meeting every three 
months.  The  Committee also  expresses reservation over the proposal to amend th e 
relevant Section of the Act which provides for quar terly meetings of the Board and 
placing it under the Rules which would fall within the scope of subordinate 
legislation.  The Committee unable to comprehend the rationale be hind such 
proposal.  It only reinforces the apprehension that the role of statutory Board would 
be further diluted.  The Committee strongly recomme nds for creating a Monitoring 
Cell for Delayed Payment in office of the Development Commissioner, MSME.   
 
7. In addition, the Advisory Committee set up under  Section 7 (2) of the Act too has 
discussed the issue of modifications in Entrepreneu rs Memoranda, issue related to 4 
th  
MSME Census and the prospects of separate SME Exchange.  
 
8. The Committee was also informed that the Governm ent has issued notifications 
regarding filing of Entrepreneurs Memorandum by the Medium Enterprises under Section 
8 of the Act. The State Governments are expected to  issue notifications in respect of 
small and micro enterprises. The Committee notes that the number of enterprises who 
had filed memoranda has increased exponentially from about 1.75 lakh in 2007-08  
 
 
 
 

 
to 2.82 lakh in 2011-12. However, the Committee obs erves reduction in number of 
registrations in successive years in case of certai n States. The Committee would like 
to explore the reasons for such reduction.  
 
9. The Committee was informed that as per the Secti on 11 Act, the Government has 
notified Procurement preference policy in March 201 2, wherein minimum 20% of 
procurement of annual requirement of goods and serv ices by all the Central 
Ministries/Departments/PSUs from MSEs, of which 4% should be sourced from the 
enterprises owned by SC/ST entrepreneurs.  
 
10. The Committee observes that the said notification does not cover the 
Autonomous organizations/Societies/ Trusts/Institut ions/ Universities and other 
Government aided organizations under the various Ce ntral Government 
Ministries/Departments. The Committee also wonders if the notification includes the 
Constitutional bodies.  The Committee recommends that the said notification  should 
include such institutions. The Committee also recom mends that the Central 
Government should persuade the State Governments to  adopt similar policies, for 
which Government can use the National Board as a fo rum where State 
Governments are also represented by rotation.  
 
11  The Committee recommends that like the Central Ministries/Departments/PSUs, 
the private sector companies should also procure a minimum of 20% of annual 
requirements of goods and services from MSEs. 
 
12. Section 20 of the Chapter V of the Act provide for the establishment of Micro and 
Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (MSEFCs) by the State Government. The Central 
Government had formulated and circulated to the States, the model rules regarding filling 
up of the vacancies of such Councils and for discha rging their functions. The Committee 
was informed that while 34 States and Union Territo ries had notified the rules, 34 
States/UTs had set up such Facilitation Councils. The Committee takes note of the 
performance of the Facilitation Councils in States. It is rather strange that in certain  
States/UTs no fresh cases were filed during year 20 11-12. Also there is large 
pendency of cases and disposal rate is rather slow.  This is clear violation of Section 
18 (5) of the Act which make disposal of references  within Ninety days, obligatory. 
The Committee also apprehends that decline in the f iling of fresh cases may be due 
to dwindling faith in the efficacy of this mechanis m. The Committee therefore 
suggests that the rate of disposal of cases should be faster. Further, it appears that 
as per Section 19 the supplier does not have right to appeal against the Award given 
by an IFC.  Considering that the IFC do not have po wers to enforce the award, the 
suppliers too should have the right to appeal.  It also reiterates its previous 
recommendation that “The Industrial Facilitation Co uncil should evolve into an 
effective forum of arbitration, to resolve the issu e of delayed payments to small and 
tiny enterprises, conferred with sufficient mandate  to execute its award, appeal 
against which could be filed only in the High Court  of the State where IFC is 
located.” The Committee also takes note of the amen dments to make IFCs more 
effective, that are under consideration of Governme nt. These amendments pertain 
to bringing earnest money/security deposit submitte d during tender and falls within 
the ambit of provisions related to delayed payment.   The amount of award given by 

the Facilitation Council should be realizable as ar rears of land revenue.   The 
amount of award given by the Facilitation Council w ould be made enforceable and 
should include earnest money and securities submitt ed during the tender . The 
Committee recommends that by brining earnest money scrutiny deposit within the 
ambit of provisions related to delayed payment in MSMED Act 2006, this delay may 
be checked and regulated.   
 
13. Apart from the inputs from the administrative M inistry of MSME, the Committee 
also received inputs from select industry associati ons. During the course of its interaction 
with the representatives of industry associations t he following major concerns were 
raised : 
 
Definition of MSME 
 
14. In view of inflation there was demand to enhanc e the limit on the investment in 
plant and machinery in micro and small scale enterp rises. It was also underscored that it 
was difficult to differentiate between private and business assets of MSMEs, hence it was 
difficult to assess the investment in assets with required exactitude.  
 
15. The Ministry in its reply generally agreed with  the contention but expressed 
constraint stating “ The present definition is in t he Act itself. These need to be defined in 
Rules rather than in Act itself. The definition sho uld be dynamic to enable the MSME to 
avail the benefits as well as handle global competition.” 
 
16.  Considering the inflation and dynamic market  sit uation, the Committee 
feels that definition of MSMEs as provided in the A ct may be revised every five 
years. 
 
Entrepreneurs’ Memorandum 
 
17. It was suggested that the filing of the Memoran da should be simplified by making 
it online. 
 
18. The Ministry agreed with the suggestion that th e filing of the Memorandum 
should be made online. It was informed that a consu ltation meeting with the States in this 
regard was held in January 2012.  
 
19. The Committee notes that the Report of the Working  Group on the MSME 
for the 12 
th  Plan, too recommended that the States should encou rage ‘online’ filing 
of Memoranda. Considering the consensus on the issu e, the Committee expects that 
necessary steps should be taken to resolve the issu e expeditiously .  The MSME 
Ministry should encourage the Micro and Small Enterprises to register themselves.     
Delayed Payment 
 
20. The Committee notes general dissatisfaction ove r the issue of delayed payment. 
The Committee also believes that this issue is crit ical for the survival of micro and small 
enterprises who work with limited working capital a nd any interruption in cash flow puts 
their survival at stake. The Committee also notes t hat the mechanism of Industrial

Rehabilitation and Exit Policy 
 
Section 25 of the MSMED Act provides for the exit policy for the closure of micro, small 
or medium enterprises. The Committee was informed that units that are not Companies or 
Limited liability partnerships, are largely governe d by provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, 
where there is no separation of personal and busine ss assets, which leads to lengthy 
litigation. The Ministry recognized the need for a separate and much simpler mechanism 
for the revival or exit of MSMEs. The Committee was  informed that the Ministry was 
working on a Draft framework in this respect which provides for setting up of Revival 
and Exit Committee of MSME Facilitation Council through which a MSME or a Creditor 
can initiate filing for either revival or exit route.  
 
The Committee also took note of the recommendations  made by the PM’s Task Force on 
the MSME in this regard, some of which are as under : 
 
 
…. The Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 (LLP) pr ovides for enabling schemes of 
revival as well as liquidation and winding up. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has also 
introduced the Companies Bill 2009 which includes a  provision for a ‘one person 
company (OPC)’. The MSMEs need to be encouraged/ in centivised to convert to these 
forms.  
(Action: MoCA/ DoR/MoMSME – no time lines) 
 
… Banks have existing mechanism/ procedures for rehab ilitation/ restructuring of 
potentially viable sick MSMEs. However, as the track record of the sick units is generally 
poor, the bankers are often reluctant to rehabilita te such units. Consequently, very few 
units are being rehabilitated by banks. Moreover th ese mechanisms do not provide 
protection from statutory dues or other creditor ac tion. There is, therefore, a need for an 
alternate mechanism to re-examine the viability of such units and implement a 
rehabilitation package in a time bound manner. It is suggested that for MSME units found 
to be unviable by the banks, an administrative mech anism may be put in place at district 
level, under the GM (DIC) to re-examine the viabili ty and implement a rehabilitation 
package, wherever necessary. The rehabilitation pac kage may comprise, besides 
additional lending by banks, of relief and concessi ons in statutory dues by the State 
Governments/autonomous bodies, Power Supply Company etc. Since the promoters often 
find it difficult to infuse fresh funds to the exte nt required by the Banks, Rehabilitation 
funds specially set up by the State Governments cou ld part-finance promoters margin 
money requirement. The Central Government may support the setting up of rehabilitation 
funds  in  the States to  facilitate  and  encourage  rehabilitation  of  potentially viable sick  
units. An appropriate scheme should be formulated b y Ministry of MSME with an 
estimated outlay of Rs.1,000 crore. District Level Committees will be convened by GM, 
DIC. The rehabilitation Cell set up in DICs will fo rm the Secretariat of these committees. 
It will receive and monitor the applications and wi ll also draw up a panel of Technical 

Officers/ Chartered Accountants to provide assistan ce in the preparation of the 
rehabilitation packages. The Rehabilitation cell in  consultation with the entrepreneur 
shall prepare the rehabilitation packages and place  before the Committee for approval. 
The entire process of preparation of rehabilitation plan to finalization of the rehabilitation 
package should be completed in 2 months time. Till the rehabilitation package is 
finalized, all statutory and bank payments will be kept in abeyance. This will be binding  
on all parties by issuance of Government order by t he State Government. The banks 
should devise a liberal One Time Settlement  policy  for small enterprises particularly 
micro enterprises found unviable by the District level Committee. 
(Action: Ministry of MSME/State Governments/Banks – 6 months) 
 
…. In place of the outdated Provincial Insolvency Act,  1920, action may be initiated to 
formulate and circulate a model Insolvency Act with in 6 months which will have 
enabling provisions for time bound revival and exit  for the unincorporated firms. The 
model Act should take into consideration the following 4 critical elements:  
 
(a) a specialized quasi-judicial body, to appraise viability and set up time bound revival/ 
closure plans;  
(b) enabling provisions for a holding period for revival;  
(c) segregation of business assets from personal assets based on reasonable norms; and  
(d) speedy winding up in case the business is determined as non-revivable. 
 
(Action: Ministry of MSME in consultation with M/o Corporate Affairs & 
Ministry of Law & Justice – 6 months)
