15. The Committee is surprised that despite 55% uti lization of funds upto 31st 
December, 2014, the Ministry has demanded almost do uble the allocation for the 
next year.  In this context, the Ministry informed the Committee that the  enhanced 
amount for the year 2015-16 was proposed for achieving the goal of Hon'ble Prime 
Minister to enhance manufacturing, competitiveness and promoting skill 
development in India. However, more thrust is to be  given on Quality of 
Technology Support Institutions & Programme (Credit  Linked Capital Subsidy 
Scheme etc.), Infrastructure Development & Capacity Building (Tool  Rooms  and 
Cluster Development Programme), Setting up of new T ool Room and Credit 
Support Programme.  
16.  The Committee had raised serious concern over unde r-utilisation of 
funds by the Ministry in its Planned schemes.  Desp ite repeated observation 
by the Committee regarding issues of under-utilisat ion of funds year after 
year in its Reports and its Action Taken Reports, i ts concerns have been 
ignored. Same pleas of procedural delays in devolution of funds, approvals  by  
 

-8- 
 
Banks etc. have been taken by the Ministry. Notwith standing Government’s 
pronouncements towards Ease of Doing Business, it a ppears that these 
procedural complexities remain insurmountable in the Ministry. How else can 
one justify 58% utilization of funds till the end o f third quarter of Financial 
Year and then sudden jump in expenditure in the fou rth quarter?  The 
Committee has repeatedly recommended that the expen diture on the planned 
schemes should not be crowded in the last quarter only. Yet, no heed has been 
given to Committee’s recommendations.   
17. The Secretary, M/o MSME tried to rationalize th e pattern of expenditure: 
“If we take the method of incurring expenditure, we  have the budget 
estimate.  There is a limitation on how much we can spend from quarter to quarter.  
So, in the first quarter, there is a limitation on how much we can spend.  Similarly, 
in the second quarter, third quarter and the fourth  quarter too.  In the existing 
arrangement, while the expenditures may look to be higher, and they are higher, 
compared to the first, second and the third quarter s, in the last quarter.  Actually, 
there is a limitation on how much we can spend with  reference to the Budget 
Estimate and RE in the last quarter.  So, even on c rowding of the expenditure in 
the last quarter, the arrangement  of the Finance M inistry, which is implemented 
through our Financial Advisor, is that there is a l imit up to which we can spend.  
And, that limit is, I think, 33 per cent of the Bud get, which can be spend in the last 
quarter.  So, it cannot be more than that”. 
18.  The Committee finds that year after year, the actu al expenditure in last 
quarter has far exceeded the limit of 33% and the C ommittee has highlighted 
the same in its earlier Reports also. This year too , till 31 
st  December, 2014, by 
Ministry’s own admission it could spent only 55% of   the  allocation with DC-
MSME utilizing  less  than 50%. If the Ministry was  not able to utilize 
remaining 45% in next three months, the money should have been  

-9- 
surrendered at RE stage. Ministry’s plea that expen ditures could not be made 
due to enforcement of Model Code of Conduct would h ave been acceptable, 
had it not been a yearly phenomenon.  Similarly, Mi nistry knew that the 
duration of last financial  year 2014-15 was shorte r one, yet it demanded 
higher funds and its allocations in BE 2014-15 were  higher than the actual 
utilization of 2012-13.  The Government has been ge nerous in allocations to 
M/o MSME regardless of its ability to spend efficiently. 
19. The Secretary justified the bulk expenditure in  the bank-linked schemes like 
CLCSS or PMEGP by explaining the structure of schem e where banks raise the 
claims on the Ministry.  His assertion was that the  Ministry disburses the money 
only after receiving the claims from the Banks   
20.  The Committee is apprehensive to accept the argume nt. The Committee 
also finds it strange that as per the Ministry’s ow n Annual Report, the Banks 
have been meeting the lending targets for MSE secto r as prescribed by the 
RBI. Yet, banks are not coming forward to support M inistry’s schemes for 
MSME  sector despite budgetary support.  Obviously, the  answer  lies  in  the 
structure of schemes and process of screening by th e Ministry and its 
agencies, that needs to be addressed .   
21.  The Committee wonders if the Banks get the applica tion only towards 
the last months of the Financial Year or they take protracted time to 
scrutinize the application. The Committee will not be inclined to recommend 
to Banks to lower their standards of scrutiny. The applications  are  processed 
by the agencies assigned by the Ministry. Whether t hese agencies scrutinize 
the applications diligently? For example, in case o f PMEGP, the applications 
are processed by DLTFC. Majority of the applications forwarded by DLTFC  

-10- 
are rejected by Banks. The Committee wonders if any  purpose is served by 
DLTFC as the applications forwarded by them are to be rejected on merit. 
The Committee had asked the Ministry to furnish the  information if the 100 
days deadline prescribed by it to settle an applica tion, was at all being 
followed. The Committee too had recommended that th e DLTFC should meet 
at least once in two months to clear the cases. The  Ministry too has launched 
E tracking system. Yet, it was not in position to identify the bottlenecks except 
for pointing at Banks for delay. For example, in ca se of PMEGP the 
Committee has repeatedly asked that the projects sh ould be sanctioned 
throughout the year. Yet, this year, within four da ys from 28 th  February to 4 th  
March, projects worth Rs 400 crores were disbursed.  
22. Another related aspect is targets.  The Committee f inds the targets of 
schemes rather moderate vis-à-vis the scope of MSME s in the country.  The 
Committee  wonders  that  despite cut in RE and further under utilization, the 
Ministry is able to meet majority of its targets.  Obviously either targets were 
kept modest or the demands for allocation were inflated.  
Unorganized Sector  
23. MSMEs are predominantly in unorganized sector.  As per fourth census, out 
of the 360 lakh MSMEs only 15 lakh are registered. 
24. The Committee also took note of the Prime Minis ter’s letter dated 31 
st  
March, 2015 to Small business persons of the countr y. In which he succinctly 
summarized the importance of this sector in the economy: 
"While many think that large companies dominate, in  reality, it is over 5.5 crore 
(55 million) small units like yours, which drive ou r economy through small 
manufacturing, trading and service businesses." 
 

-11- 
25. He sets the priority of the Government to make doing business easier for 
these units: 
“You should be able to run your business easily, no t be harassed by officials, get 
loans for your day-to-day activities, material  for  your operations and markets for 
your product." 
 
26.  On being asked whether the Ministry’s schemes were  reaching to 
remaining unregistered and unorganized sector, the Committee was informed 
in a written reply that the Ministry has not done a ny survey whether its 
Schemes are reaching to unorganized sector nor has it taken steps so far to 
facilitate doing business for the unorganized sector.   
27. The Committee also raised the issue of inaccess ibility of Government 
schemes for the unorganized sector during discussio ns with Industry associations. 
Whether such units are at all aware of the existenc e of such Schemes, it was 
informed: 
“There are some important reasons as to why most of the schemes do not percolate 
down.  Firstly, the MSME Act came into being in 200 6.  Prior to that the units 
which were registered were now supposed to be registered under the EM-Part II of 
the new Act.  The procedure is so cumbersome that  if  you  take  the statistics, only 
35 per cent are registered while 65 per cent cannot  avail any benefit under any 
scheme or even the facilitation council benefits of the recovery of receivables. 
 Sir, we all talk about ease of doing business. Mos t of the micro and small 
units are one man show.  If they have to make sever al trips to the Government 
offices, they lose the interest and then, they just  forget about the rest of the 
procedures.  Since they were already registered ear lier, it should be mandatory to 
give them registration under E.M. Part II, which wo uld solve the problem. This is 
something which needs to be looked into very urgent ly because almost 65 per cent 
of the units are deprived of the benefits.” 
 
 

-12- 
28. When the Committee raised the issue with the Se cretary, M/o MSME, 
during interaction on 25 th  March, 2015, he submitted: 
 
“The question which comes to mind is that why these micro enterprises are, 
actually, not getting registered and there we enter , the issue of ease of doing 
business, the  Inspector Raj and the  laws themselv es, which don't tend to 
distinguish between a big enterprise and a small en terprise when it comes to 
compliance, whether it is taxation laws or labour l aws or local laws, they are 
completely neutral on this; whether they are dealin g with a small enterprise or a 
big enterprise.  So, the compliance burden on the s mall enterprises is such that it 
simply does not make sense for them to register, an d that is why they are 
functioning in such a massive manner in the informa l sector.  This, I myself had 
pointed out in my Report as Chairman of the Inter-M inisterial Committee on 
Manufacturing in the MSME sector in the year 2013 itself, that  something needs to 
be done.  This particular trend is totally unsustai nable,  when the growth of the 
informal sector has been actually, much faster than  that of the formal sector.  
Again, those issues are  connected with  the ease of doing business and in  the ease 
of doing business,  there are, of course, a number of issues which have to be dealt 
with.  They are not be dealt with by the Ministry o f  MSME.  We are doing 
advocacy on behalf of the small enterprises, but these issues have to be really dealt 
with by the other Ministries in the Central Governm ent, mainly the Ministry of 
Finance and the Ministry of Labour.  Some issues, w hich are pertaining to 
pollution control, have to be dealt with by the  Mi nistry of Environment.  But there 
are also a lot of issues relating to land, clearanc es and taxation at the State level, 
by the State Government itself.” 
29. The Committee takes serious note of the situation.  Considering the 
Ministry’s admission that its schemes are mostly ta rgeted to Registered Units, 
and that only a miniscule minority of MSMEs is regi stered, the Committee 
finds the situation unacceptable. The MSMED Act, 20 06 does not make it 
obligatory upon micro enterprises to register. In e xcluding unorganized 
sector, the Ministry has gone against the statuary provisions of the Act in

29. The Committee noted that the Scheme was announced two years back 
with Rs. 2200 crores.  Yet only Rs. 3.60 crores spe nt after two years on pre-
project activities.  This year implementation of 3- 4 Technology Centres out of 
12 identified are likely to start.  The Committee express its concern over tardy 
pace of skill development and technology upgradatio n project. This is yet 
another example of Budget announcement being made w ithout institutional 
mechanism being on place to execute the projects ex peditiously.  As a result 
the Budget announcement are devoid of corresponding  budgetary support.  
(Para 85) 
30. The Committee is concerned over the employability o f trainees who 
undertake short term training at Technology Centers  (TCs).  These courses 
constitute the bulk of training programmes of TCs.  But no record of 
employability is kept.  To assess the efficiency of  such courses, employment 
record must be maintained.  The Committee reiterate s its views that 
performance audit under Audit Regulations 2007, (Ch apter 7) of the CAG 
Act, 1971, of these TCs should be done by CAG.  The  Committee may be 
apprised if these courses and institution will be t ransferred to Ministry of 
Skill Development as per Budget announcement.  
(Para 86) 
 
31. Yet on certain parameters, the targets were met.  This shows either 
figures are doubtful or the Ministry had inflated d emands. Clubbing such 
varied schemes under one umbrella  allocation, is o bviously going to be 
difficult to monitor yet the BE allocation for fina ncial year 2015-16 have been 
retained at same level as previous BE 2014-15.  Gov ernment must benchmark 
actual utilization while allocating funds.  Also Ministry must takes a hard look 
of achievement figures.  To say that there are dema nd driven schemes only 

justifies that allocation should have been benchmar ked against actual 
utilization.  
(Para 89) 
32. In every running Scheme, barring KRDP and new India  Innovation 
Entrepreneurship and Agro Industry Fund, the BE (20 15-16) is lower than 
RE (2014-15).  In both these Schemes the BE allocat ion were reduced at RE 
stage and yet again they have been enhanced in BE ( 2015-16).  However, 
considering all other MSME Schemes the pattern is low BE which is enhanced 
at RE stage.  In the context of D.C.(MSME) Schemes the allocations have been  
 
-67- 
enhanced despite lower utilization, here is case of KVIC, the budget allocation 
have been reduced vis-a –vis higher RE.  The Commit tee is unable to 
appreciate the reduction.  The Committee apprehends  that such trend in 
allocation may force the  KVIC  to crowd its expenditure  towards  the  end  of 
financial year.  KVIC is supposed to provide margin  money subsidy under 
PMEGP and Khadi Grant, the entire year, therefore i ts Budget allocation 
should be enhanced in the beginning of the financial year. 
(Para 92) 
33. The Committee has also failed to appreciate the ra tional of increasing 
budget allocation for  Khadi Reform & Development Programme (KRDP) 
during 2015-16 as Rs. 66.50 crores when the scheme is not able to use the 
money and allocation had to be reduced at RE stage.  Acknowledging that the 
scheme is largely funded by ADB assistance under ce rtain conditions, the 
Committee also takes note of protests from Khadi In stitutions against KRDP 
and the difficulties in getting the Khadi Instituti ons audited before availing 
the assistance under KRDP. 
(Para 93) 
34. The Committee notes that the allocation for Khadi Industries (Grants) 
hiked by almost double at RE stage in the year 2014 -15.  The Ministry state 
that it was done in view of increased mid year dema nd raised by KVIC.  The 
Committee finds that this has been the pattern of  allocation  in previous years 
also.  The Committee wonders about the impact on Khadi Institution if grants 
are allocated within second half of the financial y ear.  It will force the KVIC 
to release Khadi Grant only after enhanced Revised Estimates. The 
Committee also wonder if only 57% of the BE was spe nt till the 3 rd  quarter of 
financial year, why the allocation was enhanced at RE stage.  The Committee 

therefore is of the view that Ministry must stagger  the release of grant in 
installments throughout the year.  
(Para 99) 
35. The Committee notes that MDA scheme was devised to  sustain the 
Khadi institutions the year long instead of seasona l rebates. However, the 
purpose is defeated if MDA is released after the pa ssage of Financial Year. 
The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministr y must devise the 
scheme so as to ensure that MDA is staggered and is  released to khadi 
institutions year long. The Committee noted that the  khadi  institutions  were  
 
 
-68- 
working on shrinking margins and depleting capital.  Any delay in releasing 
the MDA can result in sickness and consequent unemp loyment among 
artisans.   The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministr y must 
devise method and powers to transfer the Khadi  MDA  Fund.  The Scheme 
was devised to replace annual rebate, so as  to pro vide assistance throughout 
the year.  However current expenditure defeats the objective of MDA.  
Ministry must ensure regular release of funds at an y stage of Khadi 
production.  
(Para 100)   
36. Considering that these Schemes are pending for app roval from 
competent authority, the Committee considers it as a comment on Ministry’s 
inability to defend the Scheme designed by it and s ecure approval of 
competent authority.  It is a reflection on the Min istry that approval is 
pending for years and still being included in annua l Demands for Grants of 
the Ministry.  
(Para 102) 
 
37. The Committee noted the suggestion by representati ve of Khadi 
Artisans that the Janshree Bima Yojna be replaced w ith Rashtriya Swasthya 
Yojna, which has better medical benefits. Consideri ng no expenditure under 
Janshree Bima Yojna due to delay in approval, the C ommittee recommends 
the Ministry to take appropriate note of the sugges tion given by the 
beneficiary artisans to replace Janshree Bima Yojna with Rashtriya Swasthya 
Bima Yojna  and also inform the Committee of its view. 

(Para 103) 
 
38. The Committee takes note of the Secretary’s submiss ion regarding 
scheme and wonders if allocation was made without a ny proposal from the 
Ministry. With Ministry having no plans or project to use the fund, such 
surprise allocation obviously led to delay. The Com mittee know the details of 
structures of these three schemes and are the benef iciaries identified. The 
Committee also cautions that the Ministry must make use of funds efficiently. 
(Para 105)

39. The Committee finds that despite reduction of funds  from Rs. 1418 
crores at BE (2014-15) to Rs. 1100 crores at RE (20 14-15). The actual 
utilization till 13.03.2015 was only Rs. 641.59 cro res.  However, in reply to 
subsequent query, the Ministry informed that there were about 58000 project 
sanctioned by the Banks amounting to Rs. 1238 crore s of margin money were 
pending for disbursal.  Were  the Committee to believe that remaining Rs. 600 
crores will be used in remaining 15 days of financi al year.  If yes, it will be 
despite Secretary’s assertion that not more than 33 % of allocation could be 
spent in one Quarter. It will also be despite Commi ttee’s several 
recommendations against crowding of expenditure tow ards the end of 
financial year?  The Committee would like to know h ow such crowding could 
happen despite Ministry’s instructions to disburse the money within 100 days 
of receiving the applications. The Committee too ha d recommended that 
DLTFC should meet at least once in two months to sc reen the pending 
applications thoroughly. The Committee also distressed to note that against an 
employment target of 8,24,852, only 2 lakh employment could be generated till 
13.03.2015.  The Committee feels that Ministry must  re-design the procedure 
to salvage the objective of the flagship scheme.  C onsidering that 58000 
projects were still pending with Banks for disbursa l, the Committee wonders 
why cases were referred to banks so late and withou t such screening at the 
level of DLTFC.  During the interaction, the Commit tee asked the Secretary 
to furnish the number of cases that have been settl ed within prescribed 100 
days.  Looking at the low success rate of the cases  cleared by DLTFC, the 
Committee feels that in order to streamline the pro cedure and reduce the 
time, Ministry must do  away  with the DLTFCs  and  like other  Schemes, the 
applicant should directly approach the Banks.  Anot her solution could be to 
shift the Scheme from margin money subsidy to inter est subvention scheme, 
since the investment limit in PMEGP is fixed. The C ommittee must also be 

informed as to how many districts have been able to meet 100 PMEGP project 
targets.  
(Para 110) 
 
40. The Committee noted that 800 clusters were proposed  to be developed 
during 12 
th  Plan.  71 cluster, majority of them Mini Clusters with less than 
500 artisans were to be set up in the current first  phase.  Guidelines of 
revamped SFURTI were issued only in August, 2014.  After complex and 
protracted procedure only 17 proposals have  been shortlisted for preparation 
 
-70- 
of preparatory project report and other preliminary  survey and 
documentation. The Committee in convinced that goin g by general 
performance of Ministry, it is highly improbable that 800 clusters could be set 
up during 12 th  Plan period till 2017.  It appears that the Minist ry due it own 
complex processes, is severely constricted and hamp ered in achieving its own 
targets. 
(Para 117) 
41.  The Committee feels that the previous experience h as told us that the 
Cluster based approach is essentially against the b asic character of MSME 
sector. The Units operate individually and independ ently under individual 
ownership or limited partnership.  To ask MSME unit s to form Cluster will 
only delay the process as it involves land issues a nd would require 
administrative and statutory clearances which may vary from State to State.  
(Para 118) 
42. The Committee observes that the level of Non-Plann ed expenditure 
must be reduced and  scarce resources should be use d for Planned schemes 
for the Sector and coir artisans. For this the Comm ittee had recommended to 
drastically reduce the size of Coir Board and its C ommittees. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendation and asks the Ministry to bring a comprehensive 
amendment to the Coir Act, expeditiously. 
(Para 130) 
43. The Committee has also learnt that domestic coir i ndustries are facing 
shortage of raw material as coir is being exported to China at a concessional 
duty and the finished imported Chinese Coir product s are driving the 

domestic producers out of competition in our own ma rket. The Committee 
recommends that the Government should address this duty imbalance.  
(Para 131) 
44. The Committee suggests that the possibility must b e explored to use coir 
fiber in the production of paper and packaging material.  
(Para 132) 
 
 
 
-71- 
45.     The Committee noted that the year after year, the allocations meant for 
North Eastern Region have remain almost unspent. As  per the Budgetary 
norms the 10% of the Planned allocation is allocate d to NE Region which if 
unspent goes into a non lapsable pool of fund. The basic intention of such 
initiative was to persuade Ministries to undertake developmental works in the 
region. Given the rich tradition of crafts and ecol ogy, the NE region is best 
suited for scaling up the micro, small and medium e nterprises. Yet, in 2013-
14, Rs 333 crores remained unspent. Last year, 2014 -15 the BE allocation of 
Rs 333 crores was reduced  to Rs 221 crores. This y ear, 2015-16, the BE is 
further reduced to Rs 202 crores. The Committee wou ld like to judge the 
performance of Ministry in NE region in context of the commitment made in 
the Budget speech that priority will be given for m ainstreaming the North 
Eastern Region in nations economy.  
(Para 134) 
46. The Committee is dismayed to note that its repeate d recommendations 
seeking better and efficient utilization of scarce funds for as vital sector as 
MSME, have been undermined by the Ministry despite its repeated assurance 
to   improve the  performance.  Every  year  the  M inistry  seeks  ever  higher 
allocation. Keeping in view the vast scope of the S ector, the Committee too 
would be inclined to support the demand. But utilization of scarce fund defeat 
all the arguments in favour of enhancing the alloca tion. The Committee 
recommends that Year-wise Budget Estimate, Revised Estimates and the 
Actual Expenditure should be provided on the Minist ry’s website. Also, the 
Financial Advisor and Chief Controller of Ministry’ s Accounts should post 
Scheme-wise Planned and Non Planned expenditures fo r every Quarter of the 
Financial Year.   

(Para 135)

schemes are too modest. The prospective beneficiary  units are not aware of 
existence of Ministry’s Schemes. In absence of awareness these schemes do not 
percolate to grass root level where these small uni ts exist. The outreach of the 
Ministry is limited as it does not have country-wid e institutional network and 
has to rely on State agencies. In order to raise th e awareness of Ministry’s 
Schemes and expand their outreach, the Ministry sho uld provide on its 
Website the link to the detailed structure of respe ctive Schemes, the details of 
resource agencies at District level, Proforma application and the check-list of  
 
-72- 
documents required for making application. The Comm ittee feels that these 
steps will improve performance of the Ministry and its Schemes and can be 
done with this year given Government’s emphasis on E-governance. 
(Para 136) 
 48. In fact the primary responsibility for promotion a nd development of 
MSMEs lies with State Government.  The Government o f India can only 
supplement the efforts of the State Governments.  T he role of the Ministry of 
MSME is mainly to assist the States in their effort s to promote growth and 
development of MSMEs.  However, instead of assisting the State Government, 
the Ministry has devised its own Schemes and implements them through State 
agencies like KVIBs and DICs.  Often there is overl ap of schemes or 
duplication of programmes of Center and State Governments. The Committee 
finds that though State Governments are involved in  consultative process at 
apex level, and execution level, the Central and State agencies do not converge 
institutionally.  Financial institutions like Banks  have their own schemes for 
MSME sector.  While the Ministry has often argued t hat the delay in 
implementing Schemes are mainly due to financial in stitutions and Banks. 
The Committee found that Banks have been meeting th eir annual credit 
lending targets to MSMEs.  The Ministry has to look   into the  causes as why 
do not Banks come forward to support Ministry’s Sch emes for which there is 
Budget allocation.  
(Para 137) 
49. The Committee observes that uptil 2006, the Small Scale Industries 
sector was being regulated under Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 
1951. However, with the passage of 73 rd  Constitution (Amendment) Act, 1992, 

the small and Khadi & Cottage Industries were place d in Eleventh Schedule 
under the mandate of Panchayati Raj Institutions.   As  per  the  Article      
243 G,  the  State  Legislature  has  the legislati ve power over Panchayati Raj 
Institutions. As such, the Central Government  has  limited  role  in  the  
subjects pertaining the Development of Small and Co ttage Industries and 
Khadi, with Industries (Development & Regulation) A ct, 1951 being 
superseded by the 73 rd  Constitution Amendment.  This is also corroborated  in 
the constricted outreach of the schemes of Ministry  of MSME. Despite 
generous annual allocations, the annual targets of Ministry’s schemes are too 
modest vis a vis massive scope and the Ministry is not able to utilize the 
allocations efficiently.   
(Para 138) 
 
 
 
 
-73-

the Grants of Ministry of MSME and its previous per formance in respect of

Introduction 
 
In India, the Heavy Industries Sector encompasses H eavy Engineering, Machine 
Tools, Heavy Electrical, Construction Machinery and  the Automotive Industries.  The 
output of these industries permeates almost all sec tors of the economy including basic 
infrastructure like power, rural and road transport s industries and provide heavy 
machinery that are critical to other important sect ors like mining, refineries, 
petrochemicals, fertilizers, shipping, paper, cemen t, textiles etc.  The Department of 
Heavy Industry (DHI) which looks after this industrial sector is the part of the Ministry of 
Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which was created by the President’s 
Notification dated the 15 
th  October, 1999. DHI administers 32 operating Centra l Public 
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), including 12 subsidiary  companies and 1 JV Company, i.e., 
NTPC- BHEL Power projects Pvt. Ltd. The Department also administers the following 
autonomous organizations; 
  
a)  NATRiP 
b)  FCRI 
c)  ARAI 
d)  NAB 
 
2. As per the Economic Survey, 2014-15, the Index o f Industrial Production 
suggests that the Industrial sector is recovering s lowly but steadily with a 2.1% growth in 
April-December 2014-15 against 0.1% during on the same period last year.  The recovery 
is lead by the infrastructure sectors, viz, electrical, coal & cement.  Mining Sector growth 
also turned positive during the year.  From the poi nt of view of Heavy Industries, it is 
further encouraging that Capital Goods sector appears to be on the path of recovery as the 
sector has a multiplier effect on over all economic  growth.  This trend of growth in the 
Industrial Sector coupled with the  ‘Make in India’  programme aimed to facilitate  
investment, foster innovation, enhance skill develo pment, protect intellectual property 
and build best -in -class  manufacturing infrastruc ture rolled out by the Government 
makes the Budget of year 2015-16 , a period of reckoning.

the teething issues like coal availability which ha s been hampering the growth of the

NATRiP 
 
 
21. The National Automotive Testing R & D Infrastru cture Project (NATRiP), 
approved by the Government in 2005, envisaged setti ng up of world-class automotive 
testing and homologation facilities in India with a  total investment of Rs.  1,718 crore. 
However, right from its inception, the execution of  the NATRiP has been badly delayed 
and has suffered cost escalation due to several rea sons.  The project got extended to 2012  
and thereafter, the Cabinet again extended the time  line for completion of the project up 
to 31 
st  December, 2014.  The revised cost of the project w hich was to be completed by 
December 2014 was Rs. 2288.06 crore. But the Commit tee notes with extreme concern 
that the completion of NATRiP still needed time.   
 
22. In reply to a question regarding reasons which necessitated further extension of 
time for completion and the cost escalation, DHI su bmitted that initially scheduled date 
of completion of NATRiP project was April, 2011, wh ich was extended to December, 
2012 and further to December, 2014.  The proposal f or further extension till December 
2017 was under process. The project had faced hurdl es in the initial stages on account of 
delays in acquisition of land at various sites, del ays in clearances, shifting of utilities, 
contractual complications, etc. First Revised Cost Estimate (RCE-I) of NATRIP was 
approved by CCEA in April, 2011 at Rs.2288.06 crore . During the implementation of the 
project as per RCE-I approval, it was observed that  the escalation for land cost and the 

increased cost of Civil and Infrastructure works fo r the project were captured only 
partially and there was also foreign exchange variation during the period including delays 
in implementation. The RCE-II proposal of NATRIP wi th proposed cost at Rs.3827.30 
crore with the revised date of completion of the pr oject as 31 st  December, 2017 is under 
the consideration and will be shortly submitted to CCEA for approval. 
  Main reasons for cost overrun were:  
• Increase due to price escalation (Rs.80.80 cr.),  
• Foreign exchange variation (Rs.115.09 cr.),  
• Change in scope (Rs.75.88 cr.),  
• Additions/deletions (Rs.247.23 cr.),  
• Under estimation of certain items in RCE-I (Rs.190.28 cr.),  
• Land acquisition (Rs.145.45 cr.) and  
• Other reasons (Rs.684.51 cr. mainly due to terminat ion of M/s. IVRCL 
contracts for non-performance at risk and cost basis.   
 
23. During 2014-15, an amount of Rs 241.91 crore was released to NATRIP till Oct. 
2014. Since the project completion date expired on 31.12.2014, further fund could not be 
released to NATRIP. As part of the examination of D FG 2015-16, the Department 
submitted before the Committee that Rs 300 Crore ha s been earmarked to NATRiP as 
loan during 2015-16. 
 
24. The Committee notes with apprehension that NATR iP, which was originally 
thought to be completed in 6 years from 2005, after  the expiry of two extensions 
spanning three years from 2012 to 2014, still needs  three more years, i.e., upto 2017, 
for completion.  Having taken cognizance of all sta ted reasons for delays, the 
Committee, still feels that even a flagship project  like NATRiP, which has delivered 
a lot of unprecedented results, could not escape ti me and cost overruns which are 
typical banes of the Indian administrative system.  The Committee is of the 
considered opinion that NATRiP sans the delays woul d have produced more 
spectacular results. Therefore, the Committee recom mends that every effort should 
be made to successfully wind up the project by the current period of extension being 
sought.  The details of the completion of NATRiP sh ould be presented to the 
Committee in the form of a comprehensive Status Report.

st

Capital Goods Sector 
 
 
31. The Capital Goods Sector (CGS) provides the bas e for a strong, resilient and 
vibrant manufacturing sector.  An effective manufac turing sector is essential for the 
prudent economic growth of the country.  Basic infr astructure buildup is also dependent 
on the products of the CGS.  Besides, the sector al so creates a considerable amount of 
employment opportunities.  The performance of CGS i s vital for DHI as they overlook 
the sector in India and is also in administrative c ontrol of some of the largest CPSEs of 
India that are big stakeholder in the sector. The C GS in India saw a growth of 4.9% 
during April-November 2014-15 as compared to the gr owth of -0.1% during the 
corresponding period of the last year.  
 
32. As part of the DFG examination of DHI for the y ear 2015-16, the Committee 
sought the views of major Industry associations cat ering to the sector.  The interaction 
brought forth the concern and expectations of the v arious private players in the CGS.  
Their demands included efficient and expedient impl ementation of Scheme for 
Enhancement of Competitiveness in Capital Goods Ind ustry, Purchase Preference 
Mechanism by Government and Public Sector Enterpris es for Indian companies, creation 
of level playing field for the domestic CGS in the wake of FTAs, regulation of import of 
second hand equipment, development of manufacturing  cluster and zones, demand 

creation in the power sector through enhanced publi c and private investment.  Further, 
the need for Skill Development /Skilled manpower, rectification of inverted customs duty 
structure, making transfer of technology to Indian partner mandatory, in cases of large 
imports of machinery, setting up of Technology Acqu isition Fund and Centres of 
Excellences were also stressed as the requirements of the sector.  
 
33. Regarding the dynamics of the sector, in the ov erall economy, it was 
submitted to the Committee, that whenever an econom y undergoes a bit of 
recession, this sector was the first area to be eff ected and when there is a recovery, 
this is the sector which recovers last.  Considerin g this and the fact that the CGS is 
one of the most important contributors to national growth, the Committee 
recommends that DHI should explore the possibility of acting upon the suggestions 
made by the Industrial associations and provide a r eport to the Committee on the 
basis of a detailed feasibility examination.  
 
34. In this regard the Committee further recommends tha t along with skill 
Development, the Department should consider and pro mote the system of 
apprenticeship programmes on the lines of similar a pproaches being followed in 
nations like Japan and China.  Also, the establishm ent of Centers of Excellence with 
participation of Universities, so that small player s of the  industry sectors who 
cannot invest large sums of money on R&D can also be benefited with such facilities. 
 
Scheme for Enhancement of Competiveness in Capital Goods Industry 
 
 
35. The Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness i n the Capital Goods Sector 
aims to make the Indian Capital Goods sector global ly competitive by addressing the issues of 
lack of technology and innovation, lack of industry  academia connectivity for technology 
development, non-availability of adequate infrastru ctural facility on value chain in 
manufacturing, absence of test and certification ce ntres etc. The Scheme envisages 
infrastructural intervention through Scheme components like setting up of (i) Centre of 
Excellence for technology development, (ii) Integra ted industrial infrastructure centre, 

(iii) Common Engineering Facility centre   (iv) Tes t & Certification centre and (v) 
Technology Acquition Fund.  
 
36. The Scheme, with an outlay of Rs. 2360 crore wa s proposed to Planning 
Commission in 2012- 13, i.e, during the 1 
st  year of the 12 th  Five Year Plan (2012-17). 
DHI proposed a requirement of Rs.10, 600.26 crore a s Plan budgetary support including 
the scheme of capital goods.  However, Planning Com mission on 4.1.2013 allocated only 
Rs. 4680 crore to DHI for the 12 th  plan.  This led to a drastic reduction of Plan bud getary 
support for the scheme to Rs. 581.22 crore.  Howeve r, in January, 2015 the Planning 
Commission had approved the scheme in principle. 
 
37. Regarding the delay in the approval of the sche me, DHI submitted that the 
process for obtaining approval of the Expenditure F inance Committee (EFC) was 
initiated soon after the Planning Commission commun icated it’s ‘in principle approval’.  
In a review meeting chaired by the then Secretary, HI  on 20.3.2013 it was decided to 
visit Indian Institutes of Technology (Delhi, Mumba i and Madras) to explore the 
possibilities of their intervention for technology development in collaboration with the 
domestic capital goods industry.  After interaction s with Indian Institutes of Technology 
(IITs) and  Federation of Indian Chambers of Commer ce and Industry (FICCI) on 
Technology Acquisition Fund, a  draft memorandum fo r EFC was circulated on 5.9.2013 
to the concerned Ministries/ Departments / Organiza tions with approval of the then 
Minister of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises. After receiving comments/ views 
from the concerned Ministries/ Departments/ Organiz ations note for EFC was finalized 
and sent to Ministry of Finance on 17.1.2014.  The EFC considered and approved the 
proposal in its meeting dated 26.2.2014.  However, minutes of the meeting was received 
in DHI only on 23.4.2014.  DHI agreed to comments/ recommendations of the EFC, with 
the exception that funding by GoI for Test and Cert ification Centre should be 100% as 
opposed to EFC recommendation of limiting governmen t contribution to 80% of the 
project cost. Since there has been a deviation  fro m EFC recommendations before 
approaching (CCEA), it was decided to circulate the  draft Cabinet Committee on 
Economic Affairs (CCEA) note to the concerned Minis tries/ Department/ Organizations 
inviting their comments/ views. After obtaining com ments and views the proposal on the 

scheme was sent to CCEA on 25.8.2014.  CCEA approve d the scheme with an outlay of 
Rs.930.96 crore (budgetary support Rs.581.22 crore and industry support Rs.349.74 
crore) on 15.9.2014.  The scheme was notified in the Gazette of India on 5.11.2014. 
 
38. For the current financial year, out of two proj ects approved by the Apex Committee 
formed under the scheme, 1 st  installment of Grant-in-Aid was likely to be paid to the project 
implementing authority. For infrastructural components, except technology &  
certification centre, Government funding will be li mited to 80% of the individual 
project cost. Test and Certification Centre for ear thmoving machinery will be fully 
funded by the Government. For technology acquisition fund programme, Governme nt 
contribution will be limited to 25% of the cost of acquisition/ transfer of technology subject to 
a maximum of Rs.10 crore in each case. 
 
39. During the oral evidence, when queried about th e scaling down of the originally 
conceived much larger allocation and provision of o nly a meager amount of Rs.25 crore 
for the year 2015-16, the Department submitted that  the scheme at present was a pilot 
scheme, but was initially conceived with a much wid er proposal.  It was also informed 
that there were several proposals under the scheme and DHI had chalked out a roadmap 
for obtaining proposal for incurring expenditure un der the scheme.  Further, it was also 
informed by DHI that a large number of Small & Medi um Enterprises (SMEs) in the 
private sector have come forward   enthusiastically, for the scheme.   
 
40. The Committee notes that though the scheme was originally proposed during 
2012-13, the final approval has come through only i n August, 2014.  Meanwhile, the 
original proposed outlay of Rs. 2360 crore has been  reduced to a Plan Budgetary 
support of only Rs. 581.22 crore.  This scaling dow n of fund indicates that the 
original span of activities planned under the schem e has also been shrunk.  In view 
of this, the Committee expresses its apprehension a bout the adequacy of the 
dispensation under the scheme.  Even so, the Commit tee recommends that DHI 
should work towards the effective implementation of  the scheme as approved now, 
without allowing the usual administrative and proce dural delays to creep in, 
resulting in under performance of scheme.  

 
R&D Project for “Development of Advanced Ultra Supe rcritical (Adv. USC) 
Technology for Thermal Power Plants”  
 
41. It has been submitted to the Committee that the  R&D Project for “Development 
of Advanced Ultra Supercritical (Adv. USC) Technolo gy for Thermal Power Plants” 
will be carried out jointly by BHEL, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research and 
NTPC. The objective of the First Phase of the proje ct is to undertake R&D on all 
aspects of Adv.USC technology for thermal power pla nts in order to improve power 
plant efficiency, reduce carbon-dioxide emissions a nd reduce coal consumption per 
unit of power generated.  The Thermal efficiency of  Power Plant was expected to go 
up from 38% to 45% and it would reduce the CO2 emis sion per MW substantially. 
The proposed project would enable Indian industries  to design, manufacture and 
commission higher efficiency coal fired power plant s with indigenously developed 
technology and manufacturing process. The duration of the project is estimated to be 
of two and a half years from the date of approval. 
 
42. The Ministry of Finance has approved the propos al for providing one time 
budgetary support of Rs. 1100 Crore spread over a p eriod of three years, commencing 
from 2014-15, to be provided as plan Gross Budgetar y Support to BHEL for 
implementation of the R&D project for Development o f Advanced Ultra Supercritical 
(AUSC) Technology for Thermal Power Plants, on a Mi ssion Mode. Advanced copy of 
final CCEA Note, approved by Minister of Heavy Indu stries & Public Enterprises has 
been sent to PMO & Cabinet Secretariat on 26.02.201 5. Final CCEA Note would be sent 
to Cabinet Secretariat, for obtaining approval of C CEA, following the extant instructions 
in the matter. After final approval of CCEA, action  may be taken for implementation of 
the project.  
 
43. While examining the Budgetary allocation (2015- 16) to the scheme, the 
Committee sought explanation for the reduced allocations at RE (2014-15)  to Rs 13.23 
crore from Rs 100 crore at BE (2014-15) and also ab out the proposal of being allocated 
only Rs 50 crore at BE (2015-16), half of the amoun t of the previous BE. The 
Department replied that initially it was presumed t hat the approval of Cabinet 

Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) for the projec t could be obtained in the 3 rd  
quarter and Rs.100 crore could be utilised for the project.  Therefore, in the BE 2014-
15 allocation of Rs.100 crore was made for the proj ect.  However, subsequently at the 
RE stage, it was felt that approval of CCEA for the  project could have been possible in 
the 4 th  quarter of financial year 2014-15. Hence, as per t he guidelines issued by the 
Ministry of Finance for utilisation of funds in the  4 th  quarter of the financial year, the 
allocation of funds for the project was reduced to Rs.13.23 crore in the RE 2014-15. 
For the year 2015-16, while the Department had soug ht an allocation of Rs 583 crore, 
the Ministry of Finance had allocated only Rs 50 crore. 
 
44. The Committee notes that Advance Ultra Supercri tical Technology is the 
technology of the future in thermal power generatio n.  Higher plant efficiency and 
lesser coal consumption along with reduced carbon f ootprints are its salient 
features.  The Committee is of the considered opini on that if developed quickly it 
can help BHEL acquire a definite advantage over its  competitors in the domestic as 
well as international markets. Accordingly, the Com mittee views this as an 
endeavour that can give a fillip to BHEL in it’s st rive for recapturing lost ground in 
terms of its core business of thermal power plants.   Indigenous development of this 
technology will also give the nation an impetus in its infrastructural development.  
But, being an advanced technology, its development will need financial support 
from the Government, along with quickened process of approvals.

 Jagdishpur Paper Mill 
 
 
65. Jagdishpur Paper Mills Ltd. (JPML) was incorpor ated during the year 2008 after 
CCEA approval, for setting up a modern paper mill t o manufacture 3,00,000 tonnes of 
quality Writing & Printing Paper. The estimated cost of setting up this plant was Rs. 3700 
crores. Since the date of incorporation, not much p hysical, tangible activity could be 
made as the land was not allotted by Govt. of U.P. Meanwhile, attempts were made to 
reconfigure the project keeping in view the raw mat erial availability as well as the 
infrastructure, by getting a revised DPR prepared t hrough a renowned consultant. After 

receipt of the DPR, a fresh proposal incorporating therein the usage of substitute raw 
material was made. CCEA approvals have been obtaine d during the financial year 2012-
13. After pursuing vigorously all these years for g etting the required land at Jagdishpur a 
breakthrough could finally be made only during the year 2013. Jagdishpur Paper Mill Ltd 
(JPML) was allotted 187.59 acres of land by UP Stat e Industrial Development 
Corporation (UPSIDC) at Industrial Area Utelwa, Jag dishpur, Amethi District, UP. 
Pursuant to the allotment order cited above, JPML h ad paid EMD of Rs.11.8 Crores, 
towards the allotment of 187.59 Acres of Land and a n MoU was signed on  14.12.13 
between  UPSIDC and JPML. 
 
66. Subsequently, it was learnt from UPSIDC that Ka mala Neheru Memorial Trust 
has filed writ petition before the Hon’ble High Cou rt Lucknow Bench against allotment 
of land and the Hon’ble High Court had passed an or der dt.27.11.13 which states as 
follows:- 
           “as a interim measure we direct the part ies to maintain status quo as it exists   
today. The respondents shall ensure no construction  is raised over the land in question by 
fresh allottee. Allotment made shall be subject to further orders passed by this court.”  
 
67. Considering that the matter regarding allotment  of land to JPM is sub- judice and 
was pending before the Hon’ble Supreme court and also the fact that the project itself had 
the CCEA approval in the year 2008, the Committee s ought to know the timeframe 
further required for the commencement of the Greenf ield Pulp and Paper project at 
Jagdishpur under HPC.  The Committee also wanted to  know the possibility of 
considering an alternate location for the Mill.  In  reply, the Department stated that it 
appears the even after the present  legal battle, t here was a likelihood of litigation in the 
future from the farmers cultivating the land and the encroachers of the allotted land as the 
same is not free from encumbrances as per the averm ents made by Kamala Nehru Trust 
(KNT).  
 
68. The present litigating parties i.e. Kamala Nehr u Trust and UPSIDC have been 
fighting the legal battle from the year 2007. Recen tly, UPSIDC has communicated an 
offer to procure land from farmers and allot to JPML, if JPML was agreeable to the offer. 

The said offer of acquisition of land and allotting  the same after acquisition also may not 
be free from litigation and also quite time consumi ng. Under the circumstances, DHI has 
informed that it was not be possible to give a defi nite time frame for settlement of 
litigation and acquisition of land without encumbrances in a case wherein JPML was only 
an impleaded party and as such the settlement of li tigation would much depend on the 
main litigation parties i.e. Kamala Nehru Trust and UPSIDC. Meanwhile, attempts to find 
alternate sites to locate the project duly consider ing the raw material availability, and 
other infrastructure, were being made. 
 
69. The Committee takes note of the fact that the Green field Pulp and Paper 
Mill project at Jagdishpur, estimated at Rs. 3700 crore in 2008, has not taken off the 
ground as on date due to litigation regarding allot ment of land for the project at the 
designated site. The matter being sub judice, the C ommittee refrains from making a 
comment in this regard. Nevertheless, the Committee  recommends that nothing 
should stop the Department from earnestly exploring  the possibility of establishing 
the Mill at an alternate location taking into accou nt factors like raw material 
availability and other linkages. The Committee is o f the considered opinion that it is 
unacceptable to let an important project worth Rs. 3700 crore linger on indefinitely 
without its operationalisation being expected in near future.

coupled with the favorable initiatives like the ‘Ma ke in India’ campaign of the

Modified Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (MDRS) for NPP C and the Revival process

(Para No 6)

Committee finds that for the year 2015-16 too DHI h as been given lesser Plan funds 
compared to the Non Plan allocations. As per the current classification of funds, this 
trend points towards less asset creation activities  under DHI year after year. 
Accordingly, in view of the Committee, the activiti es of DHI are gradually tilting 
towards non creative activities like winding up of CPSEs, settling dues, managing 
VRS, etc.  Though there might be a contrary view th at winding up of sick CPSEs 
also contributes indirectly to asset creation and e fficient channelisation of available 
resources, as per extant classification of Plan and  Non Plan activities, it does not 
count as a productive activity.

activities of DHI are either stagnating or getting reduced.  This would also mean 
that the Department has largely been unable to come  up with schemes necessary to 
cater to the varying needs of the extremely important Heavy Industries Sector in the 
country.  In view of the above, the Committee obser ves that DHI should strive more 
to come up with Plan schemes in a proactive manner by gauging the needs of the 
Heavy Industries Sector. Such initiatives will faci litate business environment in the 
sector.  
(Para No 10)

crucial input studies that could have benefited the  flagship schemes of DHI could

depth study for critical analysis as well as impact  assessment of Capital Goods

such studies should be done with more frequency, wh ich would in turn help DHI, 
the administrative Department of such crucial secto rs, to come up with innovative

Advance Ultra Super Critical Technology for Thermal  Power Plants will also help 
BHEL to stay a cut above their competitors. The Com mittee also observes that DHI 
should extend maximum assistance is to BHEL in this matter.  
(Para No 53) 

 
 Also, the Committee is happy to observe that BHEL i s also making use of the 
slogan “Make in India’ in Hanover to invite countri es like Germany to work in 
collaboration with India to boost the quantum of business of BHEL. 
(Para No 53) 
17. The Committee views the fall in the performance  of HEC and its pathetic 
state of affairs with extreme disappointment. In it s Report on DFG (2013-14), the 
Committee had recommended that HEC, which was a shi ning example of a CPSE 
turning around with the help of a revival package, should be extended all support in 
its modernization efforts.  However, the Committee finds that two years from then, 
HEC, though has managed to prepare a Modernization plan, is still far from its 
implementation. The Committee observes that HEC, fr om a turn around champion 
has been reduced to another victim of administrativ e lethargy and managerial 
ineptitude. In view of the above, the Committee rei terates its earlier 
recommendation of extending all possible support of  DHI to the Modernizations of 
HEC by helping them in securing the portion of fund s the Company has to raise 
through loans from financial institutions /banks.  In case, HEC is unable to secure 
the same on their own within a reasonable time limi t, DHI should even considering 
enhancing the budgetary assistance of Rs. 500 crore  appropriately.  The Committee 
is also not averse to resorting to foreign collabor ation for the Modernization of 
HEC.  However, the solution to the problems faced b y HEC has to come before the 
Company goes beyond the point of recovery. 
(Para No 58) 
18. Taking into account the present problems being face d by the company, the 
Target set by HEC for achievements during 2014-15, and 2015-16, the Committee is 
of the considered opinion that these are unreasonab ly high, especially, when during 
2014-15, they could attain only one fourth of the s et target. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends, that under the circumstance HEC should set only realistic, 
attainable targets for itself. 
(Para No 59) 

19. The Committee observes that R&C was referred to  the BIFR almost quarter 
a century ago, in 1992, but, now DHI has agreed tha t the latest revival plan of R&C 
can be implemented since it does not involve any cash assistance and the Company’s 
activities can be considered as the core activities of economy falling under the ‘Make 
in India’ campaign. In this context, the Committee recommends the DHI should 
expeditiously place the revival of R&C for approval  of the Cabinet and help the 
company in its road to revival.  
(Para No 64) 
 
20. The Committee takes note of the fact that the Green field Pulp and Paper 
Mill project at Jagdishpur, estimated at Rs. 3700 crore in 2008, has not taken off the 
ground as on date due to litigation regarding allot ment of land for the project at the 
designated site. The matter being sub judice, the C ommittee refrains from making a 
comment in this regard. Nevertheless, the Committee  recommends that nothing 
should stop the Department from earnestly exploring  the possibility of establishing 
the Mill at an alternate location taking into accou nt factors like raw material 
availability and other linkages. The Committee is o f the considered opinion that it is 
unacceptable to let an important project worth Rs. 3700 crore linger on indefinitely 
without its operationalisation being expected in near future. 
(Para No 69)

Report  
 
 
Introduction 
 
 
 Public sector units are hailed as ‘the temples of modern India.’ Government of 
India has employed the public sector enterprises to  achieve various socio-economic 
objectives. The basic difference between private an d public ownership is the difference 
lies in their objectives, viz welfare maximization by the public sector and profi t 
maximization by the private sector. The Central Pub lic Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) 
comprise enterprises established by the Government of India (GOI) as Government 
companies under Section 617 of the Companies Act, a nd wherein the equity holding of 
the GOI is more than 50 per cent. It also includes statutory corporations constituted under 
specific statutes of the Parliament. The CPSEs do n ot, however, include departmental 
undertakings, banking institutions and enterprises where equity holding of the GOI is 
50% or less.  
 
2. As per the Public Enterprises Survey (2013-14), there were 290 Central Public 
Sector Enterprises consisting of 234 operating CPSE s and 56 CPSEs under construction 
as on 31.3.2014.  The turnover of all 234 operating  CPSEs during 2013-14 stood at Rs. 
20, 61,866 crore as compared to Rs. 19, 45,814 cror e of 230 operating CPSEs in the 
previous year. The list of 64 Schedule ‘A’, 68 Sche dule ‘B’, 46 Schedule ‘C’ and 4 
Schedule ‘D’ CPSEs is placed at Annexure-I.  Also, the list containing names of the  7  
Maharatna, 17 Navratna and 72 Miniratna CPSEs is kept at Annexure-II.  
 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE)  
Mandate  
 
3. The DPE is the nodal department for all the Cent ral Public Sector Enterprises and 
formulates policy pertaining to CPSEs.  Mandate of DPE as submitted to the Committee, 
lays down policy guidelines on performance improvem ent and evaluation, autonomy and 
financial delegation  and personnel management in CPSEs. Furthermore, it  collects and 
maintains information on several areas in respect of CPSEs.  
 

4.         The Committee was also informed that as per Allocation of Business Rules of the 
Government, the following include the functions all ocated to the Department of Public 
Enterprises:- 
 
i) Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industria l Management Pool. 
 
ii)     Coordination of matters of general policy o f  non-financial  nature       
affecting all public sector industrial and commercial undertakings. 
 
iii)     Matters relating to Memorandum of Understa nding mechanism of 
improving the performance of public sector undertakings. 
 
iv)       Matters relating to Permanent Machinery o f Arbitration for the Public 
Sector Undertakings. 
 
v)        Counselling, Retraining and Rehabilitatio n of employees in Central Public 
Sector Undertakings under Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
 
 
5. The Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) was set up in 
December, 2004 to consider inter-alia , Revival/Restructuring proposals of Sick/Loss 
making CPSEs and make suitable recommendations rela ted thereto. The DPE provides 
secretariat support to BRPSE. 
  
6. In fulfilling its role, the Department coordinat es with other Ministries, CPSEs and 
concerned organization.  Some of the important task s of the Department are listed as 
follows: 
 
i)  Co-ordination of matters of general policy of non-financial  nature relating 
to Public Sector Enterprises. 
 
ii)  Issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to Public Sector 
Enterprises. 
 
iii)  Publication of the annual survey of CPSEs known as Public Enterprises 
Survey. 
 
iv)  Memorandum of Understanding between the Public Sector Enterprises and 
the Administrative Ministries/Departments. 
 
v)  Formulation of policies pertaining to Public Sector  Enterprises in areas 
like Board Structures, Personnel Management, Performance Improvement, 

Financial Management , Wage Settlement and Vigilance management, 
etc.   
 
vi)  Matters relating to reservation of posts in the Pub lic sector Enterprises for 
certain classes of citizens. 
 
vii)  Policy relating to Voluntary Retirement Scheme in CPSEs. 
 
viii)  Matters relating to Counseling, Retraining and Rede ployment Scheme 
(CRR) for rationalized employees of CPSEs. 
 
ix)  Investiture and review of Maharatana / Navratana / Miniratna status to 
CPSEs. 
 
x)  Policy matters relating to composition of Board of Directors of CPSEs, 
Categorization of top posts Scheduling of CPSEs.  
 
xi)  Notification of Pay Scales of Board level executive s as well as below 
Board level personnel and unionized workers and the  DA admissible 
thereon at periodic intervals. 
 
xii)  Policy relating to deputation of Government officer s to Public Sector 
Enterprises. 
 
xiii)  Matters relating to reservation of posts in the Pub lic sector Enterprises for 
certain classes of citizens. 
 
xiv)  Settlement of disputes through Permanent Machinery of Arbitration 
(PMA) among Public Sector Enterprises and between P ublic Sector 
Enterprises and Government Departments except dispu tes relating to tax 
matters. 
 
xv)  Matters relating to International Centre for Promot ion of Enterprises 
(ICPE).  
 
xvi)  Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE). 
 
xvii)  Matters relating to delegation of powers to Board of Directors.  
 
xviii)  Matters relating to Board for Reconstruction of Pub lic Sector Enterprises 
(BRPSE). 
 
7. The Committee notes that as per the Allocation o f Business Rules, the 
functions of DPE includes inter-alia  ` Coordination of matters of general policy of 
non-financial 
 nature affecting all public sector industrial and commercial 

undertakings'.  However, as per the submission made  before the Committee during 
the oral evidence relating to the examination of De mands for Grants (DFG)  (2015-
16), the functions of DPE includes laying down of p olicy guidelines on autonomy 
and financial  delegation.  Similar dichotomous position regarding  the mandate of 
DPE on financial matter is also reflected in the Ou tcome Budget of the Ministry of 
Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises.  This incong ruence was pointed out during 
the oral evidence of DPE and a clarification was so ught.  But DPE did not provide 
the requisite information either at the meeting or in their subsequent written replies 
to the queries raised during the meeting.   
 
8. In this context, the Committee recommends that t he ambiguity regarding the 
functions of DPE relating to whether the Department  is tasked to frame 
policies/guidelines relating to financial matters n eeds to be addressed immediately.  
Accordingly, the action taken in this direction sho uld be intimated to the 
Committee.

year because of their specific nature e.g. payment for benchmarking studies, expenditure

prescribed by the Ministry of Finance.  The Committ ee notes that DPE has sought 
exemption from Ministry of Finance to iron out this  problem.  The Committee 
observes that utilisation of funds would improve on ce this streamelining of 
expenditure as per the nature of activities underta ken has been carried out.  
However, the Committee is not convinced with the st and of DPE that it has been 
able to utilise only about 37% of funds provided to  the scheme during the first three 

years of the 12th Five Year Plan solely due to the above mentioned discrepency.  
Accordingly, it is recommended that along with secu ring the requisit exemption 
from the Ministry of Finance for the expenditure un der the scheme, it is also 
imperative that the Department takes urgent measure s to improve the utilisation of 
the allocated money.  In this context, the Committe e expects that Rs.3.58 crore

28. Realizing the need to have a safety net for the  separated employees, Government 
had established the National Renewal Fund (NRF) in February, 1992 broadly to cover the 
expenses of VRS and to provide retraining to the wo rkers in the organized sector. The 
retraining activity was administered by the Departm ent of Industrial Policy & Promotion. 
However, due to various reasons NRF was abolished o n 31 
st  March 2001. Since 2001-02, 
the Scheme of Counselling, Retraining & Redeploymen t (CRR) of separated employees 
of CPSEs was implemented by the Department of Public Enterprises.  
 
29. The objective and scope of the CRR scheme is to  provide opportunities of to the 
separated employees who are rendered surplus as a r esult of modernization, technology 
upgradation and manpower restructuring in the PSEs.  The aim of retraining of the 
employees is to reorient them through short duratio n training programmes to enable them 

to adjust to the new environment and adopt new avocations after their separation from the 
PSEs due to VRS/VSS or retrenchment due to closure / restructuring of the enterprise.

Scheme was modified in the year 2007. Some of the m ajor modifications included (i) 
Training of one dependent of each VRS optee if the VRS optee himself/herself is not 
interested; (ii) Extended duration of training from  20/30/40 days to 30/45/60 days with 
revised expenditure norms; and (iii) Dedicated amou nt earmarked in the expenditure 
norm for follow-up of trained VRS optees.

in view of  the reduced physical target  due to dec lining trend of VRS in CPSEs in recent

administrative Ministries have again been requested  to furnish latest information 
regarding vacancies of Non-officials Directors of C PSEs under their respective 
jurisdiction, period of vacancy and steps being tak en to fill these vacancies. During the 
oral evidence it was also by DPE that the Companies  Act, 2013 has made it mandatory to

Ministry to comply with this provision of the Act.

nd  Report related to DFG 2013-14 of DPE, it had been

enforcing the filling up these vacancies, through i ts policy directives, including a 
penal provision during the assessment of MoU performance of a CPSE.

39. India is a founder member of ICPE in Ljubljana,  Slovenia. The annual 
contribution of India to ICPE is US$ 1, 50,000.  Th erefore, budgetary provisions have 
been made under this head. DPE informed that the pr ovision of Rs. 0.87 crore in BE 
2014-15 consists of Rs. 0.72 crore for payment of I ndia’s membership contribution to 
ICPE. Hence, the fund allocation is in terms of con tribution as a member and does not 
come under the category of a scheme.

45. The Government constituted BPRSE  vide  Resolution dated 6 th  December, 2004 as

restructuring of CPSEs and to advise the Government  on strategies, measures and 
schemes related to them.

recommendations of BRPSE due to its statutory backi ng. Accordingly, this Committee 
recommended that when National Company Law Tribunal  (NCLT) was put in place of 
BIFR, its mandate should avoid any duplication of work with BRPSE. The Department in 
its Action Taken Note (ATN) assured the Committee t hat its recommendation would be 
represented appropriately at the time of constitution of the new body.

a new entity, DPE failed to respond.

reported to be replaced in the near future.  The Co mmittee views these proposed 
changes as a potential watershed in the area of revival /restructuring of CPSEs.  The 
Committee recalls that during their co-existence ti ll now, owing to certain overlaps 
and conflicts in the roles essayed by BIFR and BRPS E in approaching the revival

avoidable delays. Accordingly, in the backdrop of t he proposed replacement of

in the role assigned to the new entity of BRPSE and  the NCLT which has been 
conceived to replacing BIFR. Further, the new agenc ies should be conceived in such 
a manner that the revival /restructuring of CPSEs s hall be completed in a 
prescribed timeframe without lingering for years.

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action 
Taken by the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium En terprises on the 
recommendations contained in the Committee’s Two Hu ndred Fifty Ninth 
Report on Review of the implementation of Khadi and  Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC) Act, 1956  pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises in respect of the reco mmendations contained 
in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:  
 
Chapter –I   The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted

 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report.

not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies.

Committee has either not accepted replies of the Mi nistry or has asked the 
Ministry to review its reply. 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry 
should furnish logical explanations therefor. 
 
Chapter -IV    The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final

 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has 
either furnished the interim replies or couched its language in vague terms like

The Committee is of the opinion that the intent of the Act and its

supervision is given to Commission in order to ensu re its administrative 
autonomy required to facilitate its mandate. As the  Commission meets once a

affairs. In view of Sections 4(1), 5(1) and (1A) an d Rules 10, 11 and 12 made

Section 27 of the Act prescribe the Commissions pow ers to frame

Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee observed that the definitions of khad i and Poly-vastra 
are limited to cotton, woolen or silk yarns or mixt ure thereof. The definition 
does not include synthetic yarn. To that extent the  definition needs to be 
revised to include Poly-vastra. The definitions inc lude handspun fibre and 
handloom woven cloth. It does not include innovations like E-charkhas, which 
are meant to increase the productivity, which is on e of the objectives of the 
KVIC under Section 15 (2) (e). The Committee feels that the definition should 
be flexible enough to include technological advance s which are the mandate 
of the Commission. 
(Para 28) 
 
Action Taken  
 
The KVIC Act under Section 2 (d) defines: "khadi" m eans any cloth 
woven on handlooms in India from cotton, silk or wo ollen yarn handspun in 
India or from a mixture of any two or all of such y arns;”. However, “Poly-
vastra” is defined in the schedule under Section 2 (h) of the KVIC Act, the 
entry for “village industry”. Thus the two are diff erent set of products 
altogether. As far as the proposal to include synth etic yarn in the definition is 
concerned, it may be noted that as ‘Man-made-fibre’ is already included in the 
definition of ‘polyvastra’, which includes ‘synthetic yarn’ also. 
 
As regards introduction of e-charkha, all such tech nological 
advancements can be introduced for the products und er the category of 
“village industry”. This would maintain the purity and sanctity of khadi and 
would ensure the development of a niche market for it globally. The 
suggestion would be separately examined in consulta tion with main 
stakeholders.

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 
However, the Committee remains unconvinced of the statutory status of 
the KVIC Act. As per the reply of the Secretary and  the written reply, the Act 
was framed under Entry 97 of the Union List that ga ve the residuary powers 
which rest with the Union in 1956. However, with in clusion of Khadi and 
Village industries in the Eleventh Schedule enumera ting subjects under the 
powers and responsibilities of Panchayati Raj Insti tutions ( PRIs) read with 
the Article 243 (A), power of law making on the sub jects enlisted in the said 
Schedule including KVI sector, rests inter alia wit h the State legislature. And 
as such cannot be covered under the residuary power s of the Union in List I. 
Conversely, the State Government would not have the  legislative competence 
in respect of KVI sector regardless of Article 243 (A) as residuary powers are 
to be vested in the Union Government. The Committee  therefore recommends 
that the Ministry may review the statutory position  in consultation with 
relevant Ministry/agency to give KVIC firm statutory status. 
(Para 20) 
 
Action Taken  
 
The Ministry feels that the statutory status of KVI C has been 
decided already as KVIC has been formed by an Act o f Parliament. 
However, in the light of the specific recommendatio n of the committee 
to review the statutory status of KVIC, the same ma y be done by 
obtaining suitable opinion from the Law Ministry. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
The Committee may be apprised of the opinion of the Law Ministry 
in the matter.

 The Committee may be updated of the steps taken by KVIC.
