Considering that CSR had been included in the new Companies Act, 2013, the
DPE reviewed its guidelines in tune with provisions of the Act. After extensive
consultations with key stakeholders including MCA, DPE again issued the guidelines in
October, 2014 on ‘CSR and Sustainability’ to supplement the CSR Rules issued by MCA

and became effective from 1% April, 2014.

7. DPE Guidelines on CSR and Sustainability- 2014 do not supersede or override
any provision of the Act, or Schedule VII of the Act, or the CSR Rules, but only

supplement them.

8. The following Guidelines issued by DPE on October, 2014 is applicable to all
CPSEs are generally in the nature of guiding principles.
«

i) It is mandatory for all profit making CPSEs to undertake CSR activities
as per the provisions of the Act and the CSR Rules. Even the CPSEs which are not
covered under the eligibility criteria based on threshold limits of net-worth,
turnover, or net profit as specified by Section 135 (1) of the Act, but which made
profit in the preceding year, would also be required to take up CSR activities as
specified in the Act and the CSR Rules, and such CPSEs would be expected to
spend at least 2% of the profit made in the preceding year on CSR activities.

ii) All CPSEs must adopt a CSR and Sustainability Policy specific to their
company with the approval of the Board of Directors. The philosophy and spirit
of CSR and Sustainability must be firmly ingrained in the policy and it must be
consistent with the CSR provisions of the Act, Schedule VII of the Act, CSR Rules,
the Guidelines, and the policy directions issued by the Government from time to
time. The CSR and Sustainability policy of a CPSE should serve as the referral
document for planning its CSR activities in accordance with Schedule VII of the
Act and give a road map for formulation of actionable plans.

iii) If the CPSEs feel the necessity of taking up new CSR activities / projects
during the course of a year, which are in addition to the CSR activities already
incorporated in the CSR policy of the company, the Board’s approval of such
additional CSR activities would be treated as amendment to the policy.

iv) It would be mandatory for all CPSEs which meet the criteria as laid down
in Section 135(1) of the Act, to spend at least 2% of the average net profits of the
three immediately preceding financial years in pursuance of their CSR activities
as stipulated in the Act and the CSR Rules. This stipulated percentage of average
net profits is to be spent every year in a manner specified in the Act and CSR
Rules. In case a company fails to spend such amount, it shall have to specify the
reasons for not spending it. However, in case of CPSEs mere reporting and
explaining the reasons for not spending this amount in a particular year would
not suffice and the unspent CSR amount in a particular year would not lapse. It

4


would instead be carried forward to the next year for utilisation for the purpose
Jor which it was allocated.

v) While selecting CSR activities / projects from the activities listed in
Schedule VII of the Act, CPSEs should give priority to the issues which are of
foremost concern in the national development agenda, like safe drinking water for
all, provision of toilets especially for girls, health and sanitation, education, etc.
The main focus of CSR and Sustainability policy of CPSEs should be on
sustainable development and inclusive growth, and to address the basic needs of
the deprived, under privileged, neglected and weaker sections of the society which
comprise of SC, ST, OBCs, minorities, BPL families, old and aged, women / girl
child, physically challenged, etc.

vi) For CPSEs to fully exploit their core competence and mobilize their
resource capabilities in the implementation of CSR activities / projects, they are
advised to align their CSR and Sustainability policy with their business policies
and strategies to the extent possible, and select such CSR activities / projects
which can be better monitored through in-house expertise.

vii) All CPSEs are expected to act in a socially, economically and
environmentally sustainable manner at all times. Even in their normal business
activities, public sector companies should try to promote sustainable development
through sustainability initiatives by conducting business in a manner that is
beneficial to both, business and society. They are advised not to lose sight of their
social and environmental responsibility and commitment to sustainable
development even in activities undertaken in pursuance of their normal course of
business. National and global sustainability standards which promote ethical
practices, transparency and accountability in business may be referred to as
guiding frameworks to plan, implement, monitor and report sustainability
initiatives. But the amount spent on sustainability initiatives in the pursuit of
sustainable development while conducting normal business activities would not
constitute a part of the CSR spend from 2% of profits as stipulated in the Act and
the CSR Rules. se

viii) As a part of their sustainability initiatives CPSEs are expected to give
importance to environmental sustainability even in their normal mainstream
activities by ensuring that their internal operations and processes promote
renewable sources of energy, reduce / re-use / recycle waste material, replenish
ground water supply, protect / conserve / restore the ecosystem, reduce carbon
emissions and help in greening the supply chain. CPSEs are expected to behave in
a responsible manner by producing goods and services which are safe and
healthy for the consumers and the environment, resource efficient, consumer
friendly, and environmentally sustainable throughout their life cycles i.e. from the
stage of raw material extraction to production, use / consumption, and final
disposal. However, such sustainability initiatives will not be considered as CSR
activities as specified in the CSR Rules, and the expenditure incurred thereon
would also not constitute a part of the CSR spend. Nevertheless, CPSEs are
encouraged to take up such sustainability initiatives from their normal budgetary
expenditure as it would demonstrate their commitment to sustainable
development.


ix) Sustainability initiatives would also include steps taken by CPSEs to
promote welfare of employees, especially women, physically challenged, SC / ST /
OBC categories, by addressing their concerns of safety, security, professional
enrichment and healthy working conditions beyond what is mandated by law.
However, expenditure on such sustainability initiatives would not qualify as CSR
spend.

x) The philosophy and spirit of CSR and Sustainability should be understood
and imbibed by the employees at all levels and get embedded in the core values of
the company.

xi) CPSEs should extend their reach and oversight to the entire supply chain
network to ensure that as far as possible suppliers, vendors, service providers,
clients, and partners are also committed to the same principles and standards of
corporate social responsibility and sustainability as the company itself. CPSEs
are encouraged to initiate and implement measures aimed at ‘greening’ the
supply chain.

xii) As mentioned in the Act, CPSEs should give preference to the ‘local area’
in selecting the location of their CSR activities. It is desirable that the Board of
Directors of CPSEs define the scope of the ‘local area’ of their commercial units /
plants / projects, keeping in view the nature of their commercial operations, the
extent of the impact of their operations on society and environment, and the
suggestions / demands of the key stakeholders, especially those who are directly
impacted by the company’s commercial operations / activities. The definition of
‘local area’ may form part of the CSR policy of the CPSE.

xiii) After giving due preference to the local area, CPSEs may also undertake
CSR activities anywhere in the country. The Board of Directors of each CPSE
may also decide on an indicative ratio of CSR spend between the local area and
outside it, and this may be mentioned in the CSR policy of the CPSE. CPSEs,
which by the very nature of their business have no specific geographical area of
commercial operations, may take up CSR activities / projects at any location of
their choice within the country.

xiv) As far as possible, CPSEs should take up the CSR activities in project,
which entails planning the stages of execution in advance by fixing targets at
different milestones, with pre-estimation of quantum of resources required within
the allocated budget, and having a definite time span for achieving desired
outcomes.

xv) CPSEs should devise a communication strategy for regular dialogue and
consultation with key stakeholders to ascertain their views and suggestions
regarding the CSR activities and sustainability initiatives undertaken by the
company. However, the ultimate decision in the selection and implementation of
CSR activities would be that of the Board of the CPSE.

xvi) As per the CSR Rules, all companies are required to include an annual
report on CSR in their Board’s Report. The template / format for reporting CSR
activities as provided by CSR Rules should be strictly adhered to. However,
CPSEs shall also have to include in the Board’s Report a brief narrative on the
action taken for the implementation of the Guidelines so that the stakeholders are

6


informed of not only the CSR activities but also of the sustainability initiatives
taken by the CPSEs. CPSEs are further advised to prepare an Annual
Sustainability Report, which would go a long way in imparting greater
transparency and accountability to the company’s operations, apart from
improving the brand image.

xvii) It is desirable that CPSEs get a baseline/ need assessment survey done
prior to the selection of any CSR activity. It is also desirable that CPSEs should
get an impact assessment study done by external agencies of the CSR activities /
projects undertaken by them. Impact assessment is mandatory for mega projects,
the threshold value of which can be determined by the Board of a CPSE and
specified in its CSR and Sustainability policy. However, the expenditure incurred
on baseline survey and impact assessment study should be within the overall limit
of 5% of administrative overheads of CSR spend as provided for under the CSR
Rules.

xviii) Within the provisions of the Act, Schedule VII of the Act, and the CSR
Rules, CPSEs are encouraged to take up CSR activities / projects in collaboration
with other CPSEs for greater social, economic and environmental impact of their
CSR activities / projects.

xix) CSR projects taken up by CPSEs in 2013-14 under DPE guidelines on
CSR & Sustainability which were effective from Ist April 2013, may be continued
till their completion. However, CPSEs to ensure that all new CSR activities /
projects are in accordance with the CSR Rules.

xx)  CPSEs which are statutory corporations should also comply with the
provisions of the Act, CSR Rules and the Guidelines.

xxi) These guidelines will supersede the guidelines / circulars / instructions

issued earlier by DPE on the subject of CSR and Sustainability.

Preference to local Area in CSR

14... Section 135 (v) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that the local area of the
company’s and the areas around it where it operates shall be given preference to pursue
CSR activities. The Committee, during its interaction with the Ministry, wanted to know
if this section prevented the companies altogether from carrying out CSR activities in

However, there was no compulsion in this behalf and, certainly, there was no bar to

should take into account the development of remote backward areas of the country.
These are areas where the pace of industrial development has been slow due to their
geographic isolation. While neighborhood community and local area with reference

to company’s works have first claim over CSR projects, Schedule VII should also

31. An important aspect that caught the attention of the Committee Was PSUs
carrying out CSR activities going into the red and thereby their ongoing CSR activities
getting hampered. The Committee also noted that though the Companies Act, 2013
envisaged that CSR activities should be self sustaining projects, most activities under

32. In this backdrop, the Committee, perceiving the need for sustainability of CSR

maintained and whether any. corpus was set aside from the CSR funds to maintain or
sustain to assists/activities under CSR. Moreover, the Committee also wanted to know if
the CSR Rules, 2014 allowed expenditure incurred towards maintenance of social assets

or recurrent expenditure on CSR activities as expenditure under CSR.

33. While responding to these queries the MCA submitted in their written reply dated
5.12.15 in affirmation that any expenditure incurred towards maintenance of such assets
should be counted as CSR expenditure and further clarified that expenditure towards
maintenance of social assets can be met with funds under certain conditions. However,
clarification needs to be issued in this direction. Further, MCA also submitted that “Rule
4 (1) of CSR, Rules, 2014 requires corporates to undertake CSR activities in a project or
programme mode. A project by definition would have finite time frame. Sustainability of
the same is required to be factored into the project design itself at the very beginning.
15


Board of the Corporate is responsible for taking this into account and design project
accordingly. This is some kind of corporate innovation one would look forward to. No

specific clarification has been issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs in this regard.”

34. The Committee takes note of the responses of MCA and appreciates the fact
that sustainability is expected to be factored into the design of CSR projects at its
beginning. However, the Committee also takes cognizance of the fact that a good
share of CSR activities are purely welfare oriented and may not strictly fit into a
project/programme mode where sustainability can be built in. This aspect of
sustainability of CSR initiatives will be even more accentuated in the case of CPSEs
who are prone to fluctuating earnings/profits. Further, the CSR, Rules, 2014 include
‘ongoing’ activities under CSR activities. While emphasis is on the self sustaining
CSR projects, the activities listed in Schedule VII are one off activities that do not
generate revenue even to maintain these assets and are therefore non-self sustaining.
Provisions should be made for maintenance of CSR assets in successive years.
Therefore, the Committee is of the considered opinion that DPE should mention in
their guidelines for maintenance of CSR assets created under CSR budget. So that

the assets are maintained otherwise the whole funds would go waste.

Financial Audit of CSR activities.

35. The Committee at its meeting held on 18" November, 2014 raised the issue of
audit of CSR fund. MCA in their written reply submitted that Section 143 of the
Companies Act, 2013 prescribes Auditing Standard for auditing the Annual Financial
Statements of the companies, which would also include expenditure incurred on CSR by
eligible companies. Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) is developing a
“Guidance Note for the Auditors for Expenditure of CSR activities’ that will provide

guidance to auditors and it is at an advanced stage of finalization.

36. The Ministry repeated the same reply in their written communication to the
Committee again on 3" February, 2015. Thereafter, during the examination of the
Demand for Grants (2015-16), the Committee again sought to know the latest
development regarding the finalization of the ‘Guidance Note for the Auditors’ by the
ICAI. |It was informed by DPE that after ascertaining from the MCA that the “Guidance

Note for the Auditors” was still under preparation.

16


37. Considering that there was no finite answer regarding the finalization of Guidance
Note for the auditors and the fact that the mandatory disclosures of CSR expenditure
were to be made by the companies after September, 2015, the Committee again sought to
know the progress made towards the issue of the Guidance Note. To which MCA
responded by submitting that the ICAI had issued a Guidance Note on accounting for

expenditure on CSR activities that comes into effect from 1 May, 2015.

38. On the issue of auditing, the Committee further enquired that as per the Section
143(2), auditor shall have to make the report on all the financial statements required
under the Act. However, reporting CSR is not specified. Whether this includes the
reporting on the provision made in Section 135 pertaining CSR and whether the auditors
have reported on Section 135? Also, whether the National Financial Reporting Authority
constituted under Companies Act has presented auditing standards with regard to Section
35?

39. For which, the MCA has responded in writing that Section 143 of the Companies
Act, 2013 prescribes Auditing Standards for auditing the Annual Financial Statements of
the companies. This would also include auditing of expenditure incurred on CSR by

eligible companies. It was also informed that National Financial Reporting Authority

(NFRA) under the Companies Act, 2013, is yet to be constituted.

40. The Committee is of the firm opinion that since it will be the first audit of
CSR activities after CSR has been wtiade legally mandatory, auditing of expenditure
made under these activities, along a guided path, would be important for
streamlining of expenditure and ensuring transparency. The Guidance Note of
ICAI is expected to be the tool for the purpose. In view of this, the Committee
wants to be apprised of the details relating to the salient features of the Guidance
Note and compliance by CPSEs in the first audit since the coming into force the

Companies (CSR policy) Rules, 2014.

Publicizing successful CSR stories

41. During the course of the examination of the CSR activities of various PSUs, the
Committee came across certain excellent emulatable conduct of CSR activities like that

of NDMC as already mentioned. The Committee is of opinion that such success stories
17


should be published on the website of DPE and other visual and print media and
also be included in the documents like Public Enterprises Survey and Annual report
of DPE as a token of appreciation to these earnest efforts. The Committee
recognizes the efforts made by Standing Committee of Public Enterprises (SCOPE)
by compiling such success stories. This needs to be updated and be given wide

publicity.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE-AT A
GLANCE

1. DPE should issue directions or guidelines, as to how can the CPSEs extend
their CSR oversight to entire supply chain network to ensure vendors comply with
principles of CSR as per DPE guidelines. The DPE should also allow the CPSEs to
join in the Central and State Government’s Schemes like Mid-day meal, Sarva
Siksha Abhiyan as per Schedule VII. For this DPE should evolve a model
arrangements framework between the CPSEs and the nodal Government Agency
which should ensure timely release of Utilization Certificate to the CPSEs so that it
can reflect the CSR expenditure in its annual accounts. Similarly, the Company or
NGO, through which CSR projects are to be implemented, too should furnish the
Utilization Certificates in time. It must be ensured that such NGOs and Companies
should actually use the funds in time.

(Para 9)

2. The Committee recognizes that the Act gives rule making powers to Central
Government. Considering that the DPE is the nodal Department to provide non-
financial guidelines to PSEs, the Committee acknowledges that DPE guidelines have
given greater force to the CSR related provisions of the Act by introducing negative
marking in MoU for non- CSR compiled CPSEs. The DPE may assess the
performance of a PSE, against each of its CSR guidelines before rating the PSE.
(Para 10)

3. During its interaction with the CPSEs, the Committee drew the following
inferences which needed greater clarity. DPE may include these issues in the
guidelines: हु हे

(i) Lack of provisioning for cost of maintaining a durable social asset
created under CSR. we

(ii) Clarifications regarding CSR obligations of Holding companies, like
Coal India Ltd. considering that earning in form of dividend were not
to be included while computing Net income.

(iii) There is confusion whether PSUs can set up_professional/skill
development institutions as per Schedule VII in their respective area
of usual business and core competence.

(iv) Exclusion of para military veterans and widows from the definition of
armed forces.

(Para 12)

4, The Committee acknowledges that subsequent to their taking up the matter
regarding the need for the inclusion of health care in Schedule VII of the Act, in the
above meeting, the Ministry came out with its first amendment to the Schedule VII
on 31 March, 2014. Vide this amendment “promoting health care including
preventive health care” was added in the Schedule VII (i) of the Act in the place of
७०००००००००००००० promoting preventive health care”.( Annexure IT)

29

(Para 13)


oF The Committee is of the considered opinion that as provided by the
Companies Act, 2013 it is an obligation of a Company to be concerned with the well
being of its local populace and environment, the resources of which are being
directly utilized by them. However, the Committee also holds the view that CPSEs
should take into account the development of remote backward areas of the country.
These are areas where the pace of industrial development has been slow due to their
geographic isolation. While neighborhood community and local area with reference
to company’s works have first claim over CSR projects, Schedule VII should also
provide for development by individual company or jointly with other companies, in
backward areas like North East, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep,
which do not have much of industrialisation and are in need of development. The
Committee therefore, recommends that some percentage of CSR be allowed to
spend in such backward areas other than local area. Similarly, the Committee is of
the opinion that in case company contributes its CSR fund to the corpus for
National Schemes like Swachh Bharat Mission, a certain percentage of CSR fund
must mandatorily be assigned to local area around Company’s works/ projects so
that the basic ideology to start CSR policy for local area population is not defeated
and local population do not suffer because they are the first people who are socially
and environmentally affected whenever any plant of PSUs is established.

(Para 15)

6. As per the UNIDO definition CSR should be an integral part of a Company’s
business operation. This approach makes CSR more sustainable instead of the
approach taken by Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 that exclude activities
undertaken in presence of normal course of business. This approach will help
companies to align their operations with sustainable development objectives, instead
of taking up unsustainable one off projects and tendency to make financial
contribution for CSR. The DPE guidelines too require the PSUs to exploit their core
competence and mobilize their resource capacities in implementation of CSR. PSUs
have been advised to align their CSR with their business policies and strategies. This
position is concurrent with the UNIDO but contrary to Rule 4(2) of Companies
(CSR Policy) Rules, 2014. The Committee finds this approach to be more effective
and practicable.

(Para 17)

i The Committee feels such initiatives should become a model for CPSEs and
companies in other Sectors as well to come together to set up industry specific
technology institutes to cater to the demand of skilled manpower for the sectors like
defence, petroleum, etc. In this regard, the Committee also acknowledged the
pronouncement made in Budget speech (2016-17) regarding setting up of Higher
Education Financing Agency (HEFA) - ‘We have decided to set up a Higher
Education Financing Agency (HEFA) with an initial capital base of Rs 1,000 crore.
The HEFA will be a not-for-profit organization that will leverage funds from the
market and supplement them with donations and CSR funds. These funds will be
used to finance improvement in infrastructure in our top institutions and will be
serviced through internal accruals.’

(Para 18)

6


8. The Committee while keeping in mind and considering the essence of CSR,
observes that setting up of training institutions in specialized areas by companies
can be allowed regardless of its relations to its core business. This is even more
imperative considering that our country is facing an acute problem of skill deficit in
specialized fields like defence, power, petroleum, mining technologies, etc. Such
training institutions would be social assets whose pass-outs may or may not join the
Company. These institutions may be run on the terms of financial sustainability.
The senior management and engineers may join the faculty or take up research
assignments thereby evolving into scholars and professionals.

(Para 19)

9, The Committee while analyzing the provision that allows companies to
engage trust/society/NGO with ‘established track record’ to execute their CSR
activities, feels that the term as mentioned in the Rules, 'established track record'
needs further specifications to avoid any possible abuse. The Committee also feels
that it is required to exclude those trusts/societies/NGOs wherein relatives of Board
members of the CPSE, State/Central Ministries or local administration are involved
in undertaking CSR activities. DPE should issue general guidelines in this regard
amd not leave it to Board alone. DPE should also advise CPSEs to blacklist deviant
trust/society/NGO to prevent them from engaging in such activities in future. The
Committee also recognized that the Rules have been amended to provide only 5% of
the CSR budget for such overhead expenditure towards salary, etc to NGOs. Also,
rules must specify that such trusts/ NGOs must utilize the funds in time and give’
Utilization Certificate to the Company for inclusion in the annual account.

(Para 24)

10. To discount such trend, the Committee recommends that a certain
percentage of CSR budget must be assigned to CSR projects in the neighboring
community around the Company’s project. The Committee also emphasis that
Board of Directors of all PSUs while framing their CSR Policy should define the
local areas as mentioned in DPE Guidelines (point xii).

(Para 25)

11, The Committee believes that the concept of CSR would be defeated in case
CPSEs resort to mere transfer of CSR money to any fund created by Central
Government for social-economic development. Instead they should directly involve
in building community assets and maintaining them in partnership with community.
However, in cases where CPSEs contribute CSR money to Central Government
sponsored funds/schemes/programmes mentioned under Schedule VII of the
Companies Act. 2013, the Committee recommends that such contributions should be
limited to a specified percentage of the entire CSR fund of the CPSE and certain
percentage of CSR must be mandatorily assigned to neighboring communities work.
Such a specification will ensure that the CPSEs would imbibe the essence of CSR by
directly engaging themselves in such activities.

(Para 29)

ae


12. The Committee recommends that the Companies should be allowed to
identify the technologies developed by research institutions like CSIR, Universities
or start ups, incubate and commercially develop them for some years as part of CSR
and then may be allowed to market it under mutually agreed terms between
Company and the research institution.
(Para 30)

13. The Committee takes note of the responses of MCA and appreciates the fact
that sustainability is expected to be factored into the design of CSR projects at its
beginning. However, the Committee also takes cognizance of the fact that a good
share of CSR activities are purely welfare oriented and may not strictly fit into a
project/programme mode where sustainability can be built in. This aspect of
sustainability of CSR initiatives will be even more accentuated in the case of CPSEs
who are prone to fluctuating earnings/profits. Further, the CSR, Rules, 2014 include
‘ongoing’ activities under CSR activities. While emphasis is on the self sustaining
CSR projects, the activities listed in Schedule VII are one off activities that do not
generate revenue even to maintain these assets and are therefore non-self sustaining.
Provisions should be made for maintenance of CSR assets in successive years.
Therefore, the Committee is of the considered opinion that DPE should mention in
their guidelines for maintenance of CSR assets created under CSR budget. So that
the assets are maintained otherwise the whole funds would go waste.

(Para 34)

CSR activities after CSR has been made legally mandatory, auditing of expenditure
made under these activities, along a guided path, would be important for
streamlining of expenditure and ensuring transparency. The Guidance Note of
ICAI is expected to be the tool for the purpose. In view of this, the Committee
wants to be apprised of the details relating to the salient features of the Guidance
Note and compliance by CPSEs in the first audit since the coming into force the
Companies (CSR policy) Rules, 2014.

(Petra 40)

REPORT
Introduction
The Heavy Industries in India is dominated by the Capital Good Sector (CGS) and the Auto
Sector. The Indian Capital Goods Industry has enough potential but manufacturing capacity is
underutilized to the extent of 40%.  Two major hurdles faced by the sector are cheap imports and
technology gap. The Government has come up with many initiatives/schemes to make the sector
globally competitive. The Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) with a mission to achieve high
growth in Heavy Electricals and Capital Goods Industry have announced the National Capital Goods
Policy (NCGP) on 15
th February 2016 which is a landmark initiative in this regard and has been
reflected in the Budget 2016-17 by way of enhancement of Customs Duty on Heavy Electrical
equipments from 7.5 % to 10%, imposition of Countervailing Duty (CVD) on road construction
machinery and reduction of excise duty from 12.5% to 6% on parts of centrifugal pumps.  All
these measures are expected to help indigenous producers of Capital Goods to be more cost
competitive against imports.
2.. The Auto Sector contributes 45% to the Manufacturing Gross Domestic Product (GDP),
26% to the Industrial GDP and 7.1% to the National GDP hence it is evident that this sector is
critical to the manufacturing sector. The Auto sector provides 29 million job opportunities, both
direct and indirect and has made investments to the tune of  ` 70, 000 crores in the last five
Financial Years (FYs). Considering that the industry had a turnover of USD 124 billion during
2014-15 and assuming a growth rate of 10% during 2015-16, the Government expects it to achieve
around 94% of the target set for the industry in the Automobile Mission Plan (2006-16) by 2016.
An ambitious Scheme for Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid and) Electric Vehicles in
India (FAME-India) is being implemented by the Government to support the hybrid/electrical
vehicles industry and its manufacturing ecosystem to attain self-sustenance. In the Budget
2016-17, the Government announced measures aiming to invest big in infrastructure like outlay of
` 97,000 crore for road infrastructure,  `  200 crore to FAME-India scheme & National Automotive
Testing R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP), reduction in customs duty on raw materials for
catalytic converters from 7.5% to 5%, etc that are expected to provide fillip to the Auto sector
in the ensuing years.
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI)
3. The Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, comprising the Department of
Heavy Industry (DHI) and the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), was created as per the
Presidential Notification dated the 15
th October, 1999. DHI administers 31 operating Central Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), including 12 subsidiary companies and 1 JV company i.e. NTPC-
BHEL Power Projects Pvt. Ltd. (NBBPL). The Department also administers the following
autonomous organizations:
(a) NATRiP Implementation Society (NATIS) set up in July 2005, for guiding the
1

2
implementation of the National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project
(NATRiP);
(b) Fluid Control Research Institute (FCRI), Palakkad, Kerala which caters to the needs
of the flow industry for calibration;
(c) Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune, Maharashtra; and
(d) National Automotive Board (NAB).
DHI has also been allocated the following subjects/Industrial Sectors:
(a) Heavy Engineering Equipment and Machine Tools Industry.
(b) Heavy Electrical Engineering Industries.
(c) Automotive Industries, including tractors and earth moving equipment.
The 31 CPSEs administered by DHI can be categorized into 3 major groups namely,
Engineering Units, Non- Engineering Units and Consultancy/Contracting Units. The list of the
CPSEs is placed at Annexure I.
4. The main objectives of DHI are: -
(a) Optimum utilization of installed capacity of CPSEs under the Department;
(b) Management Development to ensure professional management and operations in the
CPSEs;
(c) Promotion of profitability, efficiency and productivity through restructuring,
modernization, technology up-gradation and optimal deployment of human and
material resources in the CPSEs;
(d) Closer co-ordination and interaction between the manufacturing and the user sectors;
(e) Development and growth of Sectors looked after by the Department; and
(f) Implementation of a national project in Auto sector for creating state-of-the-art
facilities for testing etc.
5. The enterprises under the Department produce wide range of products ranging from
machine tools, industrial machinery, boiler, gas/steam/hydro turbines, turbo generators, electrical
equipment, and railway traction equipment, pressure vessels, AC locomotives, prime movers,
agricultural tractors and consumer products such as watches, cement, paper, tyres and salts, etc.
The industries provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy including power,
rail and road transport. The Department also looks after the Machine Building Industry and caters
to the requirements of equipments for basic industries such as steel, non –ferrous metals,
fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, paper, cement, sugar etc.  Besides, it supports the
development of a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings forgings, diesel
engines, industrial gears and gear boxes.
(I) Detailed Demand for Grants (DDG) 2016-17
6. The Demand for Grants (DFG) 2016-17 a
ppearing at Sl. No. 44 relating to DHI has been
brought out in a pattern which is a departure from the past years. As part of the Committee’s
examination of Demands of DHI, explanation was sought regarding the changes made for the year
in comparison to the previous years and the rationale behind the changes.

3
7.  In their submission, DHI stated that as per the instructions of Ministry of Finance (MoF),
rationalization of existing plan/ non-plan schemes have been done. The aim is to rationalize all
programmes/schemes by merging the relatively small schemes into a logical large schematic
framework. Rationalized final set of schemes will lead to well defined measurable outcomes which
can be monitored. Schemes/sub-schemes reflected in the Detailed Demand for Grants are also to
be suitably merged /eliminated to yield a more compact framework for schemes/programmes,
which will help the Ministries/Departments gain more flexibility in execution of the schemes and
guard against spreading the resources too thin. MoF have stressed upon the need for rationalizing
Central Sector Schemes so as to ensure that schemes having small outlays could be done away
with or merged with bigger schemes, and the feasibility of achieving the intended objectives
through merger/clubbing could be explored.
8. With this aim, meetings on rationalization of the Central Sector Scheme in respect of DHI
were held in the MoF and accordingly, following three major Umbrella Schemes have been framed
after merging of existing plan/non-plan schemes and accordingly Budget Estimates for the year
2016-17 has been allocated to the tune of  `  300 crore (Plan) and  `  1000 crore (Non Plan).
Sl. Rationalized/ New Umbrella Scheme

– Adv- USC) Technology for Thermal Power Plants

4
9. On account of rationalization of existing schemes, only Umbrella Schemes are reflected in
the Statement of Budget Estimates (SBE) 2016-17 and accordingly Budgetary allocations for
2016-17 have been made. Therefore, SBE 2016-17 has been divided into two parts. Part-I with
heading Budget Estimates (BE) 2016-17 has reflected only Budgetary allocation for 2016-17 as per
the Umbrella Scheme. Part-II with heading Revised Estimates (RE) 2015-16  reflects the Actual
2014-15, BE-2015-16 and RE-2015-16 and this part is almost similar to the pattern of SBE 2015-16.
10. The Committee notes that the Demands for Grants (2016-17) for DHI has followed
a new pattern of depiction of allocation of funds when compared to the last year. On a quick
reference of Demands No. 44, the new pattern may appear difficult to comprehend due to
the absence of comparative details upfront. But, in reply to a query on this, the Department
has preferred to an explanation of bunching of smaller schemes under larger umbrella
schemes for the purpose of imparting more flexibility in the execution of schemes and to
guard against spending the resources too thin. The Committee finds reason in the rational
provided by DHI and appreciates the new initiative of the MoF.  It is expected that the new
system of Umbrella Schemes will result in timely implementation of schemes by reallocating
funds between sub schemes as per operational expediencies which should in turn curb
underutilization of funds as well.
11. The Department also submitted that depending on the nature of expenditure, the funds of
` 282.06 crore for the Development of Automobile Industry have been allocated in the following

12. It has been observed that on account of rationalization of existing schemes, Umbrella
Scheme, namely, Development of Automobile Industry has been reflected in the SBE 2016-17 and
an amount of  `  282.06 crore (Plan fund of  `  199.91 crore and Non Plan fund of  `  82.15 crore)
was allocated for the 2016-17. Schemes/Sub-Schemes reflected in the Detailed Demand for Grants
have been suitably merged/eliminated to yield a more compact framework for Schemes/
Programmes, as per the instructions of Ministry of Finance in order to facilitate the Ministries/
Departments to gain more flexibility in execution of the schemes and guard against spreading the
resources too thin.
13. Token provision has been made under the Major Head 6858 under the Umbrella Scheme
Development of Automobile Industry because funds to NATRiP can be released in the form of
Grant-in-aid (Major Head 2852- Revenue Section) as well as in the form of Loan (Major Head
6858- Capital Section). Since, there is lesser possibility of expenditure against NATRIP in the form
of Loan, only token provisions have been kept under Capital Section (under 6858).
14. Regarding the allocation of funds to schemes under Development of Automobile
Industry, the Committee observes that funds for the same purpose has been allocated under
two different Heads, with one Head witnessing only a miniscule allocation and the other
reflecting majority of the funds.  The Department’s explanation for differential allocation
is that token allocations in two Heads have been made to cater to the possibility of funds
being allocated to NATRiP in the form of Grants–in-Aid as well as in the form of Loan, even
though the loan possibility is low. The Committee would have found it more appropriate if
the Government would have at least by now decided the manner in which funds to NATRiP
are to be provided, i.e. either as Loan or as Grants. Such uncertainties can affect the
lucidity of the Demand and the transparency with which allocations are made.

18. The Committee takes note that under the Head, Grants to CPSEs, funds have been
reflected under two different Heads – on Depiction Head and on Operational Head. On this
duality of funds, it has been informed that funds under the Depiction Head will be
transferred to the Operational head for executing expenditure.  This arrangement has been
done under the directives of Government of India (GoI). Further, it is encouraging to take
into cognizance that DHI is one of the few Departments of the GoI where all fund transfers
are being made on-line through PFMS and under this system funds can be transferred only
to those Heads which atleast have some token allocation.  The Committee observes that the
PFMS will hasten up the release of funds and eliminate avoidable delays and
mismanagement.
19. However, the Committee also wonders whether it is not ironical that while on the one

schemes for the benefit of simplification of procedure and facilitating financial flexibility, on
the other hand it is complicating matters by adding more Heads for allocations and
expenditure of funds under a single umbrella scheme.

(1) Development of Automobile Industry
22. Auto Industry has been an engine of growth in most developed countries and it is essaying

10
the same role in India too. Indian Automobile industry, which was at its nascent stage at the
beginning of the 21 st century, has now become a huge industry that contributes majorly to growth
and development of Indian Economy. The industry witnessed two difficult Financial Years (FYs)
2013 and 2014, in which the segments across the industry witnessed de-growth, carrying nearly
60% surplus production capacity. However, this situation was reversed in the first half of financial
year 2015-16. But it was submitted to the Committee that ban on registration of new Diesel
V ehicles with more than 2000 ml capacity, imposed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court for National
Capital Region (NCR) in Dec 2015, resulted in flattening of sales graph of such vehicles.
23. In the last few years, Government has taken many proactive steps for improvement of
safety and emission norms for the vehicles. About 60 mandatory safety requirements have been
duly notified by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.  Besides, Government has also
announced the introduction of BS VI compliant vehicles with effect from 1
st April, 2020.  One of
the major actions taken for controlling vehicular pollution is initiation of National Mission on
Electric Mobility. Under this mission, DHI has formulated a holistic scheme to promote electric and
hybrid vehicles along with necessary infrastructure development with Faster Adoption and
Manufacturing of Electric (& Hybrid) vehicles in India (FAME India).
(i) National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP)
24. The aim of NATRiP is to create world-class automotive testing, validation, Research &
Development (R&D) and homologation facilities in line with emerging requirements of the National
Automotive Safety and Emission roadmap. These are being created in the three principal hubs of
North, West and South India. NA TRiP was approved by the GoI in 2005, with a total investment
of `  1,718 crore, which was revised to  `  2286.06  crore. The initial scheduled date of completion
of NATRiP project was April, 2011, which was first extended to December, 2012, then to
December, 2014 and the current extension is upto December, 2017. The GoI does majority funding
of the project and also granted full customs exemption duty to all project imports while the State
Governments have offered land at concessional rates. Plan provision had been kept for NATRiP for
the installation and commissioning of the equipments in various ongoing projects.

26. DHI as part of its written submission to the Committee stated that the BE for 2015-16 for
NATRiP was in the form of plan loan of Rs, 300.00 crore which was reduced to zero at RE stage
due to low plan RE ceiling intimated by Ministry of Finance. However,  `  100.00 crore was sought
at RE stage.  As per the Revised Cost Estimate (RCE-I), the loan provision is  `  511.28 crore, and
accordingly  `  411.28 crore was sought by the Department. The Grant-in-aid portion as per RCE-
I has already been released to NA TRiP. The RCE-II has been approved by Expenditure Finance
Committee (EFC) and is yet to be considered by CCEA.
27. Further, during the oral evidence on the current Budgetary allocations of the Department,
it also made the following submission about NATRiP-
“This year, out of  `  199.01 crore earmarked in the automobile sector,  `  75 crore is
earmarked for NATRiP. It is a provisional allotment, and the remaining  `  25 crore for FAME- India
Scheme. Out of  `  75 crore earmarked for 2015-16, only a balance of  `  70, 000 is left out.  The
remaining `  125 crore projected in the next year’s Budget, we are more than sure that the
allocation would be utilized.
The same scheme was originally sanctioned for two years, but as you deduce from that
` 75 crore and  `  125 crore, only  `  200 crore would be utilized in two years. It has to spill over
in the third year also. As far as the NATRiP is concerned, the extended time mandate has been
given up to 31 st December, 2017.  But,  I am afraid by that time, probably, some activity would
still remain, and a fresh time extension would be needed to be sought.”
28. The Committee takes into account the status of completion of various components
of NATRiP as submitted by the Department. It also notes the explanation given by the
Department on how it is to utilize the plan loan of  ` ` ` ` `  300 crore allocated to the project
during 2015-16 over a period of 3 years ending in 2017-18. In this regard, the Committee
recognizes that this spread of expenditure warrants yet another extension of NATRiP,
beyond currently extended period upto December, 2017.  The Committee expresses concern
over the fact that a project which has already seen three extensions is looking for further
extension.  In the view of the Committee, this unending continuation of the flagship project
of DHI, which was originally intended to be time bound, is a pointer to mismanagement
along with lack of foresight and accordingly, recommends that a performance audit of
NATRiP with specific focus on lapses in project management shall be conducted.
(ii) Schemes for Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid and) Electric
Vehicles in India –(FAME- India).
29. GoI approved the National Mission on Electric Mobility in 2011 and subsequently National
Electric Mobility Mission Plan 2020 (NEMMP) was unveiled in 2013 to provide clean mobility
solutions to the people while reducing the Country’s dependence on fossil fuel. As part of the
mission, DHI has formulated a scheme, namely, Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid &)
Electric Vehicles in India (FAME-India). The overall scheme is proposed to be implemented over
a period of 6 years i.e. till 2020.  The objective of the scheme is to encourage faster adoption
(Market creation & related activities), domestic technology development (Research & Development)
and manufacturing of full range of cleaner electric vehicles technologies that include mild hybrid,
full hybrid vehicles (HEVs), plug in Hybrids Vehicles (BEVs) (collectively termed as HEVs) thereby

13
leading to creation of a strong, globally competitive, viable & self-sustaining electric vehicle
industry and its eco-system in India.
30. The scheme shall have 4 focus areas, i.e. Technology Development, Demand Creation, Pilot
Projects and charging Infrastructure. The Phase-I of the scheme shall be implemented over a
2 years period commencing from 1 st April, 2015 to 31 st March, 2017  i.e.  FY 2015-16 and FY
2016-17. The scheme has four verticals and progress made in each of these verticals is as given below.

32. The Committee considers FAME – India as one of the most forward looking schemes
of the Government in the face of heightened environmental concerns and depleting fossil
fuel reserves.  Though the scheme is picking up, the Committee, while examining the
submissions of the Department, finds that in respect to R&D and creation of Charging
Infrastructure there has already been complaints of shortage of funds extending up to
````` 25.63 crore and  ` ` ` ` `  87.00 crore, respectively. The Committee would want the Department
to submit the reasons for the said shortages and the curative action taken, if any. It is
imperative that such teething problems are to be eliminated at early stages itself to
preclude them from developing into systematic deficiencies.
33. Further, during it examination of the Demands of DHI 2016-17, the Committee felt
that there was a need for more impetus on R&D, specifically related to the development
of original technology in the field of electrical vehicles, probably in the development of
electrical motors, which will have direct application in the manufacturing of indigenous
electrical vehicles.  The Committee also feel that DHI should draw a road map with the help
of industry experts in the filed of electrical vehicles with a definite time frame so that the
objectives set up by the DHI are achieved to justify the money spent and also to reduce the
emission of carbon in the environment.
(2) Development of Capital Goods Sector.
(i) National Capital Goods Policy, 2016 (NCGP).
34. The National Capital Goods Policy, 2016 was announced on 15
th February, 2016 in Mumbai.
Initially, a Joint Task Force (JTF) was put in place to prepare a base paper on Capital Goods Policy
and sought comments of various stakeholders on the same. Other than the base paper, three sub
groups were formed under JTF on Technology and depth, Demand creation and Trade and Export.
Based on the response on the draft paper and inputs from Sub Groups as well as regional
roundtables, JTF completed formulation of a draft policy by October, 2015. Thereafter, the same
uploaded in the DHI website with a view to seeking comments/ views on the same. An Inter-
Ministerial Meeting was held in November, 2015 and a draft Cabinet Note on the National Capital
Goods Policy was circulated to the Ministries/ Departments concerned in December, 2015. After
receiving comments/ views of the Ministries/ Departments concerned, the Note was sent to the
Cabinet on 8.2.2016. This was followed by a Supplementary Note on 10.2.2016. However, the
meeting of the Cabinet scheduled to be held on 10.2.2016 was postponed. Therefore, the case was
moved for seeking approval of Hon’ble Prime Minister under Rule 12 of the Transaction of
Business Rules with a view to launch the Policy during ‘Make in India week’ in Mumbai.
The National Capital Goods Policy 2016 is available on the website of the Department (dhi.nic.in) .
35. The policy has made various key recommendation such as (i) integration of major capital
goods sub-sectors as priority sectors to be envisaged under ‘Make in India’ initiative; (ii) creation
of an enabling scheme as a pilot for ‘Heavy Industry Export & Market Development Assistance
Scheme (HIEMDA)’ with a view to enhance the export of Indian made capital goods; (iii)

16
strengthening existing capital goods scheme by increasing the budgetary allocation & scope of the
present ‘Scheme on Enhancement of Competitiveness of Capital Goods’; (iv) launching a
Technology Development Fund under Public Private Partnership (PPP) model to fund technology
acquisition, transfer of technology, purchase of  Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) designs &
drawings and for commercialization of such technologies; (v) creation of a ‘Start-up Center for
Capital Goods Sector’; (vi) mandatory standardization and (vii) up gradation of testing
infrastructure; (viii) skill development through a Scheme to develop existing training centers and
setting up 5 new State of the art skill development centers and; (ix) modernization of existing CG
Sector units especially in Small and Medium Enterprises segment through a scheme based on
capital subsidy to promote manufacturing of quality products.
(ii) Scheme for Enhancement of Competiveness in the Indian Capital Goods
Sector:
36. The Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector was
approved by the CCEA in its meeting dated 15.09.2014. The scheme subsequently was notified in
the Gazette on 05.11.2014 and was launched, thereon. The Scheme envisages infrastructural
intervention through Scheme components like setting up of (i) Centre of Excellence for Technology
Development, (ii) Integrated Industrial Infrastructure Centre, (iii) Common Engineering Facility
Centre (iv) Test & Certification Centre and (v) Technology Acquisition Fund.

Under the scheme, the first installment of grant was released on 31.3.2015 to Central

41. The R&D Project for “Development of Advanced Ultra Supercritical (Adv. USC) Technology
for Thermal Power Plants” is to be carried out jointly by Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL),
Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) and National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd.
(NTPC). The objective of the First Phase of the project is to undertake R&D on all aspects of
Advanced Ultra Super Critical (Adv-USC) technology for thermal power plants in order to improve
power plant efficiency, reduce carbon-dioxide emissions and reduce coal consumption per unit of
power generated. The proposed project would enable Indian industries to design, manufacture and
commission higher efficiency coal fired power plants with indigenously developed technology and
manufacturing process. The duration of the project is estimated to be of two and a half years from
the date of approval. The Department informed the Committee that the fund of Rs 50 crore
allocated for the project in BE 2015-16 was surrendered because the project has yet not been
approved by the GoI. In the BE 2016-17 a token provision of Rs one lakh has been made for the
project. Further, the Department also updated the Committee on the progress made during 2015-
16 on the project.
42. DHI submitted that pursuant to the decision taken in a meeting held on 20-05-2015 under
the Chairmanship of Secretary, DHI, BHEL had committed to enhance its contribution for the
project from Rs 220 crore to Rs 270 crore. NTPC had confirmed the contribution of Rs 50 crore
for the project and IGCAR was to contribute Rs 234 crore for the project. The balance amount
of Rs 1000 crore was to be funded by GoI. Further, certain pre-project R&D activities were taken
up with funding of approx. Rs 25 Crore provided by the Office of Principal Scientific Advisor
(PSA), GoI, wherein two out of five small projects have been successfully completed and work
on the balance three is underway. However, the work on R&D Phase of the main project would
be taken up based only on the finalization of funding pattern. Final Note was sent to Cabinet
Secretariat on 3-3-2015 for obtaining approval of CCEA. However, the Cabinet Secretariat vide its
O.M dated 16-7-2015 returned the copies of CCEA Note with the direction that DHI may take
necessary action to finalize the note afresh as per Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) direction on the
issue.
43. The Principal Secretary to Prime Minister took a meeting on 20-08-2015 on the above
mentioned subject wherein the following were decided:
(1) NTPC and BHEL need to reconsider their commitment for financial support to the
project. Further, a suggestion was put forward that an amount of Rs 200 crore may
be contributed by the NTPC and Rs 400 Crore each by BHEL and IGCAR. The
remaining amount will be provided as support by the GoI.

19
(2) If the project is to be taken up, the funding of Phase-I & II needs to be finalized
upfront. The sharing pattern for phase-II should also be the same as for Phase-I.
Further, there needs to be a tight Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between
GoI, IGCAR, BHEL & NTPC, delineating their respective responsibilities clearly.

BHEL
57. BHEL, one of the largest CPSEs in India and is the only Maharatna under DHI.  It is
engaged in design, engineering manufacture, construction, commissioning and servicing of a wide
range of products and services for the core sectors of the economy viz. Power, Transmission,

24
Industry, Transportation, Renewable Energy and Oil & Gas.  BHEL has maintained a consistent
track record of growth, performance and profitability, since its inception more than five decades
ago. However, contrary to this claim, the status of BHEL has been indicated as ‘Weak’ as per
DHI’s classification of its CPSEs based on the new guidelines of DPE.
58. The Committee asked BHEL to present its case regarding the “Weak” categorization by its
administrative ministry, in the presence of the representatives of DHI. As part of their explanations,
both BHEL and DHI harped on reasons which had been placed before the Committee time and
again, which included dampened demand for products, both domestic and international, difficulties
in coal linkage, peculiarities in some of the provisioning in the balance sheet, stranded orders,
problems in securing environmental clearances, etc.  Hope was also expressed by BHEL that owing
to the impetus of the Government on power infrastructure through schemes like Ujjwal DISCOM
Assurance Yojana (UDAY), corrective action taken towards successful execution of orders with
better interaction with customers, diversification into areas including defence solar power and other
alternative energy options, etc, the performance of the company would pick up in the coming
years.  However, the Committee found it difficult to buy the reasons put forward for the poor
plight of BHEL.
59. DHI’s further submission to the Committee on the matter regarding BHEL being categorized
as a “Weak” CPSE stated that according to BHEL the yard-sticks/criteria formulated for the
classification did not factor the operating business environment and the severe competitive intensity
faced by the Company from both domestic and international players. As such, the DPE criteria on
the matter were made applicable for all CPSEs, irrespective of their type of operations/category/
sector which should not be the case.
60. The Committee notes that the performance of BHEL has slackened over the last two
to three years owing to a slew of reasons given by the Company viz. retarded demand,
delayed environmental clearances, stranded orders, etc. In the view of the Committee, the
reasons put forward by BHEL portrays an impression that these have been ‘beyond the
control’ of the company. Even while considering that BHEL might have taken steps to check
the slide in its performance, the fact remains that their performance seems to have dipped
despite these efforts. Accordingly, the Committee finds it difficult to isolate the reasons for
the lackluster performance of BHEL to those quoted by the company alone. Therefore, the
Committee’s conclusion is that there has been a delay on the part of BHEL in responding
to the challenges thrown to them by the market and other factors.  Though, the Committee
does not completely discount the reasons put forth by BHEL, it is the Committee’s firm
belief that BHEL’s current situation is the outcome of their poor performance in the area
of risk analysis and business foresight, both of which would have allowed the Company to
anticipate rough business weather and for effective and commensurate course correction.
61. In the area of diversification of business also the Committee finds that the efforts
taken by BHEL does not seem to be of the quality of the top most companies in India to
which BHEL belongs. Efficient and timely diversification could have acted as a buffer to
absorb the shocks in the core business. Since this has not happened it will not be out of
place to presume that the diversification initiatives of BHEL do not bring in the desired
results. And for DHI, the Committee opines that DHI should have pressed BHEL firmly for

25
implementation of timely corrective measures. Under these circumstances, the Committee
cannot but recommend strict measures to ensure accountability for lapses in business
decisions to the extent possible.  Accordingly, it is further recommended that a forensic
audit for BHEL shall be ordered with a view to identify instances of deficiencies in business
decisions and take suitable measure so that those are not repeated.

62. HEC, Ranchi was incorporated on 31
st December, 1958. It has three manufacturing units
viz: Heavy Machine Building Plant (HMBP), Heavy Machine Tools Plant (HMTP), Foundry Forge

implemented till FY 2008. This mostly included non-cash assistance like waiver/conversion,
implementation of wage revision, etc and helped improve the performance of the company when
coupled with some efforts to modernize facilities. But this period of operational profits continued

th March 2016 for final discussions related to the press modernization

st March 2016

for major part of the Project. For financing of other schemes covered under open tender, Company
was trying for loan from SBI and generate fund from state government which had shown keen

65. The Company has signed agreements with Russian Government Company for technology
transfer in the areas of manufacturing clean steel technologies and heavy casting / forgings for
different clientele. These technologies would be implemented in HEC and all items would be
manufactured within HEC. These are rare technologies and would be developed specially for needs
arising from demands of various sectors within the country. As per DHI it would be a perfect

26
example where these item s under ‘Make in India’ initiative will be manufactured at HEC and would

66. Modernization Plan of HEC prepared by M/s MECON as Consultant was envisaged by the
Management of HEC with a total proposed outlay of Rs 976.60 crore comprising of budgetary
assistance from the Government of Rs 500 crore and the remaining amount of Rs 476.60 crore

of the cost of modernization. As such the allocation of Rs 50 crore in BE 2015-16 was withdrawn

67. As part of the examination of budgetary allocations (2016-17) to DHI, the Committee heard
some select CPSEs. HEC was one among them wherein they updated the Committee that they have
handed over some land to the Government of Jharkhand, and, against that, they were getting
around `  740 crores but that is not sufficient for modernizing of their plant. Their requirement for
modernization was  `  1,000-odd crores and they require another  `  300 crore which they were
trying to get from the State Bank of India. This excludes their other liabilities of vendors ranging

of this, they have already generated  `  750 crores by disposing of land to the Government of
Jharkhand. At the end of their submission HEC sought the Committee’s support to get them some
sort of financial assistance from the Government of India.
68. The Committee is aware that HEC had once set an example how a sick company can
revive and turn around to generate profits again with efficient managerial approach and
Government support. Therefore, the Committee in its reports on DFG of DHI 2013-14 and
2015-16 had recommended the Modernization of HEC, so that the Company could sustain
the gains made through the revival package. In its 2015-16 report the Committee even
suggested that DHI should consider enhancing the budgetary assistance of  ` ` ` ` `  500 crores,

69. It is evident from HEC’s submission before the Committee that the modernization
of HEC is getting stalled due to shortage of funds. The Committee has in the past
repeatedly asked the Government to help and hasten HEC’s plan for modernization, but it

recommends DHI to provide all requisite support to HEC in their search for funds and
consider providing proposed guarantee for bank loan or enhancement of budgetary supports
beyond ` ` ` ` `  500 crores.  It is the firm opinion of the Committee that, the management will
be equally responsible to help themselves to make available the required funds for its
modernization and utilize the same efficiently.
70. However, the worrisome factor for the Committee is the lethargic approach of the
parties involved which is the typical cause for delay in respect of revival of CPSEs.  The
Committee apprehends that this fac
tor may creep into the case of HEC as well.  Therefore,

the Committee warns both the administrative ministry and HEC from falling prey to this
cliché situation.

72. HPC was incorporated on 29.05.1970 with the objective of establishing pulp and paper/
