two units are the only 100% bamboo based mills in India. NPM and CPM, achieved 100% capacity
utilisation during 2000-01 and 2005-06, respectively.
73. While hearing select CPSEs as part of its discussion on Demands of DHI, representatives
of HPC placed before the Committee issues related to NPM & CPM.  According to them, HPC
was making profit and paying dividend till the year 2008-09.  Thereafter, the misfortune of
Company started because of large-scale gregarious flowering of bamboo in the North-East Region,
which remained for about five years.  During this period, they could not operate in full capacity.
As informed to the Committee, once this problem of flowering was over and they started getting
bamboo up to the required quantity, National Green Tribunal (NGT) put a ban on mining and
transportation of coal in the State of Meghalaya, from where they used to resource 100 per cent
coal for Cachar Paper Mill and 60 per cent for the Nagaon Paper Mill.  As a result, there was
no other way to bring coal to that area, the plants were closed.
74. NPM was closed in 1990 and it went to BIFR.  Finally, in 2013, GoI approved an outlay
for `  489 crore for its revival. But final permission from BIFR came only in the month of January,
2015 and thereafter, they started the process of tendering etc.  The price discovery has shown that
the project, which was sanctioned ` 489 crore in the year 2013, now is costing about  `  861 crore.
The Revised Estimates have been approved by the competent authority. As there are different
stages, they are likely to put up to the competent authority for that. In that particular ` 489 crore,
there were 14 packages. Out of them, 7 have already been approved and allotted to the people and
7 are in the process for want of funds.  Progress is also taking place gradually but due to law
and order conditions, some disturbances keep coming. HPC expect that by the month of December,
2016, at least, NPM shall be able to manufacture some quantity of paper by buying pulp or
diverting some pulp from our local mills so that some commercial activity starts from there and
it start generating some funds also.
75. Cachar Paper Mill was closed from the month of April, 2015.  All the cost and fixed cost,
they were spending from Nagaon Paper Mill.  As a result, their working capital got eroded and
they are facing trouble on that. Fortunately, it is a good sign that Ministry of Development of North

28
Eastern Region (M/o DoNER) has given a sanction of  `  20 crores for laying of a railway line and
for conversion of metre-gauge to broad-gauge for six kilometers.  That will be over within four
months and will facilitate CPM.  Because of the working capital shortage, as they have to incur
the cost of CPM also, they are not in a position to run NPM plant also in full capacity. Therefore,
the Company has requested the Government to give a working capital support for  `  400 crores,
which is under consideration. According to HPC, it is the only industry in the North-Eastern Region
on which almost 2 lakh people around 200 kilometers are dependent on that and Bamboo, which
is the basic raw material for paper.  Bamboo is grown by the marginal farmers and 70 per cent
of NER Paper industry requirement is met by them only.  HPC is confident that after conversion
of metre gauge to broad gauge, which will cost about  `  60 crore per year, that Company will turn
into a profitable venture. Added to the presentation of HPC, DHI stated that they have been
working on the revival of HPC.  Unfortunately, before it could reach a logical fruition, now code
of conduct has been made effective because of impending Assam elections.  DHI would be moving
to Election Commission for seeking relaxation.  In case it is provided, they will go ahead.
Otherwise, after election results are announced, when code of conduct ceases to exist, DHI would
be going for Cabinet approval for HPC revival.
76. Regarding NPM, the Committee is aghast the way in which revival/restructuring of
CPSEs can be dealt with in this Country.  It took long 25 years from 1990 to 2015 for NPM
to finally get its revival plan approved from BIFR. Expectedly, the outlay made in 2013 of
````` 489 crore will now grossly fall short of the current costing of  ` ` ` ` `  861 crore. The Committee
wants to be apprised regarding the specific  reasons which lead to this delay of 25 years.
Despite such grim background, the management of NPM nurturers the hope of producing
some quantity of paper by December, 2016 and start generating some funds. The Committee
sincerely hopes that this believe bears fruits through the earnest efforts of DHI & HPC and
observes that the approval for the revised cost shall be pursued vigorously as NPM is
important to NER in terms of employment and other developments.
77. As far as CPM is concerned, the Committee notes that the Ministry of DoNER has
given a sanction of  ` ` ` ` `  20 crore for laying of a railway line and for conversion of metre-
gauge to broad-gauge for six kilometers, which would help CPM to being a profitable unit
of HPC.  Also, that DHI enhanced BE 2015-16 of ````` 50.00 crore to ````` 83.50 crore for meeting
the additional requirement of CPM as Grant-in-aid General for NER as transport subsidy as
per CCEA approval dated 28.02.2014. But the presentation also suggests that the Company
has requested the Government to give a working capital support for  ` ` ` ` `  400 crore, which is
under consideration.
78. Accordingly, the Committee is pleased to observe that different Ministries of the
Government are coming together for reviving a sick unit back to its capacity. At the same
time, it hopes that DHI could get timely working capital support that HPC require, with the
apprehension that unexpected delay, as in the case of NPM, may lead to dampening of all
the good efforts made so far.
(v) Nagaland Pulp and Paper Corporation (NPPC)
79. NPPC was incorporated in 1971 with the objective to construct and manage a modern
integrated pulp and paper mill at Tuli in Nagaland. The commercial production commenced in 1982.

29
It was incorporated as joint venture between Government of Nagaland (GoN) & HPC, wherein,
HPC holds 94.78% equity and GoN holds 5.22% equity. NPPC is a schedule ‘C’/BIFR/BPRSE
referred CPSE.
80. Regarding the revival plans of NPPC, DHI informed the Committee that  GoI sanctioned the
Revival & Up-gradation Plan of NPPC in June 2013 with a projected cost estimate of  `  489 crore.
Accordingly, Modified Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (MDRS) submitted to BIFR and the same got
approved for circulation on February, 2015. NPPC has floated global tenders for all the main plant
packages which have been opened progressively and LoI/ Work Order has been given for 7 (seven)
main plant packages, out of 14 (fourteen), with an estimated commitment of  `  250 crore. Four
packages viz. Evaporator Plant, Chlorine Di-Oxide Plant, Water Treatment Plant and Recovery &
Pulp Mill, for which negotiation at the highest level has already been completed and is on the verge
of placement before BoD for approval and issuance of LoI / WO, the approximate value of which
is `  230 crores. Work for all the plant packages have started on right earnest and barring some
unforeseen contingencies, trial run is expected by November, 2016 and commercial production in
December, 2016. Some of the packages overshoot the estimated cost, as such, NPPC is in the
process of submission of Revised Cost Estimate.
81. As part of its examination of Demand of DHI, reasons were sought by the Committee on
major variations between BE and RE for 2014-15 and reasons of surrender/savings in 2015-16
made to NPPC. The Department replied that for 2014-15 a Budget provision of  `  25.00 crore was
kept in the financial year for the NPPC as a part of its revival plan. ` 100 Crore was already
released in the year 2013-14 as a part of its revival plan, which could not be utilized completely.
Though tendering evaluation and recommendation of remaining 7 packages was completed,
awarding of the contracts to MDRS could not be made for want of BIFR clearance, which was
accorded only on 29
th January, 2015. It is expected that the remaining amount also would be
required for payment in the next 3-4 months in the financial year. Hence, no funds were likely to
be released in the year and BE was reduced to zero at RE stage. Thereafter, the major work for
the project was started. In anticipation, a provision of  `  54.00 crore was made in the year
2015-16, however, in the absence of Utilization Certificates in respect of funds released in the year
2013-14, again BE was reduced to zero at RE stage.
82. The Committee note that though a revival package amounting to  ` ` ` ` `  489 crore was
sanctioned to NPPC in 2013, the approval of BIFR was obtained only by the end of January,
2015.  The Committee observes that it is this sought of delay in the final clearance of
revival/restructuring package of sick PSUs that defeat the very purpose of its revival. Such
delays lead to cost escalation resulting in revised costs which in turn again requires
approval of competent authority and the painful vicious cycle of delays is set forth. Under
such circumstance, the Committee sincerely hopes that the new revival/restructuring
mechanism being put in place by the Government will address such teething problems of the
previous system.
83. Further, the Committee also notes that during 2013-14,  ` ` ` ` `  100 crore was released for
RMDP project work to NPPC. However, this could not be utilized completely by the
Company.  Accordingly, during 2014-15 the BE  ` ` ` ` `  25 crore for that year was withdrawn at
RE stage.  The same story was repeated during 2015-16, wherein the BE of  ` ` ` ` `  54 crore was

30
reduced to zero at RE due to absence of Utilization Certificate in respect of the funds
released in the penultimate year i.e. 2013-14.
84. The Committee, while taking into account the undue delay on the part of the
Government/ BIFR, is equally disappointed that NPPC could not utilize the funds allocated
in 2013-14 timely and also could not produce the Utilization Certificate for the same which
curtailed allocation of funds thereafter. Here, the Committee observes that the funds for
revival of CPSEs are provided by the Government after a long fought approval process.  In
this individual case, after a long drawn process of approval and sanctioning of fund, the
management of NPPC has failed squarely to make best use of the funds.  As per the new
guidelines of DPE for revival/restructuring of CPSEs, the administrative ministry has the
primary responsibility regarding the health of its CPSEs. Accordingly, it is recommended
that DHI should take measures to properly guide the management of NPPC in the
implementation of the revival plan and see to that they steer clear of such lapses in the
times ahead.
(v) Hindustan Newsprint Limited (HNL)
85. HNL which was incorporated as a wholly owned subsidiary of Hindustan Paper Corporation
in 1982 with the major objective of taking over the business of Kerala Newsprint Project is a unit
of HPC Limited. HNL has experienced a brief streak of three years (2013-2015) of losses and it
is expecting better results in the current FY . When queried about the reasons for the losses and
the steps taken to address them DHI submitted the following developments:
1. Forest Based Raw Materials:  Government of Kerala (GoK) is committed to HNL by
means of a long term agreement to supply 1,80,000 MT of Forest based raw
material every year for use in the process of manufacturing paper. The price of raw
material payable by HNL is however fixed by the Government every year.
However, in view of the losses incurred in the last three years, the company
represented to the Government for considering a concessional pricing of raw
material in order to improve the profitability and sustain its operations. Considering
the request, Government of Kerala has consented for concessional pricing of Forest
Based Raw Materials viz. Wood, Reed and Bamboo for the next six years with
effect from 2015-16. The GoK has agreed to reduce the price from the existing
level of  `  2,600/2,900 per MT to  `  1,000 per MT. This concession is expected to
reduce the cost by a significant amount.
2. To supplement the requirement of forest based raw materials, HNL has also forayed
into its own Captive Plantation. As on date, it has all together 2,670 hectares under
Captive Plantation of various species of pulpwood trees covering several districts of
the State. Since modern techniques of plantation like Clonal propagation are adopted
by HNL Forestry team, the yield per hectare is better than the average Government
plantation. Consequently, the cost of production of Raw material in HNL’s captive
plantation is much cheaper than that of the GoK supplies.
The GoK was originally committed to provide 5,600 Hectares of land on lease basis
for Captive plantation. However, it could only provide 2,670 hectares. Now, the

31
Govt. has also decided to allot the balance 3,000 Hectares in a time bound manner.
Out of which 1,500 hectare has already been identified for immediate allotment, and
the balance will be allotted in the course of another six months. With the allotment
of additional land under Captive plantation, HNL is expected to ensure continuous
supply of raw material at a cheaper cost.
3. Power Supply: In the FY 2014-15 the Company has started purchasing of Power
under the Open access trading portal of Power Trading Corporation. Under the
scheme, the company is able to bid for purchase of power at a price significantly
lower than that of the State Electricity Board. Even though, the price of traded
power may not always be cheaper than the State Board, it remains significantly
lower during winter and rainy season. The rates are also generally lower on holidays
and weekends. Taking advantage of the same phenomenon, the company is able to
save a significant sum of money on power cost. With the implementation of
purchase of power by trading from National Grid, the Company is expected to save
significantly in energy cost.
4. Cost Control Measures: In addition to the above, the Company has also started
different cost control measures like reduction of Employee cost by minimizing
Overtime Wage, streamlining the overhead costs by rationalizing manpower
requirement for factory maintenance, bulk tendering for Imported Coal for ensuring
better quality at a cheaper price, and overall monitoring of plant operations for
avoiding wastages of all sorts.
In view of the above positive developments and corrective measures undertaken by
the Company, it is expected that the cost of production will reduce significantly, and
Sales realization will also improve, which in turn will provide a competitive edge to
the Company. With the above the company is expected to turn around.
86. It was further submitted to the Committee that HNL proposes a Mill Development Plan with
an estimated project expenditure of ` 455 crore. On its implementation, there would be no qualms
so far quality of newsprint is concerned. The problem HNL is encountering is the realizable value
as Newsprint is in the Open General License and can be imported duty free, whereas HNL pays
Customs Duty on all its imports. Newsprint sold to the customers registered with Registrar of
Newspapers in India (RNI) is exempted from Excise Duty whereas manufacturers of Newsprint
have to invariably incur a heavy expenditure on paying Excise Duty on the inputs purchased and
Service Tax for services but the CENV AT credit is not available to them as the Newsprint itself
is free from Excise Duty. If these anomalies are removed specially imposition of Custom Duty on
import of Newsprint which used to be 10 % earlier is restored, HNL would be in a position to
substitute the imported newsprint, so far being dumped by the foreign manufacturers with cheaper
cost, and would be in a position to save lots of foreign currency for the Country.
87. The Committee notes that HNL has taken efficient and practical steps aimed at
revival of the Company. These proactive steps are expected to bring down the production
cost of newsprint and provide HNL a comparative advantage in the market.  The Committee
observes that the steps adopted by Government of Kerala are highly supportive of the cause
of HNL and the management of HNL would do well to make efficient use of it.  Further,

32
it is recommended that alongwith cost cutting measures, HNL should also revisit its
marketing strategies to be able to fully translate the benefits brought by the expected cost
advantage to tangible financial gains for the company.
88. As informed by DHI the Company is expected to turn around after a three-year
streak of losses.  In this regard, it is expected that DHI will monitor and guide HNL step
by step towards the turn around and provide all necessary support as expected from an
administrative ministry. The Committee further takes into cognizance the hardships faced
by HNL due to customs and excise duty liabilities. HNL claims that restoration of 10 %
customs duty on imported prints would help the Company immensely and they would be in
a position to substitute imported material. In view of this, the Committee recommends that
DHI should proactively take up the duty rationalizations requested by HNL with the
appropriate agencies.

(III)  Auto and Capital Goods Associations.
98. As part of the examination of Demands for Grants (2016-17) of DHI, the Committee heard
the representatives of select Auto Associations and Capital Goods Sectors in India.  The
Associations represented were ACMA, SIAM, ASDC, FICCI, ASSOCHAM, CII, IMTMA and
others.
99. In nutshell, the proposal placed before the Committee by these associations include
allocation of more funds for NEMMP 2020; more initiatives in investing in Charging Infrastructure
for electric vehicles; streamlining/eliminating inconsistencies in taxation of hybrid/electric vehicles
across various states in India; promotion of automobile skill development initiatives; impetus on
bridging technology gap in Machine Tool sector; measures to ensure level playing field to Indian
CGS companies in global tenders floated by major CPSEs; compulsory domestic value addition to

36
an appropriate percentage to be made part of all major CG imports, higher depreciation allowance
on Indian Machine Tools to generate greater demand and to heighten emphasis on technology
up-gradation, exclusion of Machine Tools and other Capital Goods from FTAs entered into
countries that have strong and surplus Capital Goods Sector; effective measures to counter fake
certificates of ‘Country of Origin’ under FTAs, Indian Embassies & High Commissions in different
countries to be allowed to promote India’s business interests with the help of Commercial Attaches,
Implementation of the Heavy Industry Export and Market Development Assistance Scheme
(HIEMDA), etc.
100. The Committee’s observation after hearing the representatives of Auto & Capital
Goods Sector associations is that the need of the hour is to focus more on urban & rural
infrastructure, road & highways, satellite cities, etc to generate demands at home in both
these sectors.  For auto industry, the Committee is of the opinion that they should start
looking for export markets in the face of saturating domestic arena while formulating
business expansion plans. Also, they should earnestly try and develop indigenous technology
in the field of electric vehicles. CG associations should come up with a concrete plan in tune
with the NCGP, 2016 objectives of the Government to triple the size of Indian CGS in a
decade.
101.  The Committee takes into account through the submission of DHI that they have
already taken into cognizance the areas put forth by the industry associations seeking
attention of the Government. Nevertheless, the Committee recommends that the
Government should look into the issues submitted by these associations before the
Committee and act upon them in best possible manner. This will encourage the private
sector to be more participative in the broader initiatives of nation building.

1. The Committee notes that the Demands for Grants (2016-17) for DHI has followed
a new pattern of depiction of allocation of funds when compared to the last year. On a quick
reference of Demands No. 44, the new pattern may appear difficult to comprehend due to
the absence of comparative details upfront. But, in reply to a query on this, the
Department has preferred to an explanation of bunching of smaller schemes under larger
umbrella schemes for the purpose of imparting more flexibility in the execution of schemes
and to guard against spending the resources too thin. The Committee finds reason in the
rational provided by DHI and appreciates the new initiative of the MoF.  It is expected that
the new system of Umbrella Schemes will result in timely implementation of schemes by
reallocating funds between sub schemes as per operational expediencies which should in
turn curb underutilization of funds as well. (Para No 10)
2. Regarding the allocation of funds to schemes under Development of Automobile
Industry, the Committee observes that funds for the same purpose has been allocated under
two different Heads, with one Head witnessing only a miniscule allocation and the other
reflecting majority of the funds.  The Department’s explanation for differential allocation
is that token allocations in two Heads have been made to cater to the possibility of funds
being allocated to NATRiP in the form of Grants–in-Aid as well as in the form of Loan, even
though the loan possibility is low. The Committee would have found it more appropriate if
the Government would have at least by now decided the manner in which funds to NATRiP
are to be provided, i.e. either as Loan or as Grants. Such uncertainties can affect the lucidity
of the Demand and the transparency with which allocations are made. (Para No 14)
3. The Committee takes note that under the Head, Grants to CPSEs, funds have been
reflected under two different Heads – on Depiction Head and on Operational Head. On this
duality of funds, it has been informed that funds under the Depiction Head will be
transferred to the Operational head for executing expenditure.  This arrangement has been
done under the directives of Government of India (GoI). Further, it is encouraging to take
into cognizance that DHI is one of the few Departments of the GoI where all fund transfers
are being made on-line through PFMS and under this system funds can be transferred only
to those Heads which atleast have some token allocation.  The Committee observes that the
PFMS will hasten up the release of funds and eliminate avoidable delays and
mismanagement. (Para No 18)
4. However, the Committee also wonders whether it is not ironical that while on the one
hand the Government is moving towards integration of small schemes under larger umbrella
schemes for the benefit of simplification of procedure and facilitating financial flexibility, on
the other hand it is complicating matters by adding more Heads for allocations and
expenditure of funds under a single umbrella scheme. (Para No 19)
37

38
5. The Committee notes that during 2015-16 money allocated as BE to NATRiP, Scheme
of R&D Project Development of Advanced Ultra Super- Critical (Adv-USC) Technology for
Thermal Power Plants and Heavy Engineering Corporation Limited  (HEC) had to be
completely withdrawn at RE stage. As informed by the Department, such surrender of funds
had to be effected as the requisite approval from the final competent authority was not
received in time to sustain the funds for the year.  The Committee feels that amounts
which have not been approved by the final competent authority should not be reflected in
full as BE.  Instead, reflection of a token allocation will give a much realistic picture to the
Demands as funds can be sought at the RE stage when the final approval materializes
during the course of time. (Para No 21)
6. The Committee takes into account the status of completion of various components
of NATRiP as submitted by the Department. It also notes the explanation given by the
Department on how it is to utilize the plan loan of  ` ` ` ` `  300 crore allocated to the project
during 2015-16 over a period of 3 years ending in 2017-18. In this regard, the Committee
recognizes that this spread of expenditure warrants yet another extension of NATRiP,
beyond currently extended period upto December, 2017.  The Committee express concerned
over the fact that a project which has already seen three extensions is looking for further
extension.  In the view of the Committee, this unending continuation of the flagship project
of DHI, which was originally intended to be time bound, is a pointer to mismanagement  along
with lack of foresight and accordingly, recommends that a performance audit of NATRiP
with specific focus on lapses in project management shall be conducted. (Para No 28)
7. The Committee considers FAME – India as one of the most forward looking schemes
of the Government in the face of heightened environmental concerns and depleting fossil
fuel reserves. Though the scheme is picking up, the Committee, while examining the
submissions of the Department, finds that in respect to R&D and creation of Charging
Infrastructure there has already been complaints of shortage of funds extending up to
````` 25.63 crore and  ` ` ` ` `  87.00 crore, respectively. The Committee would want the Department
to submit the reasons for the said shortages and the curative action taken, if any. It is
imperative that such teething problems are to be eliminated at early stages itself to
preclude them from developing into systematic deficiencies. (Para No 32)
8. Further, during it examination of the Demands of DHI 2016-17, the Committee felt
that there was a need for more impetus on R&D, specifically related to the development
of original technology in the field of electrical vehicles, probably in the development of
electrical motors, which will have direct application in the manufacturing of indigenous
electrical vehicles. The Committee also feel that DHI should draw a road map with the help
of industry experts in the filed of electrical vehicles with a definite time frame so that the
objectives set up by the DHI are achieved to justify the money spent and also to reduce the
emission of carbon in the environment. (Para No 33)
9. The Committee is pleased to observe that the scheme launched in November, 2014,
has made reasonable progress.  However, the NCGP exhorts a growth of the India Capital
Goods Sector from  ` ` ` ` `  2,30,000 crore in 2015 to  ` ` ` ` `  7,50,000 crore by 2025.  According to the
Committee, India in 68 years could muster only a  ` ` ` ` `  2,30,000 crore Capital Goods Sector.

39
For an ambitious aim of tripling the size of the sector in a decade, there is a need for a
clear cut road map and commensurate funds. Further, in this venture, equal participation
of the Private Industry along with the Government will be a foregone conclusion. In view
of this, the Committee recommends that in tune with the objectives of NCGP, required
managerial and financial support ought to be provided to the sector through the Scheme for
Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector and the components of
the scheme should be kept organic and continuously updated as per policy priorities and
industrial needs and developments. (Para No 40)
10. The Committee finds it extremely disappointing that the scheme originally conceived
in 2014-15 is yet to be operationalized, for want of requisite approvals. It is understood that
the latest impediment in the approval of the scheme has been disagreement on the funding
pattern. It is also understood that there was an initial agreement on the financial
contribution of the participants and the disagreement emerged after the direction from the
PMO to upscale their individual contributions. However, the participating entities BHEL,
NTPC, IGCAR have found it not possible to further increase their contribution to the
scheme.  In this scenario, the Committee observes that the finalization of the funding
patterns has to be taken up on a top priority by DHI.  Advanced Ultra Super Critical
Technology for Thermal Power Plants is a technology of future as it provides cleaner and
more efficient avenues of thermal power. Hence the development of the same getting
delayed because of indecision of funding pattern is disappointing. The Committee is of the
opinion that the onus of taking initiative to find a solution to this imbroglio lies with DHI
and recommends that the matter should be taken up at all reconciliatory fora including the
Cabinet, if needed.  The Committee wants DHI to come back to it with the progress made
in this regard. (Para No 46)
11. The Committee notes with concern that none of the CPSEs under DHI have been
found to be operating in a healthy manner.  The status of CPSEs has been classified as
weak, incipient sick or sick.  In the case of DHI, even the prestigious Maharatna BHEL has
been termed as a ‘Weak’  CPSE. The Committee considers this as an extremely alarming
situation which calls for decisive intervention by DHI, the administrative department.  As
per the New Guidelines of DPE, the primary responsibility for ensuring profitable
functioning of CPSEs lies with the respective administrative ministries.  In this regard, the
Committee is aware that the Government has come up with a lot of new initiatives to
reshape the avenues for revival /restructure of CPSEs.  This includes the winding up of
Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BRPSE), constitution of National Council
of Law Tribunal (NCLT) and other similar measures.  The subject of revival /restructuring
of CPSEs have repeatedly attracted the attention of the Committee and every time the
Department comes up with some generalized reasons and solutions to the entire problem.
However, the Committee has found that the lack of foresight and timely action can be
termed as one of the main causes for the poor plight of the CPSEs. In this scenario, the
Committee would like to strongly recommend that DHI desperately needs some workable
roadmap on the performance of each of its 31 CPSEs regardless of their current
classification.  It is also recommended that some appropriate mechanism for fixing
responsibility with the management of the CPSEs for the distress of CPSE concerned has
to be drawn up. (Para No 54)

40
12. In this matter, the Committee is unanimous in its opinion and is in full support of
the view of the Department regarding disposal of assets of sick/loss incurring CPSEs that
the immovable assets, i.e., land and/or buildings of such CPSEs would be transferred only
to Central/State Government or Central /State Government entities/PSUs. Accordingly, the
Committee strongly recommends that the Government should retain the above stand as this
would avoid sell out of landed property of CPSEs to private persons. The Committee feels
that land/building of such CPSEs can be utilised to start ITI or other technical institutions
under the scheme “Skill India”. (Para No 56)
13. The Committee notes that the performance of BHEL has slackened over the last two
to three years owing to a slew of reasons given by the Company viz. retarded demand,
delayed environmental clearances, stranded orders, etc. In the view of the Committee, the
reasons put forward by BHEL portrays an impression that these have been ‘beyond the
control’ of the company. Even while considering that BHEL might have taken steps to check
the slide in its performance, the fact remains that their performance seems to have dipped
despite these efforts. Accordingly, the Committee finds it difficult to isolate the reasons for
the lackluster performance of BHEL to those quoted by the company alone. Therefore, the
Committee’s conclusion is that there has been a delay on the part of BHEL in responding
to the challenges thrown to them by the market and other factors.  Though, the Committee
does not completely discount the reasons put forth by BHEL, it is the Committee’s firm
belief that BHEL’s current situation is the outcome of their poor performance in the
area of risk analysis and business foresight, both of which would have allowed the
Company to anticipate rough business weather and for effective and commensurate course
correction. (Para No 60)
14. In the area of diversification of business also the Committee finds that the efforts
taken by BHEL does not seem to be of the quality of the top most companies in India to
which BHEL belongs. Efficient and timely diversification could have acted as a buffer to
absorb the shocks in the core business. Since this has not happened it will not be out of
place to presume that the diversification initiatives of BHEL do not bring in the desired
results. And for DHI, the Committee opines that DHI should have pressed BHEL firmly for
implementation of timely corrective measures. Under these circumstances, the Committee
cannot but recommend strict measures to ensure accountability for lapses in business
decisions to the extent possible.  Accordingly, it is further recommended that a forensic
audit for BHEL shall be ordered with a view to identify instances of deficiencies in business
decisions and take suitable measures so that those are not repeated. (Para No 61)
15. The Committee is aware that HEC had once set an example how a sick company can
revive and turn around to generate profits again with efficient managerial approach and
Government support. Therefore, the Committee in its reports on DFG of DHI 2013-14 and
2015-16 had recommended the Modernization of HEC, so that the Company could sustain
the gains made through the revival package. In its 2015-16 report the Committee even
suggested that DHI should consider enhancing the budgetary assistance of  ` ` ` ` `  500 crores,
appropriately. (Para No 68)
16. It is evident from HEC’s submission before the Committee that the modernization

41
of HEC is getting stalled due to shortage of funds. The Committee has in the past
repeatedly asked the Government to help and hasten HEC’s plan for modernization, but it
seemed to have brought in little results. Accordingly, the Committee again strongly
recommends DHI to provide all requisite support to HEC in their search for funds and
consider providing proposed guarantee for bank loan or enhancement of budgetary supports
beyond ` ` ` ` `  500 crores.  It is the firm opinion of the Committee that, the management will
be equally responsible to help themselves to make available the required funds for its
modernization and utilize the same efficiently. (Para No 69)
17. However, the worrisome factor for the Committee is the lethargic approach of the
parties involved which is the typical cause for delay in respect of revival of CPSEs. The
Committee apprehends that this factor may creep into the case of HEC as well.  Therefore,
the Committee warns both the administrative ministry and HEC from falling prey to this
cliché situation. (Para No 70)
18. As the Committee reads, the only silver lining in the cloud will be the MoU, HEC
has signed with Russian Government Company for technology transfer in the areas of
manufacturing clean steel technologies and heavy casting/forgings for different clientele. It
is indeed good news that because of this move items under ‘Make in India’ initiative could
be manufactured at HEC. (Para No 71)
19. Regarding NPM, the Committee is aghast the way in which revival/restructuring of
CPSEs can be dealt with in this Country. It took long 25 years from 1990 to 2015 for NPM
to finally get its revival plan approved from BIFR. Expectedly, the outlay made in 2013 of
````` 489 crore will now grossly fall short of the current costing of  ` ` ` ` `  861 crore. The Committee
wants to be apprised regarding the specific reasons which lead to this delay of 25 years.
Despite such grim background, the management of NPM nurturers the hope of producing
some quantity of paper by December, 2016 and start generating some funds. The Committee
sincerely hopes that this believe bears fruits through the earnest efforts of DHI & HPC and
observes that the approval for the revised cost shall be pursued vigorously as NPM is
important to NER in terms of employment and other developments. (Para No 76)
20. As far as CPM is concerned, the Committee notes that the Ministry of DoNER has
given a sanction of  ` ` ` ` ` 20 crore for laying of a railway line and for conversion of metre-gauge
to broad-gauge for six kilometers, which would help CPM to being a profitable unit of HPC.
Also, that DHI enhanced BE 2015-16 of ````` 50.00 crore to ````` 83.50 crore for meeting the
additional requirement of CPM as Grant-in-aid General for NER as transport subsidy as per
CCEA approval dated 28.02.2014. But the presentation also suggests that the Company has
requested the Government to give a working capital support for  ` ` ` ` `  400 crore, which is under
consideration. (Para No 77)
21. Accordingly, the Committee is pleased to observe that different Ministries of the
Government are coming together for reviving a sick unit back to its capacity. At the same
time, it hopes that DHI could  get timely working capital support that HPC require, with
the apprehension that unexpected delay, as in the case of NPM, may lead to dampening of
all the good efforts made so far. (Para No 78)

42
22. The Committee note that though a revival package amounting to  ` ` ` ` `  489 crore was
sanctioned to NPPC in 2013, the approval of BIFR was obtained only by the end of January,
2015.  The Committee observes that it is this sought of delay in the final clearance of
revival/restructuring package of sick PSUs that defeat the very purpose of its revival. Such
delays lead to cost escalation resulting in revised costs which in turn again requires
approval of competent authority and the painful vicious cycle of delays is set forth. Under
such circumstance, the Committee sincerely hopes that the new revival/restructuring
mechanism being put in place by the Government will address such teething problems of the
previous system. (Para No 82)
23. Further, the Committee also notes that during 2013-14,  ` ` ` ` `  100 crore was released for
RMDP project work to NPPC. However, this could not be utilized completely by the
Company.  Accordingly, during 2014-15 the BE  ` ` ` ` `  25 crore for that year was withdrawn at
RE stage.  The same story was repeated during 2015-16, wherein the BE of  ` ` ` ` `  54 crore was
reduced to zero at RE due to absence of Utilization Certificate in respect of the funds
released in the penultimate year i.e. 2013-14. (Para No 83)
24. The Committee while taking into account the undue delay on the part of the
Government/ BIFR, is equally disappointed that NPPC could not utilize the funds allocated
in 2013-14 timely and also could not produce the Utilization Certificate for the same which
curtailed allocation of funds thereafter. Here, the Committee observes that the funds for
revival of CPSEs are provided by the Government after a long fought approval process.  In
this individual case, after a long drawn process of approval and sanctioning of fund, the
management of NPPC has failed squarely to make best use of the funds. As per the new
guidelines of DPE for revival/restructuring of CPSEs, the administrative ministry has the
primary responsibility regarding the health of its CPSEs. Accordingly, it is recommended
that DHI should take measures to properly guide the management of NPPC in the
implementation of the revival plan and see to that they steer clear of such lapses in the
times ahead. (Para No 84)
25. The Committee notes that HNL has taken efficient and practical steps aimed at
revival of the Company. These proactive steps are expected to bring down the production
cost of newsprint and provide HNL a comparative advantage in the market.  The Committee
observes that the steps adopted by Government of Kerala are highly supportive of the cause
of HNL and the management of HNL would do well to make efficient use of it.  Further,
it is recommended that alongwith cost cutting measures, HNL should also revisit its
marketing strategies to be able to fully translate the benefits brought by the expected cost
advantage to tangible financial gains for the company. (Para No 87)
26. As informed by DHI the Company is expected to turn around after a three-year
streak of losses.  In this regard, it is expected that DHI will monitor and guide HNL step
by  step towards the turn around and provide all necessary support as expected from an
administrative ministry. The Committee further takes into cognizance the hardships faced
by HNL due to customs and excise duty liabilities. HNL claims that restoration of 10 %
customs duty on imported prints would help the Company immensely and they would be in
a position to substitute imported material. In view of this, the Committee recommends that

43
DHI should proactively take up the duty rationalizations requested by HNL with the
appropriate agencies. (Para No 88)
27. As per the facts placed before the Committee it is noted that the RMDP of NEPA is
progressing reasonably well. The total Budgetary support of  ` ` ` ` `  157 crore approved to the
Company and as per DHI, an amount of  ` ` ` ` `  109.09 crore is purported to be utilized by March,
2016 in the form of 3 installments during the years, 2014-15. However, it is also noted that
NEPA has to secure a bank loan of  ` ` ` ` `  128 crore to complete the funds required for RMDP.
The Committee is made to understand that request for Bank guarantee has been pending
with MoF since September, 2015.  The Committee feels that it is high time a decision is
taken on the request, as the same is already badly delayed. It is therefore, recommended
that the execution of RMDP shall be expedited and all further delays are prevented. DHI
shall come back to the Committee on the progress made on the issue and efforts taken to
pursue the MoF for a decision on the above request. The Committee also wants DHI to
consider continuing the working capital support to NEPA Ltd as the company is so close to
standing on its own feet and might lose its way if support is withdrawn at this stage. As
already recommended in other similar cases, it will not be out of place to mention that DHI
should also ensure the responsibility of the management of NEPA in the timely execution
of RMDP and also in the follow up with the MoF. (Para No 95)
28. The Committee notes that in the Demands for Grants, the IEBR figures of CPSEs
portray a very unrealistic picture.  In most instances, the BE IEBR is greatly reduced or
even comes to naught at the RE stage. The explanation for such reductions provided by the
Government/ CPSEs range from deferred investments, decrease in profit, incurring of loss
by the companies, the companies being or becoming sick, reductions in tune with business
requirements, delay in securing loans, etc.  The Committee feels that though each variation
in IEBR figures are backed up with reasons by Government /CPSEs, it remains a fact that
the overall picture drawn while going through the Demands as such is confusing and borders
on misleading information as a considerable portion of the amount is disappearing at RE
stage. This is also because IEBR of a company comprises of resources generated by
Company concerned through profit, loans, equity and other funds to be secured by the
company, etc and in most cases these figures are assumptive. Accordingly, the Committee
observes that the Demand should contain an explanation to IEBR figures of each of the
CPSEs indicating the nature of the funds projected as IEBR. (Para No 97)
29. The Committee’s observation after hearing the representatives of Auto & Capital
Goods Sector associations is that the need of the hour is to focus more on urban & rural
infrastructure, road & highways, satellite cities, etc to generate demands at home in both
these sectors.  For auto industry, the Committee is of the opinion that they should start
looking for export markets in the face of saturating domestic arena while formulating
business expansion plans. Also, they should earnestly try and develop indigenous technology
in the field of electric vehicles. CG associations should come up with a concrete plan in tune
with the NCGP, 2016 objectives of the Government to triple the size of Indian CGS in a
decade. (Para No 100)

44
30.  The Committee takes into account through the submission of DHI that they have
already taken into cognizance the areas put forth by the industry associations seeking
attention of the Government. Nevertheless, the Committee recommends that the
Government should look into the issues submitted by these associations before the
Committee and act upon them in best possible manner. This will encourage the private
sector to be more participative in the broader initiatives of nation build ing. (Para No 101)

REPORT
Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) were set up to serve the broad macro-economic objective
of higher economic growth, self-sufficiency in production of goods and services, long term
equilibrium in balance of payment and low and stable prices besides meeting socio- economic
obligations. Performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), during the year 2014-15,
is summarized below:
(i) There were 298 Central Public Sector Enterprises (excluding 7 insurance companies)
under the administrative control of various Ministries/Departments as on 31.3.2015.
Out of these 298 CPSEs, 235 were in operation and 63 CPSEs have yet to
commence business. Schedules-wise list of the CPSEs and list of Maharatna,
Navratana and Miniratna CPSEs are placed at Annexure I and II, respectively.
Out of 235 operating CPSEs as many as 157 CPSEs showed profit and 77 CPSEs
incurred losses during 2014-15.
(ii) The cumulative investment (paid up capital plus long terms loans), which was
` 29 crores in 5 enterprises at the time of first Five Year Plan ( i.e. as on 31.3.1951),
has gone up to ` 10,96,057 crores in 298 CPSEs as on 31.3.2015. While the increase
in ‘investment’ in all the CPSEs went up by 10.48% in 2014-15 over 2013-14, the
increase in ‘capital employed’ went up by 7.40% during the same period.
(iii) The ‘net profit’ of 157 profit making CPSEs was ` 1,30,363 crores in 2014-15 as
against 164 profit making enterprises in 2013-14. The ‘net loss’ of 77 loss making
enterprise stood at ` 27,360 crores during the year as against 70 loss making
enterprises in 2013-14.
(iv) In comparison to 2013-14, the profitability ratios in terms of net profit to turnover/
revenue, net profit to capital employed, net profit to net worth, sales to capital
employed have declined, whereas interest to gross profit show an increase in
2014-15.
2. The Financial Year (FY) 2015-16 saw some important milestones in the realm of CPSEs in
India.  The revival/restructure/closure of sick CPSEs had evolved into a painful delayed process.
To address this, Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) brought out guidelines to “Streamlining
the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick, incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector
Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of restructuring” in October, 2015. The guidelines
enumerated the criteria for identifying the CPSEs as sick, incipient sick and weak. Subsequently,
the formal closing down of Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE), one
of the agencies involved in the revival/restructuring process of CPSEs, was announced in
November, 2015. After the closing down of BRPSE, the administrative Ministries/Departments were
put in charge of the primary responsibility of keeping watch over the health of CPSEs under them.
Further, the restructuring mechanism was also made time bound. The proposed National Council

process the revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs in India thereby ending the hitherto existent multi

3. Further, in the Budget 2016-17, the Finance Minister announced that the assets of CPSEs
had to be leveraged for generation of resources for investment in new projects.  DPE has been
assigned the responsibility of monitoring Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) by CPSEs in infrastructural
projects. The Budget also contained an announcement that a comprehensive approach for efficient
management of Government investment in CPSEs would be adopted.  Regarding disinvestment/
strategic sale of CPSEs, the Government also had laid out a new method wherein the NITI Aayog
has been tasked with identifying the CPSEs for disinvestment, mode of sale, percentage of sale and
methods of evaluation.  DPE has been made part of the process of disinvestment at its different
stages and the same is in tune with the enhancement of the mandate of DPE carried out in the
second half of the year 2015.
Department of Public Enterprises- Mandate
4. In their 52
nd Report, the Estimates Committee of 3 rd Lok Sabha (1962-67) stressed the need
for setting up a centralized coordinating unit, which could also make continuous appraisal of the
performance of public enterprises which led to the setting up of the Bureau of Public Enterprises
(BPE) in 1965 in the Ministry of Finance.  Subsequently, as a result of the reorganization of the
Ministries/Departments of the Union Government in September, 1985, BPE was made part of the
Ministry of Industry.  In May, 1990, BPE was made a full-fledged Department known as the
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE).  Presently, it is part of the Ministry of Heavy Industries
and Public Enterprises.
5. The Department of Public Enterprises is the nodal department for all the Central Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and formulates policy pertaining to CPSEs. It lays down, in particular,
policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, autonomy and financial delegation
and personnel management in CPSEs. It furthermore collects and maintains information in the form
of a Public Enterprises Survey on several areas in respect of CPSEs.
6. In fulfilling its role, the Department Coordinates with other Ministries, CPSEs and
concerned organizations. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the following
subjects have been allocated to the DPE:
Residual work relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industrial
Management Pool.
Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public Sector Enterprises.
Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, including the
Memorandum of Understanding mechanism.
Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of Arbitration for the Public Sector Enterprises.
Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public Sector Undertakings
under V oluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS).

The Department of Public Enterprises implements two Plan Schemes viz. (i) Scheme of
Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment (CRR) for the rationalised employees of CPSEs and (ii)
Scheme of Research, Development and Consultancies (RDC) on Generic issues related to Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs and SLPEs).
7. During the oral evidence as part of the examination of Demands for Grants (2016-17) of
DPE, the Committee pointed out that the mandate of the Department was significant and it had the
responsibility of overseeing the working of the CPSEs in India which had a cumulative turnover
of ` 22,00,000 crore. Further, the Committee also took into cognizance the expansion of the
mandate of the Department which now included evaluation of CPSEs, the monitoring of their
performance and the review of CAPEX by the CPSEs. Besides, DPE also had the responsibility of
running the PMA mechanism.
8. The Secretary, DPE while answering the queries of the Committee stated that-
“DPE has a chequered history. We started as a bureau and when we became a
Department, we were given certain responsibilities that have, sometimes, been changing.  At
one point of time, DPE was doing disinvestment, but some years back, the Department of
Disinvestment has been created.  So, that issue has been separated.  Just in August, we were
given the role of monitoring CAPEX and hon. Member has raised a point on that issue.
We are monitoring that from August last year only and we are trying to improve our system.
I do agree that there has been delay in projects.  But the delays in the projects of CPSEs
are being monitored now as closely as we can and we will keep on trying to improve the
system. There has also been a point made about the PMA mechanism.  The Departments
sometimes go to courts; the corporates also, sometimes, go to courts.  This issue has been
coming up again and again and we have had meetings at higher level in Cabinet
Secretariat and the Departments have been asked to desist from going to court and try to
settle it at the level of PMA. The pendency is there.  But, definitely, it has been a
mechanism that has helped us.  In certain issues which are not accepted by the parties
concerned, the appeal would lie with the Secretary, Law, and it is always settled within the
ambit of the Government without resorting to going to Courts.”

9. In their written replies to the queries of the Committee regarding the enhancement of
mandate, the Department submitted that the Amendment of Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961 has been done vide Presidential Notification in August, 2015 to enhance the
role of DPE in monitoring of performance of CPSEs and effective management of their assets by
allocating some additional subjects to DPE. These included review of capital projects and
expenditure in CPSEs, measures aimed at improving performance and rendering advice relating to
revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises including the mechanisms therefor.
DPE had accordingly initiated steps for monitoring the CAPEX projects of 33 CPSEs, Railway
Board and four other organizations. Similarly, for strengthening of performance evaluation process,
MoU guidelines for 2016-17 had been revised and parameter proposed were result oriented rather
than process oriented. Guidelines for Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of
sick/ incipient sick and weak CPSEs were issued on 29 October, 2015.
10. The Committee notes that the mandate of DPE has been augmented with the addition
of roles in monitoring of performance of CPSEs and effective management of their assets.
This has been done by addition of subjects to the Allocation of Business of DPE.  The
Committee is of the considered opinion that though the Budget allocation of DPE is small
compared to the major Ministries/Departments of the Government, the role to be essayed
by them is critical.  As the nodal Department of all CPSEs in India, their effective
evaluation and monitoring is going to be ‘humongous task.   The newly added responsibility
of CAPEX monitoring, measures to improve performance of CPSEs and other capacity
building initiatives and advice regarding revival/restructuring/closure of CPSEs will render
the working of DPE pivotal to the way CPSEs perform in the country.
11. Accordingly, the Committee observes that DPE should realize and imbibe the
magnitude and importance of the responsibilities that have been entrusted to them and take
more proactive measures to play out this role.  Rather them imagining themselves just as
a nodal coordinating agency, DPE should reinvent themselves as an arm of the Government
which can take decisive steps on its own or in coordination with other Ministries/
Departments   to create a facilitative milieu for CPSEs to perform to their potential.  The
Committee is of the firm view that DPE should not be restricting themselves to just issuing
guidelines and providing advice.  The new mandate gives them ample space to effectively
follow up the implementation of the advices rendered by them through their guidelines.
Accordingly, the Committee recommends that to be able to do this, DPE has to equip
themselves better and come out with measures implementable on ground and also
endeavour to create a coordinative platform involving the respective administrative
Ministries and other relevant Government agencies through which matters relating to the
working of CPSEs in the country can be resolved at a single stage avoiding time lag in
administrative decisions, the single most degenerative factor in case of decisions related to
CPSEs.

12. When asked about to provide an overview of the CPSE ecosystem in the country during
the Twelfth Plan Period (2012-17) till now, and to bring out all major events/factors that made an
impact in the Sector by providing a brief outline of the initiatives of the Government during this

5
period, it was submitted by the Department that the global economic performance has been
subdued over the previous couple of years and the developing economies were struggling to cope
with the declining commodity prices, reduced capital inflows into their economies and increasing
financial volatility. The CPSEs in India were performing to the best of their abilities in the prevailing
economic scenario. Brief outline of the initiatives of the Government during this period were as
under:-
Amendment of Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 has been
made vide Presidential Notification in August 2015 to enhance the role of DPE in
monitoring of performance of CPSEs, effective management of their assets and capacity
building in Good Governance practices by allocating some additional subjects particularly
Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector Enterprises.
Winding up of Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) has
been done by Government in November 2015 to reduce the number of layers for expeditious
decision on restructuring/ revival of CPSEs.
Guidelines on streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/
incipient sick and weak CPSEs have been issued in October 2015 by Department of Public
Enterprises. A criterion has been laid down in the said guidelines for identifying the CPSEs
as sick, incipient sick and weak CPSEs.
13. The Committee notes that DPE claims that the CPSEs in India are performing to the
best of their abilities in the prevailing economic scenario of declining commodity prices,
reduced capital inflows into their economies and increasing financial volatility. Even while
taking the claim of DPE in its face value and acknowledging the fact that the Committee
is not in knowledge of the performance of all the CPSEs in India, the Committee cannot
but share its observation that the current status of all the 31 CPSEs under the Department
of Heavy Industry (DHI) is sick / incipient sick and weak as per DPEs guidelines for
“Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick / incipient sick and weak
Central Public Sector Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of restructuring”.
Accordingly, the Committee observes that the stand taken by DPE that CPSEs are
performing well under the given conditions as status-quoits and wants the Department to
adopt a new forward looking stance.

Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment (CRR) Scheme for separated Employees of CPSEs.
20. Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment (CRR) Scheme is a scheme run by DPE to
provide opportunities of self/wage employment to the employees or dependents of Central Public
Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) separated under V oluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)/Voluntary
Separation Scheme (VSS) or retrenched due to closure/restructuring of the enterprise. The Scheme
aims at providing short duration skill development/entrepreneurship development training
programmes to equip the beneficiaries for self/wage employment including for new vocations and
has been implemented since the year 2001-02. It was subsequently notified in November, 2007 in
order to wider its scope and coverage.
21. While examining the Demands 2016-17 of DPE, it was noted that the Budget Expenditure
(BE) for the CRR Scheme of ` 3.20 crore (for the year 2016-17) had been allocated under two
Heads i.e. ` 0.20 crore under Major Head 2552 and ` 3.0 crore under Major Head 2852. The
Committee wanted to know the reasons for allocation of money under two different Heads. To this
query, the Department replied that under Major Head 2852, funds to the tune of ` 3.00 crore had
been allocated during 2016-17 under the Scheme of CRR. Major Head 2552 was meant for
allocation of funds earmarked for NE Region and thus ` 0.20 crore was earmarked under CRR
Scheme for the NE Region during 2016-17.

23. When the Committee wanted to know about the outcome of the reviews of the scheme
undertaken by the nodal agencies and the modifications done in the CRR scheme after the review,
the DPE submitted that in the year 2012-13, National Institute of Entrepreneurship and Small
Business Development (NIESBUD), an autonomous body of the Ministry of Micro, Small and
Medium Enterprises was engaged to evaluate the CRR Scheme. Major findings and

10
recommendations had been circulated to Nodal agencies for compliance. Some of the key findings
and recommendations were as under:
Adoption of DPE’s strategic approach of mixing both private and Government sector
organisations as nodal agencies has paid dividend. With varied experience, these nodal
agencies have been able to infuse synergy for the furtherance of the CRR Scheme over
the years at grassroots.
The widening of the ambit of the scheme by involving dependents of separated employees
has proved to be beneficial. This provision has been continued while implementing the
scheme in the current year.
The analysis of quantitative data posted by VRS optees/dependents points towards greater
fulfilment of objectives and goals as outlined in the scheme.
Academic orientation of the training imparted by nodal agencies has market friendly ideology
with scope for self-employment in case of both Government and private agencies.
CRR Scheme necessitates involvement of State based Government organisations engaged in
skill development and livelihood promotion activities.
More stress is needed on follow-ups and redeployment after linking with micro credit/
finance. In this context, Nodal Agencies have already been directed to explore possibilities
of hand holding projects and linkages particularly in context with training to dependents
under CRR to enhance redeployment/self-employment opportunities.
The quality of mobilisation (motivation) by nodal agencies in relation to counselling of VRS
optees/dependents has been found to have moderate impact on (i) retention of expected
motivation during the training; and (ii) in the job employment or in self- employment
activities.
More stress is needed to explore the possibility of formation of Self Help Group (SHGs)
by the agencies. Nodal Agencies have been asked to form SHGs wherever feasible with
provision for creation of corpus funds. Nodal Agencies have also been advised to have
sessions on bankable projects and hand holdings with participation of financial institutions.
24. The Committee has always been appreciative of the objectives served by the CRR
scheme which basically offers a social security net to employees of CPSEs who optees for
VRS or get retrenched. The Committee takes into cognizance the fact that NIESBUD had
undertaken an evaluation of the scheme in 2012-13 and had recommended a host of
improvements. One of the major recommendations was the need to stress more on follow
ups and redeployment after linking with micro credit/finance. Handholding projects and
linkages were also recommended to enhance redeployment/self employment opportunities of
the former employees and their dependents trained under the scheme. DPE have submitted
that there recommendations had been circulated to the Nodal Agencies for compliance.
However, Committee finds that the number of people redeployed after being trained under
the scheme has always hovered around 50% or less of the total trained personnel. The

11
situation has continued even after the recommendations of NIESBUD made in 2012.
Accordingly, the Committee strongly recommends that the Department should take
appropriate measures expeditiously to improve the number of trainees who get redeployed
subsequent to the training under the scheme.  In this regard, the Committee also wants
DPE to consider focussed Skill Development under current impetus accorded to skill
development by the Government.  The Nodal Agencies under the Scheme should identify the
skill sets that are in demand in the local area in terms of employability and provide
training to people under the Scheme. To the Committee, this is one of the measures that
can be taken to improve the redeployment ratio. Further, this will also contribute towards

Scheme of Research, Development and Consultancies on Generic issues related to Public
Sector Enterprises.
25. On the scheme of Research, Development and Consultancies (RDC) on Generic issues of
Public Sector Enterprises, DPE informed that the scheme was introduced in the year 2007-08 and

(ii) conduct seminars and workshops on the Generic issues to adopt collaborative and cooperative
learning for experience sharing; (iii) conduct training programmes for capacity building and skill
development;  (iv) constant improvement in performance evaluation and management processes of
Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs); (v) incentive best practices in focus areas through grant
of awards/incentives to CPSEs and SLPEs; and (vi) to deal with any other pertinent issue related
to Department of Public Enterprises (DPE).
26. During the examination of Demands 2016-17 of DPE, questions were raised on the BE
allocation for RDC scheme of ` 6.80 crore being made under two Major Heads- ` 0.80 crore under
the Major Head 2552 and ` 6.00 crore under Major Head 2852. In reply to this, DPE submitted
that the Plan funds are allocated separately for Major Head 2852 and Major Head 2552 which was
meant for North-East Areas. During the year 2016-17, ` 6.00 crore under RDC Scheme has been
allocated under Major Head 2852 while ` 0.80 crore has been allocated under Major Head 2552
for the North-Eastern Areas. It was further submitted that with a view to rationalize Plan Schemes
as per direction of Ministry of Finance, Skill Development/Training Programme of Executives of
State Level Public Enterprises (SLPEs) has been merged with RDC Scheme in the year 2016-17.
Payment of Government of India’s annual membership International Centre for Promotion of
Enterprises (ICPEs) which was earlier made through non-plan expenditure had also been included
in the revised RDC Scheme. Therefore, no separate allocation for contribution to ICPE was made
in 2016-17. Accordingly, from 2016-17 onwards RDC scheme will operate as an umbrella scheme
with wider scope and objectives.
27. However, regarding the allocation and utilisation of the funds of RDC during 2015-16, the
Committee noted that the BE for the scheme was ` 3.5 crore which was curtailed to ` 2.81 crore

12
at RE. The Committee wanted to know the actual utilization made under the scheme. The
Department informed that ` 1.89 crore had been utilized under the scheme till 14 th March, 2016.
It was also submitted that since the scheme had been made an umbrella scheme from 2016-17
onwards with broader coverage, the utilization of funds under the scheme was expected to
improve.

by CPSEs during 2014-15 through the available resources in the Department.  Further, the matter
of setting-up a monitoring system within DPE has also been taken up with the MoCA.
31. The Committee is happy to know that the Department has already initiated steps to
act on its recommendation regarding setting-up of a monitoring system to look into CSR
fund utilization by CPSEs. It is also appreciated that the matter has also been taken up

DPE should work in synchronisation with the MoCA in the matter relating to the

monitoring of the CSR fund utilization to ensure efficient internalisation of the CSR
