Revival/Restructuring of sick/loss incurring CPSEs.
32. As part of its examination of DFG 2016-17 of DPE, the Department was asked to explain,
step by step, the mechanism which was in place now and before i.e. , when Board for
Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) was in existence (till November, 2015) for
revival/restructuring/closures of CPSEs while bring out the roles of each agency, i.e.  the
administrative Ministry, BRPSE, BIFR and various other approving authorities in the process. The
Department was also asked to make a comparison of the erstwhile process of dealing with a sick
CPSE with the process made effective beyond November, 2015 with the NCLT and the NITI Ayog,
as the authorities of approval.
33. In reply, DPE submitted that before the winding up of BRPSE, proposals relating to revival/
restructuring of sick CPSEs received in DPE from the administrative Ministries/Departments
concerned, were referred to BRPSE for its recommendations. BRPSE considered the restructuring
or revival plan of CPSEs and gave its recommendations. The recommendations were advisory in
nature. The administrative Ministry/Department concerned processed the recommendations of
BRPSE and obtained approval of the competent authority and thereafter implemented the
decisions.
34. Consequent upon the decision of the Government (on 7.10.2015) for winding up of BRPSE,
DPE issued guidelines on 29.10.2015 on “Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring
of sick/incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enterprises”. The administrative Ministry/
Department concerned was now responsible to monitor the sickness of CPSEs functioning under
them and take timely redressal measures for revival/restructuring/disinvestment of sick/loss making
CPSEs with the approval of the competent authority.
35. Based on the information available in Public Enterprises Survey, 2014-15, DPE has prepared
a list of sick, incipient sick and weak CPSEs as on 31.3.2015 and has sent the list to the
concerned administrative Ministries/Departments of CPSEs on 10.2.2016 to confirm the
classification (identification of sick/incipient sick and weak CPSEs) for taking action as per the
DPE guidelines dated 29.10.2015 regarding revival and restructuring of sick and weak CPSEs.
36. Regarding the roles of different agencies involved in the process, DPE submitted that NCLT
and BIFR came under MoCA and Department of Financial Services, respectively. The role of DPE
was formulation of policy guidelines for dealing with sickness in CPSEs as per its guidelines issued
for revival/restructuring of sick CPSEs on 29.10.2015. The role of other agencies could be
explained by the administrative Ministries/Departments concerned. Further, the Department also
stated that the setting-up of NCLT is likely to replace BIFR. Ministry of MoCA was yet to notify
the setting-up of NCLT. In that case, BIFR would continue with its extant functions. DPE also
stated that the details regarding the setting-up of NCLT and the future of BIFR have been sought
from MoCA and Department of Financial Services, respectively.
37. During the oral evidence of DPE, the Committee further queried on the reasons behind
winding up of BRPSE for which the Department replied that the Government felt that the BRPSE

14
was an additional layer and needed to be removed.  In that process, the responsibility was given
to the administrative Ministry concerned to watch, to see and to review the performance. DPE has
prescribed a few things to do as part of this to the administrative Ministry. One of them was to
see whether they have become sick or they have become weak. If it falls in that category, DPE
instructed the administrative Ministry to keep a close watch and try to turn them around and do
mid-course correction and, wherever necessary, move for its restructuring or improving its
performance.  As per DPE guideline issued 29 th October, 2015 it had been always the role of the
administrative Ministry/Department concerned to address the issues of sick and weak CPSEs and
to take timely redressal measures for revival/restructuring/disinvestment of sick/loss making CPSEs
with the approval of the competent authority in a time bound manner.
38. During the oral evidence, the Committee asked DPE to submit in writing the salient features
of the guidelines of DPE issued on 29
th November, 2015 on streamlining the mechanism for revival/
restructuring of sick/incipient sick and week CPSEs in India, specially identifying the role of NCLT,
NITI Ayog, BIFR, DPE and the respective administrative Ministry in the case of such CPSEs.
39. Regarding the role of other agencies, it was submitted by DPE that the Companies Act,
2013 vide Section 407 to 434 (both inclusive), provide inter-alia  for setting-up of (a) the National
Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and (b) the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).
The Act provided for revival and rehabilitation of sick companies which were enumerated in
Section 253 to 269 of the Companies Act, 2013.  However, since these sections were yet to be
notified by MoCA, NCLT and NCLA T were yet to be operationalised. At present, the Board of
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR)/Appellate Authority for Industrial and Financial
Reconstruction (AAIFR) were authorized in the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act,
1965 for approval of revival and rehabilitation of Sick Companies, including CPSEs. DPE added
that MoCA had informed that the NCLT would replace (a) the existing Company Law Board;
(b) BIFR; (c) AAIFR and; (d) would also acquire the jurisdiction of the High Courts in the matter
where it was vested in the High Courts under the Act. Bodies referred at (b) and (c) would stand
abolished upon notification of the SICA (Repeal) Act, 2003.  MoCA has further informed that the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2015 had been introduced in the Parliament and it also proposed
to amend the Companies Act, 2013 with regard to insolvency (revival as well as winding up)
related provisions.
40. Firstly, the Committee notes with dissatisfaction the disowning by DPE of the subject
matter related to the agencies involved in the revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs in India.
The Committee is critical of the tendency of the Department to compartmentalise the
replies by contending that the roles of NCLT and BIFR would be explained by the respective
Ministry/Department concerned. As the nodal Department for the overseeing of all CPSEs
in the country, DPE is expected to provide a cogent reply to the Committee even if the
subject matter falls under the domain of other Ministries/Departments/Agencies. The
responsibility of action on the subject being with another Ministry/Department/Agency can
be justified, but that should not preclude the collection of information on the subject.
41. The Committee notes that the Government has come up with some important
initiatives in the area of revival/restructure/closure of CPSEs.  As the Committee gathers,
the earlier mechanism involved the administrative Ministry/Department, the BRPSE, the

15
BIFR and finally the approving authority, the Cabinet. This multiplicity of agencies involved
delay in granting approval to revival plans and most of the revival proposals when finally
approved would have already become redundant due to escalation of costs owing to the time
over run.  This vexed situation contributed to the further downfall of the sick/loss incurring
and weak CPSEs.
42. Now, as per the new system the respective administrative Ministry/Department will
oversee the performance of its CPSEs based on the guidelines for “Streamlining the
mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/incipient sick and weak Central Public
Sector Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of restructuring” issued by DPE.
Further, the Government has done away with the BRPSE and BIFR and AAIFR and they
would stand abolished once the NCLT is constituted.  The NCLT, provided for in the
Companies Act, 2013, will henceforth be the sole entity to decide upon the revival/
restructure proposals of CPSEs. Also, the revival/restructure process has been rendered
time bound.  In this regard, the Committee observes that the step taken to put the
administrative Ministry/Department in-charge of the monitoring of the health of their
respective CPSEs is an appropriate decision as mid-course correction and other reformative
measures can be taken swiftly without any time lapse as no third party is getting involved.
The Committee expects that all the lacunae which plagued the earlier system will be
eliminated in the new mechanism.
43. Further, it is observed that now with the enhanced mandate, DPE can also have a
proactive role to play in the process. The NCLT has been envisaged for all type of companies
in India, not just CPSEs. In this scenario, the Committee recommends that DPE has to take
this into account and take appropriate measures in coordination with the MoCA to ensure
that the CPSEs, due to their particular requirements of meeting socio-economic obligations,
are not put at a disadvantaged position in their efforts to get revived/restructured as they
would be treated as per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
New policy on management of Government investments in PSEs, including disinvestment
and strategic sale.
44. In his Budget speech, the Finance Minister announced that a new policy would be put in
place for management of Government investments in PSEs, including disinvestment and strategic
sale. In this regard, the Committee queried whether any road map has been put in place for the
same, the suggestions of DPE on framing the new policy and as to which nodal Ministry would
be responsible for formulating and implementing the policy.
45.  In reply, DPE submitted that the issue of disinvestment and strategic sale would be handled
by Department of Disinvestment. DPE also stated that the Government, on a proposal of
Department of Disinvestment, has decided for a multi-tier structure of decision making and
implementation of the decisions on strategic disinvestment/sale of CPSEs. As per the approved
structure, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) is at the apex level, then a Core
Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD), which would function as a supervisory and
recommendatory body, and there would be an Evaluation Committee (EC) for valuation and
suggesting a reserve price, opening financial bids and giving recommendations on price.

16
46. Further, DPE submitted that the Government has approved the following procedure and
mechanism for strategic disinvestment to be carried out by Department of Disinvestment, now
renamed as Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM):
(i) The NITI Aayog would identify CPSEs for strategic disinvestment. NITI Aayog
would also advice the Government on mode of sale, and the percentage of shares
to be sold of the CPSEs and suggest methods for valuation of the CPSE.
(ii) Constitution of CGD and its functions: (a) consider the recommendations of the
NITI Aayog on strategic disinvestment and recommend to CCEA on mode and
quantum of disinvestment; (b) lay down guidelines for evaluation by Evaluation
Committee; (c) recommend to CCEA on the terms and conditions of sale, the price
of sale and the strategic partner; and (d) supervise and monitor the process of
implementation of CCEA decision on strategic disinvestment.
(iii) Constitution of Evaluation Committee (EC) for strategic disinvestment and its
functions: the recommendations of the Administrative Department/Ministry on
valuation will be considered by the EC, which will fix the reserve price, open and
evaluate financial bids and make its recommendations to CGD.
(iv) Appointment of Independent External Monitor (IEM) to vet the process and settle
grievances; and
(v) Authorizing Ministry of Finance to put in place an appropriate mechanism for
protection of strategic disinvestment.
Secretary, DPE is a member of the CGD while Joint Secretary, DPE is a member of
Evaluation Committee that would consider the recommendations of the administrative Ministries/
Departments on valuation of the Company for strategic disinvestment/sale. Also, the Institute of
Chartered Accountants of India has issued Accounting Standard (AS) 10 on “Accounting for Fixed
Assets”. This included accounting for land, including its re-valuation.
47. On 13
th January, 2016, the Department of Economic Affairs constituted a Committee under
the Chairmanship of Department of Economic Affairs for suggesting broad guidelines on the issues
relating to Procedure for Exchange, Transfer, Leasing and Sale of Land held by the Government,
Government Controlled Statutory Authorities and CPSEs. DPE has representation in the Committee.
The recommendation of the Committee may be reviewed by the Cabinet Secretary before
finalization and submission of the report of the Committee.
48. Having representatives in the CGD, and the EC, the Committee asked DPE to clarify the
stand/decision/policy of the Government regarding disposal of land assets of CPSEs, but the
Department was non-committal in their reply to the Committee. With a view to have a deeper
understanding of the new policy of disinvestment, the Committee wanted to know the role of NITI
Aayog in disinvestment of CPSEs and why DPE was not given the assignment. For which
Secretary, DPE replied that the NITI Aayog would be the authority to identify CPSEs in which
disinvestment would need to be carried out and also wherever there was a need for strategic
alliances or strategic sale, and perhaps even those which need to be closed down.  After the
recommendations were made, the responsibility would not vest with the DPE, but with the

17
Department of Disinvestment. The Department of Disinvestment would take it forward. DPE was
to give them information and other backups wherever it was required. As far as the policy for
disinvestment was concerned, there was a Committee in the Ministry of Finance (MoF) which was
working on the policy of sale and how to utilize the excess land or the disposable land or the land
not in use with the CPSEs and autonomous bodies.  The approach was being worked out by the
Committee and as per the present approach the land would be first offered to the Government and
then to the CPSEs for the Government schemes and programmes. As per DPE, the controversial
part was the sale to private people. It was further submitted in this regard that such type of policy
was being deliberated at the moment as to how the Government would approach that issue. The
Committee was looking into it and DPE as a member in that would be giving feedback on the
subject.
49. The Committee notes that the Finance Minister has made couple of important policy
pronouncements – first, regarding disinvestment of Government share in CPSEs and second,
on the disposal of fixed assets of the CPSEs identified for winding up/closure.  The
Department has submitted that a mechanism has been structured to look into the
operationalisation of the said announcements. The multi-tier structure has CCEA at the
summit, NITI Aayog would identify the CPSEs and the critical parameters for
disinvestments/strategic sale. The CGD is to function as supervisory and recommendatory
body and an EC to valuate the assets of CPSEs concerned. The Committee has taken
specific note of the submission of DPE that this entire subject falls under the purview of
the Department of Disinvestment. However, the Committee observes that the subject will
have a profound bearing on the CPSEs in the country and DPE should evince keen interest
in the way things shape up on this front. This is even more important considering that the
very mandate of DPE has been enhanced on these lines and, it being member in all the
relevant Committees of disinvestment, the Department has to make more holistic
interventions on the issues/policies pertaining to CPSEs.
50. Further, the Committee has always taken a firm stand that the fixed assets,
particularly land, of wound up CPSEs should be retained with the Government or its
agencies. It is apprehended that the sale of such land to private players might have the
potential to generate many unethical practices. Accordingly, the Committee is of the strong
and unanimous opinion that the land belonging to wound up CPSEs shall be retained with
the Central Government or State Government or other Government agencies. Since
Secretary, DPE is the member of CGD it is firmly recommended that this view of the
Committee should be emphatically placed before the CGD while formulating any policy in
this area, for the present or in future. The Secretary has agreed to place the view point
of this Committee before CGD, when they deliberate on the approaches to be followed for
disposal or usage of land which is in the hands of sick PSEs or autonomous bodies.  The
Committee sincerely hopes that the view point would be considered in CGD.

RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE—A T A GLANCE
1. The Committee notes that the mandate of DPE has been augmented with the addition
of roles in monitoring of performance of CPSEs and effective management of their assets.
This has been done by addition of subjects to the Allocation of Business of DPE.  The
Committee is of the considered opinion that though the Budget allocation of DPE is small
compared to the major Ministries/Departments of the Government, the role to be essayed
by them is critical.  As the nodal Department of all CPSEs in India, their effective
evaluation and monitoring is going to be humongous task. The newly added responsibility
of CAPEX monitoring, measures to improve performance of CPSEs and other capacity
building initiatives and advice regarding revival/restructuring/closure of CPSEs will render
the working of DPE pivotal to the way CPSEs perform in the country. (Para 10)
2. Accordingly, the Committee observes that DPE should realize and imbibe the
magnitude and importance of the responsibilities that have been entrusted to them and take
more proactive measures to play out this role.  Rather them imagining themselves just as
a nodal coordinating agency DPE should reinvent themselves as an arm of the Government
which can take decisive steps on its own or in coordination with other Ministries/
Departments   to create a facilitative milieu for CPSEs to perform to their potential.  The
Committee is of the firm view that DPE should not be restricting themselves to just issuing
guidelines and providing advice.  The new mandate gives them ample space to effectively
follow up the implementation of the advices rendered by them through their guidelines.
Accordingly, the Committee recommends that to be able to do this, DPE has to equip
themselves better and come out with measures implementable on ground and also
endeavour to create a coordinative platform involving the respective administrative
Ministry and other relevant Government agencies through which matters relating to the
working of CPSEs in the country can be resolved at a single stage avoiding time lag in
administrative decisions, the single most degenerative factor in case of decisions related
to CPSEs. (Para 11)
3. The Committee notes that DPE claims that the CPSEs in India are performing to the
best of their abilities in the prevailing economic scenario of declining commodity prices,
reduced capital inflows into their economies and increasing financial volatility. Even while
taking the claim of DPE in its face value and acknowledging the fact that the Committee
is not in knowledge of the performance of all the CPSEs in India, the Committee cannot
but share its observation that the current status of all the 31 CPSEs under the Department
of Heavy Industry (DHI) is sick/incipient sick and weak as per DPEs guidelines for
“Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/incipient sick and weak
Central Public Sector Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of restructuring”.
Accordingly, the Committee observes that the stand taken by DPE that CPSEs are
performing well under the given conditions as status-quoits and wants the Department to
adopt a new forward looking stance. (Para 13)

charge of the monitoring of the health of their respective CPSEs is an appropriate
decision as mid-course correction and other reformative measures can be taken swiftly
without any time lapse as no third party is getting involved.  The Committee e xpects
that all the lacunae which plagued the earlier system will be eliminated in the new
mechanism. (Para 42)
13. Further, it is observed that now with the enhanced mandate, DPE can also have a
proactive role to play in the process. The NCLT has been envisaged for all type of companies
in India, not just CPSEs.  In this scenario, the Committee recommends that DPE has to
take this into account and take appropriate measures in coordination with the MoCA to
ensure that the CPSEs, due to their particular requirements of meeting socio-
economic obligations, are not put at a disadvantaged position in their efforts to get
revived/restructured as they would be treated as per the provisio ns of the Companies Act,
2013. (Para 43)
14.  The Committee notes that the Finance Minister has made couple of important policy
pronouncements – first, regarding disinvestment of Government share in CPSEs and second,
on the disposal of fixed assets of the CPSEs identified for winding up/closure.  The
Department has submitted that a mechanism has been structured to look into the
operationalisation of the said announcements. The multi-tier structure has CCEA at the
summit, NITI Aayog would identify the CPSEs and the critical parameters for
disinvestments/strategic sale. The CGD is to function as supervisory and recommendatory
body and an EC to valuate the assets of CPSEs concerned. The Committee has taken
specific note of the submission of DPE that this entire subject falls under the purview of
the Department of Disinvestment. However, the Committee observes that the subject will
have a profound bearing on the CPSEs in the country and DPE should evince keen interest
in the way things shape up on this front.  This is even more important considering that the
very mandate of DPE has been enhanced on these lines and it being member in all the
relevant Committees of disinvestment, the Department has to make more holistic
interventions on the issues/policies pertaining to CPSEs. (Para 49)
15. Further, the Committee has always taken a firm stand that the fixed assets,
particularly land, of wound up CPSEs should be retained with the Government or its
agencies. It is apprehended that the sale of such land to private players might have the

22
potential to generate many unethical practices.  Accordingly, the Committee is of the strong
and unanimous opinion that the land belonging to wound up CPSEs shall be retained with
the Central Government or State Government or other Government agencies. Since
Secretary, DPE is the member of CGD it is firmly recommended that this view of the
Committee should be emphatically placed before the CGD while formulating any policy in
this area, for the present or in future. The Secretary has agreed to place the view points
of this Committee before CGD, when they deliberate on the approaches to be followed for
disposal or usage of land which is in the hands of sick PSEs or autonomous bodies.  The
Committee sincerely hopes that the view point would be considered in CGD. (Para No 50)

Evolution and Mandate  
The Government of India established the Ministry of  Small Scale Industries 
and Agro & Rural Industries (SSI & ARI) in October,  1999 as the nodal Ministry for 
formulation of policies and Central sector programm es/schemes, their 
implementation and related coordination and for sup plementing the efforts of the 
States/Union Territories for promotion and developm ent of small scale, agro and 
rural industries in the country.  Subsequently, in September, 2001 the Ministry of SSI 
and ARI was bifurcated into two separate Ministries, namely, Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Ministry of Agro and Rural Industrie s.  In 2006, “Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises Development Act (MSMED), 2006” w as enacted by the 
Parliament.  Pursuant to this enactment, the Minist ry of Agro and Rural Industries 
and the Small Scale Industries were merged into a s ingle Ministry, namely, Ministry 
of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
Composition of the Ministry 
 
2. The Ministry of Micro Small & Medium Enterprises  is having two divisions 
called Small & Medium Enterprises (SME) Wing and Ag ro & Rural Industry (ARI) 
Wing.  The SME Wing is allocated the work, inter-al ia, of administration, vigilance 
and administrative supervision of the National Smal l Industries Corporation (NSIC) 
Ltd., a public sector enterprise and NIMESE an auto nomous national level 
entrepreneurship development/training organizations .  The Wing is also responsible 
for implementation of the schemes relating to Perfo rmance and Credit Rating, 
Assistance to Training Institutions and preparation  and monitoring of “Make in 
India” initiative among others.   
3. The ARI Wing looks after the administration of t wo statutory bodies viz. the 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coi r Board and a society called 

2 
 
Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Industrialisation  (MGIRI).  It also supervises the 
implementation of the Prime Minister’s Employment G eneration Programme 
(PMEGP).  Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) and 
A Scheme for Promoting Innovation, Rural Industry and Entrepreneurship (ASPIRE) 
4. The implementation of policies and various progr ammes/schemes for 
providing infrastructure and support services to MS MEs is undertaken through its 
attached office, namely the Office of the Developme nt Commissioner (O/o DC 
(MSME), National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC ), Khadi and Village 
Industries Commission (KVIC), the Coir Board and tr aining institutes viz., National 
Institute for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises ( NI-MSME), Hyderabad and 
Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation (MGIRI), Wardha.

7. The Committee feels that CLCSS and NMCP should b e separated. As per 
the current practice, the CLCSS which draws much la rger budget is clubbed 
with six components of NMCP that draw meager budget . CLCSS is essentially 
an interest subvention scheme like ISEC and should be kept as a credit support 
scheme whereas the NMCP is technology upgradation scheme.

MSME could not utilize even 67% of BE allocated to them. Some key Schemes 
like SFURTI and ASPIRE could not be implemented due  to late receipt of

and Programme that include skill and entrepreneursh ip development 
programmes have been below par and likely to increa se towards the end of

21. Scheme like India Inclusive Innovation Fund whi ch was launched towards 
beginning of current Five Year Plan with an  initia l corpus of Rs 500 crores to 
promote and finance grass root level innovations, w as allocated modest amount 
which remained unspent and now towards the end of F ive Year Plan, the Fund 
is being reconsidered. The Committee may be informe d of the reasons as to why 
this Scheme could not be operationalised through out the current Five Year Plan 
and under what conditions it is being reconsidered.  The Ministry may also 
inform the Committee of efforts made by it to operationalise the Scheme.   
 22. The Committee considers these Schemes a reflec tion of inadequate

24.  The Committee has observed the background not furnished by the 
Ministry that there was under-utilisation of Planne d Funds allocated under 
SCSP, TSP and NE Region. These funds are earmarked under the stated policy 
of Government of India for the marginalized section s of the society and remote 
areas of NE but could not be utilized due to lack o f proposals/demand not only 
indicates inefficiency on the part of Ministry but alsoshows  insensitivity. These 
Sections have traditional skills which need to be r efined, trained and 
commercialized, and the Ministry has utterly failed  to upscale their enormous   
skill pool. As an indicator in the success of MUDRA  Scheme, it is the Shishu 
loans meant largely for such marginalized sections,  are the biggest contributor. 
Yet the Ministry of MSME has not been able to reach  out to these sections. The 
Committee recommends that utilization of SCSP, TSP and NER should be 
monitored regularly at the highest levels in the Mi nistry and that the Financial 
Advisor must periodically report the Ministry of Fi nance in case of under-
utilisation of these Funds. The Ministry must launch special campaigns for these 
sections.

forward to. The financial limit for these schemes are :-

MUDRA’s delivery channel is conceived to be through  the route of refinance 
primarily to Banks/NBFCs/MFIs. Non–Corporate Small Business Segment (NCSB) 
comprising of millions of proprietorship / partners hip firms running as small 
manufacturing units, service sector units, shopkeep ers, fruits / vegetable vendors, 
truck operators, food-service units, repair shops, machine operators, small industries, 
artisans, food processors and others, in rural and urban areas are the target groups. 
54. The Committee has been monitoring the progress of this important scheme in 
different States and with different Banks. For year  2015-16 a target of Rs 1.22 lakh 
crores was set. Till the first week of February 201 6, loan amounting Rs 97000 crores 
to some 270 lakh borrowers was distributed of which  some 248 lakh were Shishu 
borrowers with Rs 50,000 and less.  
55. Though Committee recognized the progress made i n MUDRA Yojna, it 
found that lending Banks were not coming forward to  avail re-finance from 
MUDRA Bank.  Of the first tranche of Rs 5000 crores  to MUDRA, till the first 
week of February, 2016 only Rs 2184 crores were san ctioned for refinancing of 
which only Rs 1364 crores were disbursed. The Commi ttee found that 
refinancing of MFIs and NBFCs have been rather slug gish as compared to 
Scheduled Banks. The Committee is of the opinion th at MFIs have scarce funds 
and need cheap and prompt refinance and should be n atural partners in 
MUDRA Yojna instead of cash-rich Banks whose RIDF forms the corpus for the 
MUDRA Yojna. Also, the Committee would like to know  the reasons for 
sluggish refinancing under MUDRA Yojna. The Committ ee apprehends that 
perhaps Banks find the interest cap prescribed unde r re-financing conditions, 

24 
 
too restrictive. The Committee would like to know t he assessment of Ministry in 
this regard.  
56. The Committee also finds that while the MFIs ha ve the advantage of 
outreach and minimal paperwork, the actual interest  rate permissible to MFIs 
under MUDRA Yojna was around 19%, which is too high . Whereas the interest 
rate permissible for Scheduled Banks under Mudra Yo jna is at around 8-9% 
which was lower than the prevailing interest rate c harged by Banks. The 
Committee therefore recommends that interest rates for MFIs should be capped 
at a reasonable rate.

loans involving Margin Money worth 116% of BE but a ctual disbursal was only 
71% of BE. Ministry has stated having disbursed Rs 725 crores by February, 
2016, that was short of BE allocation by some Rs 30 0 crores. Also, the

207. The Committee was informed that in order to ex pand the scope of PMEGP, 
negative list of the PMEGP Guidelines has been modi fied. Under the Modified 
Guidelines, the following activities have now been allowed: 
 
• As per clause 4(ix) of the guidelines that provid es “Existing units (under 
PMRY, REGP or any other scheme of GOI or State Govt ) and the units that 
have already availed Government Subsidy under any o ther schemes of GOI or 
State Govt. are not eligible for PMEGP MM subsidy. It is however clarified 
here that such units are open to schemes available for other purposes like, 
guarantee benefits under CGTMSE scheme and other sc hemes of MSME for 
their growth and development as well as for making them more productive and 
competitive. 
 
• Industries such as processing of Pashmina wool an d other products like hand 
spinning and hand weaving have been removed from th e negative list, which 
means that khadi units are permitted under PMEGP. K VICs proposal for 
keeping handloom/powerloom out of the purview of PM EGP has not been 
agreed to and therefore, in addition to khadi units , handlooms and powerlooms 
units are eligible for funding under PMEGP. However, the subsidy/benefits for 

81 
 
setting up of such units can be claimed from one sc heme of Govt. of India 
only. 
 
• In order to encourage the setting-up of manufactu ring units under PMEGP, a 
ceiling of 10% on the extent of projects to be fina nced for transport activities 
may be imposed in the states/UTs except in specific  regions (hilly region, 
A&N Islands, Goa, Puducherry, Lakshadweep, Daman & Diu, Dadra Nagar 
Haveli, J&K and LWE affected districts). 
 
• Business/trading activities in the form of sales outlets may be permitted in 
North Eastern Region (NER), LWE-affected districts and A&N Islands. The 
LWE-affected districts, the extant classification on MHA may be adopted. The 
same was obtained from MHA’s ID dated 08.02.2012. 
 
• Retail outlets backed by manufacturing (including  processing)/service facilities 
may be permitted (Across the country) 
 
• The maximum cost of the project for business/trad ing activities may be Rs.10 
lakhs (at par with the maximum project cost for ser vice sector). Maximum 
10% of the Margin Money allocation in a year in a s tate may be used for 
business/trading activities as above.

constrained due to negative list prescribed in the PMEGP. The Committee is of

choice of vocation depending upon local resources, skill sets, market 
opportunities, instead of unduly constraining them. That a similar scheme is run

with the concerned State Government/ UT administration.

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with  the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises  (Department of Public Enterprises) 
on the recommendations contained in the Committee’s  Two Hundred and Seventy- 
Fourth Report on the Demands For Grants (2016-17) p ertaining to Department of Public 
Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Heavy Industries 
and Public Enterprises (Department of Public Enterp rises) in respect of the 
recommendations contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows: 
 
Chapter I -  The recommendations/observations, which have bee n accepted by the 
Ministry. 
 
 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Minis try has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report. 
 
Chapter -II -  The recommendations/observations which the Commi ttee does not desire 
to pursue in view of the Government's replies. 
 
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic 
and explanations advanced by the Ministry and there fore do not want to pursue them for 
the present. 
 
Chapter -III -  The recommendations/observations in respect of w hich the Committee has 
not accepted replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry to review its reply. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-i mplementation of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desi res that the Ministry should furnish 
logical explanations thereof. 
 
Chapter -IV - The recommendations/observations in respect of wh ich final replies of the 
Ministry have not been received. 
 
 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV , the Ministry has either 
furnished the interim replies or couched its langua ge in vague terms therefore; the 
Committee desires that the Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of 
recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention 
and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the ATR are being discussed in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 
(iii) 
 
 

 
 
 
CHAPTER – I 
 
The Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the Government has come up  with some important 
initiatives in the area of revival / restructure / closure of CPSEs. As the Committee 
gathers, the earlier mechanism involved the adminis trative Ministry / Department, the 
BRPSE, the BIFR and finally the approving authority , the Cabinet. This multiplicity of 
agencies involved delay in granting approval to rev ival plans and most of the revival 
proposals when finally approved would have already become redundant due to escalation 
of costs owing to the time over run. This vexed sit uation contributed to the further 
downfall of the sick / loss incurring and weak CPSEs involved.    
Para No 41 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Now, as per the new system the administrative Minis tries will oversee the 
performance of its CPSEs based on the guidelines fo r”streamlining the mechanism for 
revival and restructuring of sick / incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector 
Enterprises: General principles and mechanism of re structuring” issued by DPE. Further, 
the Government has done away with the BRPSE and BIF R and AAIFR and they would 
stand abolished once the NCLT is constituted. The NCLT, provided for in the Companies 
Act, 2013, will henceforth be the sole entity to de cide upon the revival / restructure 
proposals of CPSEs. Also, the revival / restructure process has been rendered time bound. 
In this regard, the Committee observes that the ste p taken to put the administrative 
Ministry in charge of the monitoring of the health of their respective CPSEs is an 
appropriate decision as mid-course correction and o ther reformative measures can be 
taken swiftly without any time lapse as no third pa rty is getting involved. The Committee 
expects that all the lacunae which plagued the earl ier system will be eliminated in the 
new mechanism.   
Para No 42 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 The recommendations of erstwhile BRPSE were adviso ry in nature and final 
decision regarding acceptance of such recommendatio ns rested with the administrative 
Ministries/Departments. In order to streamline the multiple mechanism for revival of sick 
CPSEs, the Government approved on 7.10.2015 for win ding up of Board for 
Reconstruction of Public Enterprises (BRPSE). Accor dingly, the BRPSE was wound up 
vide notification dated 9 
th  November, 2015.  
 
 DPE has issued guidelines issued for revival/restr ucturing of CPSEs. The 
administrative Ministries/ Departments are empowere d and made responsible to monitor 
the health of CPSEs functioning under their control  and take timely redressal measures 
for revival/ restructuring/disinvestment of sick/lo ss making CPSEs with the approval of 
the competent authority in a time bound manner .    
1 

 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the Finance Minister has made couple of important 
policy pronouncements – first, regarding disinvestm ent of Government share in CPSEs 
and second, on the disposal of fixed assets of the CPSEs identified for winding up / 
closure. The Department has submitted that a mechan ism has been structured to look into 
the operationalisation of the said announcements. The multitier structure has CCEA at the 
summit, NITI Aayog would identify the CPSEs and the  critical parameters for 
disinvestments / strategic sale. The CGD is to func tion as supervisory and 
recommendatory body and an EC to valuate the assets  of CPSEs concerned. The 
Committee has taken specific note of the submission  of DPE that this entire subject falls 
under the purview of the Department of Disinvestmen t. However, the Committee 
observes that the subject will have a profound bear ing on the CPSEs in the country and 
DPE should evince keen interest in the way things s hape up on this front. This is even 
more important considering that the very mandate of  DPE has been enhanced on these 
lines and, it being member in all the relevant Comm ittees of disinvestment, the 
Department has to make more holistic interventions on the issues / policies pertaining to 
CPSEs.   
Para No 49 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 DPE has noted the views of the Committee. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
 
 
 

CHAPTER–II 
The Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the Government's replies 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Committee note that while replying to the query  on Mid Term Review 
(MTR) of schemes during XII Five Year Plan, the Dep artment has restricted themselves 
by just submitting that no review has been undertak en.  The Committee observes that the 
Department while replying to the Committee should keep in mind that answers given to a 
Parliamentary Committee should be holistic and self -contained.   In the absence of a 
substantial reply, the Committee is precluded from comprehending the reason for not 
undertaking the MTR.  This information has to be provided to the Committee. 
 
Para No 15 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 
 The observations of the Committee are noted for co mpliance.  The Mid Term 
Review Schemes was earlier being done at the level of Planning Commission and it did 
not take place during XII 
th  Plan Period.  Hence, it was reported to the Commit tee that 
MTR for DPE schemes in XIIth Plan has not been undertaken. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
 

CHAPTER–III 
The Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry and has asked the Ministry to review its replies 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that DPE claims that the CPSEs in India are performing to 
the best of their abilities in the prevailing econo mic scenario of declining commodity 
prices, reduced capital inflows into their economie s and increasing financial volatility. 
Even while taking the claim of DPE in its face valu e and acknowledging the fact that the 
Committee is not in knowledge of the performance of  all the CPSEs in India, the 
Committee cannot but share its observation that the  current status of all the 31 CPSEs 
under the Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) is sic k / incipient sick and weak as per 
DPEs guidelines for  ”Streamlining the mechanism fo r revival and restructuring of sick / 
incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enter prises: General principles and 
mechanism of restructuring”. Accordingly, the Commi ttee observes that the stand taken 
by DPE that CPSEs are performing well under the giv en conditions as status-quoits and 
wants the Department to adopt a new forward looking stance. 
Para No. 13 
Action Taken Replies 
 The performance of CPSEs as per Public Enterprises Survey 2014-15 is given 
below: 
 Total turnover/gross revenue from operations of al l CPSEs during 2014-15 stood 
at Rs.19.96 lakh crore compared to Rs.20.66 lakh cr ore in 2013-14 showing a reduction 
in turnover of 3.40%. Overall net profit of all 235  CPSEs during 2014-15 stood at 
Rs.1.03 lakh crore compared to Rs.1.28 lakh crore i n 2013-14 showing a decrease in 
overall profit of 19.71 %. The net worth of all CPS Es went up from Rs.9.45 lakh crore in 
2013-14 to Rs.9.85 lakh crore in 2014-15 registerin g a growth of 4.12 %. Contribution of 
CPSEs to Central Exchequer decreased from Rs.2.20 l akh crore in 2013-14 to Rs.2.00 
lakh crore in 2014-15 showing a decline of 9.23 %.  
 
 DPE has issued guidelines for revival/restructurin g of CPSEs. As per the 
guidelines, the administrative Ministries/ Departme nts are responsible to monitor the 
health of CPSEs functioning under their control and  take timely redressal measures for 
revival/ restructuring/disinvestment of sick/loss m aking CPSEs with the approval of the 
competent authority. 
 
Further Recommendations  
 
 The Committee finds that the reply of DPE has not a ddressed the concerns 
flagged by the Committee in its recommendation. DPE  should base their opinion on 
the actual individual performance status of CPSEs o n their own guidelines rather 
than echoing the macro performance details of the P ublic Enterprises Survey 2014-
15. Even from the performance figures provided by D PE from the Public 
Enterprises Survey, the Committee does not find jus tification for the sweeping 
opinion of DPE that all CPSEs in the country are pe rforming to the best of their 
abilities under the given circumstances.  
 
4 

 Accordingly, the Committee reiterates its recommen dation that the stand of 
DPE regarding the performance of CPSEs is status-qu oits and expects a more 
coherent response from DPE in this regard. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5 

CHAPTER – IV 
Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry 
have not been  received 
 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 The Committee notes that the mandate of DPE has be en augmented with the 
addition of roles in monitoring of performance of C PSEs and effective management of 
their assets.  This has been done by addition of su bjects to the Allocation of Business of 
DPE.  The Committee is of the considered opinion th at though the Budget allocation of 
DPE is small compared to the major Ministries/ Depa rtments of the Government, the role 
to be essayed by them is critical.  As the nodal De partment of all CPSEs in India, their 
effective evaluation and monitoring is going to be humongous task.  The newly added 
responsibility of CAPEX monitoring, measures to imp rove performance of CPSEs and 
other capacity building initiatives and advice rega rding revival/ restructuring/ closure of 
CPSEs will render the working of DPE pivotal to the way CPSEs perform in the country. 
Para No. 10 
Action Taken Replies 
 Department of Public Enterprises is compiling the C APEX of select CPSEs on 
monthly basis and submitting it in the prescribed format. 
 
 Department of Public Enterprises has issued MoU Gu idelines 2016-17 under 
which (i) “CAPEX” MoU parameter has been prescribed  as one of the mandatory targets 
for CPSEs with weightage of 15-20.  It has been fur ther explained that CAPEX may be 
decided on the basis of viable projects available f or expansion, modernisation or 
diversification, cash and bank balance or parked fu nds, net worth, borrowings etc., and, 
(ii) “CAPEX” under the title “Leveraging Net Worth”  has been prescribed as one of 
mandatory targets for CPSEs with weightage of 5-15. 
 
Further Recommendations/ observations 
 
 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that DPE has started compiling the 
CAPEX data of CPSEs. The Committee waits to be info rmed of the methodology 
adopted for the analysis of the above said data and  how DPE proposes to utilize the 
information so obtained with respect to the extant guidelines of the Department in 
this regard. 
 
 
Recommendation/ observation 
 Accordingly, the Committee observes that DPE shoul d realize and imbibe the 
magnitude and importance of the responsibilities th at have been entrusted to them and 
take more proactive measures to play out this role.  Rather them imagining themselves

Action Taken Replies 
                                        Capital Sector 
 
 As far as Capital Goods sector is concerned, the d epartment has undertaken 
extensive consultation with the industry chambers namely, CII and FICCI and core sector 
industry associations of capital goods industry in the last one year.  The National Capital 
Goods Policy has been drawn up on the basis of view s, suggestions, recommendations 
and   regular interaction with the industry, indust ry associations and chambers.  The draft 
recommendations were   also examined in consultatio n with all stakeholders Ministries 
and Departments. Capital Goods Policy was submitted  for approval of the Cabinet.   
National Capital Goods Policy has been approved by the Cabinet in its meeting held on 
25.05.2016.  The Policy envisages increasing produc tion of capital goods from ~Rs. 
230,000 Cr in 2014-15 to Rs. 750,000 Cr in 2025 and  raising direct and indirect 
employment from the current 8.4 million to ~30 mill ion. It envisages increasing exports 
from the current 27% to 40% of production while inc reasing share of domestic 
production in India's demand from 60% to 80%, thus making India a net exporter of 
capital goods. The Policy also aims to facilitate i mprovement in technology depth across 
sub-sectors, increase skill availability, ensure ma ndatory standards and promote growth 
and capacity building of MSMEs. 
 
 The Department is already taking steps to formulat e schemes for obtaining 
approval as per the roadmap of the policy intervent ions in a time bound manner. The 
schemes being framed are based on the PPP model and  are directed towards the 
development and growth of the Capital Goods sector for both private as well as public
